issues.body:
Core tries to keep at least one outbound full-relay peer on every network it can reach (IPv4, IPv6, Tor, I2P, CJDNS). If a reachable network has none, it opens an extra full-relay connection to it every 5 minutes on average, and its eviction logic protects the only peer on a network. satd has the protection but not the extra connection.

## What Core does (v31.1)

- In `CConnman::ThreadOpenConnections` (`src/net.cpp`, the branch after the feeler), `CConnman::MaybePickPreferredNetwork` (`:2526`) picks a reachable network with no manual or full-relay outbound, where addrman has addresses. The node then draws an extra full-relay outbound from that network only (`Select(false, {*preferred_net})`).
- `EXTRA_NETWORK_PEER_INTERVAL{5min}` (`src/net.cpp:91`) paces it.
- It runs only when the full-relay count is at its target and the operator has not lowered the target with `-maxconnections`.
- Outbound eviction protects a peer that is the only one on its network (`MultipleManualOrFullOutboundConns`, `:2520`), so another peer is evicted instead.

## satd

satd's surplus eviction already keeps "the only manual or full-relay connection on its network". Nothing ever opens the connection that rule would protect, so a node with `-onlynet` covering several networks can run with no peer on one of them.

- Add the timer, the network pick, and the network-filtered draw.
- This depends on the dial-pool change in #1148 (drawing from the whole book). Onion candidates come from a separate list until onion addresses move into the book (#1157).
- Tests:

  - the extra peer survives eviction as the only peer on its network;

issues.body:
satd never opens a feeler on its own. `ConnType::Feeler` exists, and the close-after-`version` path for it is in place (`node/src/net/manager.rs:14090` at 64516c1a), but the only way to open one is the hidden `addconnection` RPC. The comment on `automatic_dial_order` says so: "satd opens no feelers of its own".

## What Core does

- A feeler timer, exponentially distributed with a 2 minute mean (`FEELER_INTERVAL`, `src/net.h:61` at v31.1), checked only once the full-relay and block-relay-only targets are met (`src/net.cpp:2770`, the `else if` after the outbound and block-relay branches).
- The feeler tests the test-before-evict incumbent first (`SelectTriedCollision`, `src/net.cpp:2821`), otherwise a new-table entry (`Select(true)`, `:2826`).
- Netgroup is not a skip reason for a feeler. A feeler needs only the services that make the peer's address book useful (`MayHaveUsefulAddressDB`), and starts after a random delay of up to 1 s (`FEELER_SLEEP_WINDOW`, `src/net.cpp:88`).
- On success the address is marked good and moves to tried.

## Why it matters

Without feelers, new-table addresses are tested only by being dialled as real outbound connections, and the tried table grows only from those. Since #1127, the test-before-evict incumbent is tested by the next automatic dial instead of a feeler.

## Suggested fix

- Add the timer and the feeler selection above, reusing the existing close-after-`version` path. A completed feeler calls `mark_good`, and a failed one counts an attempt.
- Move the incumbent test from the automatic dial to the feeler.
- Tests:
  - no feeler while the outbound targets are unmet;
  - a feeler moves a new-table entry to tried;
  - the incumbent is tested by a feeler, not by a full-relay dial.
- Live run against real testnet4 peers before merging.

Closes #1157.

The address book was keyed by `SocketAddr`, so the onions the node learned from `addrv2` gossip, and its onion seeds, went to a separate in-memory list (`connect_peer_addrs`, at most 512). A restart forgot all of them, and they had none of the book's tried table, test-before-evict or draw odds. The book is now keyed by `PeerAddr` and holds Tor v3 onions, as Core's addrman holds every BIP 155 network.

## What changes

- **Grouping.** An onion's network group is Core's for Tor (`NetGroupManager::GetGroup`): the network and the first four bits of the key, which gives sixteen groups. `-asmap` groups IP addresses only.
- **Per-source share.** One source's network group holds at most `MAX_NEW_PER_GROUP` (64) onion entries in the new table, and a full share makes room by dropping a terrible one. Onions are free to make in every group, so without this one peer's `getaddr` answer could fill the onion part of the book. The old list kept the same share (#1120). Core bounds a source through its source-group buckets, which satd's flat new table does not have. `CORE_DIFFERENCES.md` notes this.
- **`peers.dat` v3.** An onion entry or source is stored as its 32-byte key (tag 2). Version 1 and 2 files still load. In a v2 file an onion tag is garbage, and reading stops there. An older satd refuses a v3 file and starts with an empty book; the release notes cover that downgrade.

issues.body:
The address book (`node/src/net/addrman.rs`) is keyed by `SocketAddr`, so it holds no onion addresses. Onion peers learned from `addrv2` gossip go on a separate in-memory dial list (`connect_peer_addrs` in `node/src/net/manager.rs` at 64516c1a), capped at `MAX_ONION_CONNECT_ADDRS`. As a result:

- they are not written to `peers.dat`, so a restart forgets every onion peer the node learned;
- they get none of the address book's protections: new/tried tables, per-group buckets, `is_terrible` eviction, test-before-evict;
- the dial-order and feeler work (#1148, #1149) and the per-network extra peer cannot draw them like other addresses.

Core's addrman holds every BIP 155 network in one book (`CAddress` / `CNetAddr`) and buckets Tor, I2P and CJDNS addresses like the rest. Their netgroups are per address, because their bits carry no routing meaning.

## Suggested fix

- Key the book by a network address that covers onion (and I2P/CJDNS if satd adds them), not `SocketAddr`.
- Bump the `peers.dat` format version. Loading a v2 file must still work.
- Retire `connect_peer_addrs`.
- Tests:
  - an onion address learned from gossip survives a restart;
  - it is drawn, tried and evicted like a clearnet one;
  - `-onlynet=onion` draws only onion entries.
- Lands after #1148.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #1187.

A `headers` message took `accept_lock` on the P2P task, through `ChainState::accept_headers` → `commit_accepted_headers`, and a block connect holds that lock for its whole length, script verification included. A batch that arrived during a long connect parked the task, the way a stored block did before #875 (#1185): no other peer's messages, no block requests, no ping replies until the connect let go. The proof-of-work checks on up to 2,000 headers also ran on the task.

The commit has to stay under `accept_lock`: rows above the tip are only safe while the tip can't move (`state.rs` `commit_accepted_headers`). So this moves the work off the task instead of narrowing the lock.

One thread takes jobs in arrival order, so header-sync state sees each batch's result in order, as it did inline. A push past the bound waits for room. That costs the task what an inline batch did, and only under a flood. An empty queue takes any message.
- **Ordering.** Core handles one connection's messages in order, and peers rely on it. So while the queue holds work, the block-relay messages behind it are queued too and handled on the headers thread in arrival order: an `inv` naming a block, `cmpctblock`, `blocktxn`, and `block` outside IBD. issues.body:
Follow-up to #875 (fixed by #1185).

#1185 moved IBD block storage off the P2P task, so a block that arrives during a connect no longer waits there on `accept_lock`. A `headers` message still does. `handle_message` → `handle_headers` (`node/src/net/manager.rs:7167`) → `ChainState::accept_headers` (`node/src/chain/state.rs:2960`) → `commit_accepted_headers`, which takes `accept_lock` (`node/src/chain/state.rs:2774`). The IBD connector holds that lock for a whole block connect, script verification included. A `headers` message that arrives during a long connect therefore parks the P2P task the same way #875 described: no other peer's messages, no block requests, no ping replies until the connect finishes.

This is rarer than the block case. Once header sync is done, headers arrive about once per new block. The cost on the task is also larger than the wait alone: proof-of-work checks on up to 2,000 headers plus one index batch write, all inline.

Correction to the earlier comment on #875: it says header acceptance does not take `accept_lock`. It does, through `commit_accepted_headers`.

Direction: move header acceptance off the P2P task as #1185 did for block storage, or keep the PoW checks on the task and hand only the locked commit to another thread. Either way the header-sync state machine has to see the result in order, so this belongs with that code rather than as a drop-in queue.

Closes #1148. A1 of the peer-discovery work: the automatic dial pool becomes the whole address book, as in Core's `ThreadOpenConnections`.

- **The whole book is the dial pool.** `automatic_dial_order` draws from addrman directly. The 256-entry startup preload (`load_addrman(path, 256)` → `select_n`) and the `learned_addrs` list are gone. Before, only those 256 entries plus whatever gossip added later were ever dial candidates; the rest of `peers.dat` (up to 16,384 entries) waited for a peer to gossip it again. `-connect` still turns automatic dials off: `may_dial` gates every candidate as before, and the pass now returns nothing under it without reading the book.

A drawn entry is taken with those odds, or the next draw from the same table runs at 1.2× the odds, as in Core's `Select_` (`src/addrman.cpp:713`). The existing structure stays as it was: a tried/new coin toss, a bucket drawn first within tried, and the test-before-evict incumbent first. issues.body:
#1118 and #1127 brought the automatic dial order close to Core: a tried/new coin toss per candidate, a bucket drawn first within tried, the 10 min / 30 tries rule, and test-before-evict. Three gaps remain between satd's dial pool and Core's `Select()`.

## 1. The dial pool is not the whole address book

`automatic_dial_order` (`node/src/net/manager.rs:5101` at 64516c1a) orders `learned_addrs`, not addrman. At startup `load_addrman` puts only `AddrMan::select_n(256)` on that list (`satd/src/main.rs:2767`, `manager.rs:2693`), and `select_n` returns a fixed order: most recently successful tried entries, then most recently seen new ones. Anything learned later is appended. The rest of `peers.dat`, up to 16,384 entries, is never a dial candidate until gossip names it again.

Core draws every automatic outbound from the whole book (`CConnman::ThreadOpenConnections`, `src/net.cpp:2542` at v31.1).

## 2. No attempt weighting

Core accepts a drawn entry with probability `AddrInfo::GetChance` (`src/addrman.cpp:94`): ×0.01 if it was tried in the last 10 minutes, and ×0.66 per failed attempt up to 8. satd's book already stores `attempts` and `last_try`, but the dial order does not use them. An address that has failed 8 times is drawn as often as a fresh one.

## 3. No pre-dial bad-port or service skip

- Core skips IPv4/IPv6 candidates on a bad port for the first 50 tries (`IsBadPort`, `src/net.cpp:2876`). satd has no bad-port check.
- Core skips a non-feeler candidate whose stored services lack the desirable flags (`HasAllDesirableServiceFlags`), before dialling it. satd checks desirable services only after the handshake (`manager.rs:14063`), so it spends the connection first.

## Suggested fix

- Take candidates from addrman directly. Drop the 256-entry preload and `learned_addrs`. `-connect` must still turn automatic dials off.
- Weight the draw by `GetChance`.
- Add the bad-port and stored-services skips in Core's order.
- Tests:
  - an address loaded from `peers.dat` outsi

agent_prs.body:
## Cause

jemalloc's `configure`, run by `tikv-jemalloc-sys`, probes the build host and bakes the result into `satd`. On x86_64 it runs `cpuid` for the virtual-address width: 48 bits on most CPUs, 57 on CPUs with 5-level paging. That value sizes jemalloc's radix tree, so a `satd` built on a 57-bit host differs from one built on a 48-bit host in `.text`, `.rodata`, `.eh_frame` and `.bss`. `sat-cli` doesn't link jemalloc, which is why it always matched.

GitHub's hosted x86_64 runners are a mix of both kinds of CPU, so the two-replica check failed whenever the two replicas landed on different kinds. This branch caught one such run: an AMD EPYC replica (48-bit) and an Intel Xeon replica (57-bit) of the same commit differed by 17.3M bytes, with `.bss` at 2,148,032 vs 313,024 bytes. Building jemalloc locally once with `LG_VADDR=48` and once with `=57` reproduces the same 1,835,008-byte `.bss` difference.

## Changes

- `flake.nix`: on x86_64, sets `JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_LG_VADDR=48`, `JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_LG_PAGE=12` and `JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_LG_HUGEPAGE=21`, which jemalloc otherwise reads from the build host. 48 is what nearly every host already detected. It is also safe on a 5-level-paging kernel, which maps above 47 bits only on request.
- `nix.yml`: each replica uploads its binaries and a short record of the build host's CPU. On a mismatch, the compare job reports a per-section hash diff and the count of differing bytes, so a future failure can be diagnosed from the run itself.
- Manual (packaging, "Determinism hazards addressed"), CHANGELOG and the 0.7.1 release notes.

## Testing

Eight `workflow_dispatch` runs of `nix.yml` on this branch:
- Before the fix: one mismatch (an AMD/Intel pair) and one match (AMD/AMD).
- After the fix: six matches, two of them AMD/Intel pairs.

Every replica built its dependencies from scratch, and every fixed build produced the same `satd` hash that the 48-bit hosts produced before the fix.

Fixes #321

The Nix reproducibility check (`nix.yml` → `nix repro / compare`, which asserts two independent runners produce byte-identical binaries of the same commit) **intermittently fails for the `satd` binary**. `sat-cli` was reproducible in the same runs — only `satd` diverged.

This is a real (if intermittent) break of the reproducible-build guarantee documented in the Operator Manual's packaging chapter (§"Determinism hazards addressed"). It is **not** a build *failure* — both replicas build successfully; their outputs just differ.

## Evidence

First observed on PR #320 (a docs-only PR that incidentally triggered `nix.yml` by touching `contrib/repro/`):

agent_prs.body:
The node puts a resume cursor only on a connected block and on a confirmed match. A resilient watch or subscription with no `FromCursor` / `from_cursor` and an empty cursor store therefore had nothing to resume from until one arrived. A reconnect in that window sent no `SetCursor`, got no `CursorAccepted` and didn't replay the outage, and any event in flight at the drop was lost. With instrumentation, the old `TestE2EWatchSetLoaderRebuildsFromTruthOnReconnect` predicate, which cut on the unconfirmed match, failed 6 of 6 runs this way: no resume cursor at the reconnect, and the block's confirmed events never delivered.

**Node.** `Subscribe` and `Watch` responses now carry a `satd-head-cursor` header in the form `<height>:<tx_index>:<mempool_seq>:<instance_id>`. That is the cursor a `BlockConnected` at the tip would carry, with the publisher's envelope sequence as the mempool watermark. It is read after the stream subscribes to the live bus. So every event above it is either delivered on the stream or replayed by a `SetCursor` / `from_cursor` from it. A block that races the read is at worst delivered and also replayed, and the SDKs' monotonic high-water mark absorbs the duplicate. The header is omitted when there is no block source. It is documented in `docs/api/streaming.md`.

**SDKs.** The Go and Rust `ResilientWatch` and `ResilientSubscription` take the head cursor as their resume anchor when they have none. They don't send it on the stream it came from, so the next reconnect re-anchors there. Commit-on-poll persists it, so a restart resumes there too. `Stream.HeadCursor()` (Go) and `EventStream::head_cursor()` (Rust) expose it. An older node, or a client that ignores the header, behaves as before. The resilient types run over gRPC only, so the WS/SSE carrier is unchanged; the spec describes the additive equivalent.

**Tests.**
- Server: the header is present and correct on both RPCs, and absent without a block source.
- Go and Rust unit tests: a drop before any c

issues.body:
`TestE2EWatchSetLoaderRebuildsFromTruthOnReconnect` fails intermittently, in CI and locally, with:

```
--- FAIL: TestE2EWatchSetLoaderRebuildsFromTruthOnReconnect (180.58s)
    resilientwatch_test.go:249: resilient watch Next (saw map[Heartbeat:180]): context deadline exceeded
```

### Reproduction

Back-to-back runs of the same binary at the same commit:

```sh
cd clients/go/e2e
SATD_BIN=../../../target/debug/satd SATD_E2E_TIMEOUT_MULT=3 \
  go test -tags e2e -count=1 -run TestE2EWatchSetLoaderRebuildsFromTruthOnReconnect .
```

run 1: `ok … 16.0s` — run 2: `FAIL … 180.8s`, same signature. Roughly one run in two.

### What is and isn't happening

The node is healthy throughout — queried while the test was stuck, it answered `getblockchaininfo` (height 141) and `getserverstatus` normally, with the events listener bound. The client is connected too: it receives **180 heartbeats**, one a second, for the whole wait. So the stream reconnects fine after `proxy.cutAll()`.

What never arrives is the `CursorAccepted` the test waits for. On reconnect, `ResilientWatch` only sends a `SetCursor` when it has a resume cursor:

```go
if resume != nil {
    if err := h.SetCursor(ctx, *resume); err != nil { return nil, err }
}
…
w.reanchorPending = resume != nil
```

With no anchor sent there is no ack to wait for, and a caller watching for `CursorAccepted` waits forever. Worth checking whether `resume` is nil at reconnect in the failing runs, and if so why the pre-cut `ScriptMatched` events did not advance it — the test's pre-cut loop calls `Next` with a 5-second context it cancels and re-creates repeatedly, which is the cancel-safety path #455 dealt with.

### Why it matters beyond the test

Reconnect-and-replay is the SDK's contract. If a watch can come back from a reconnect without re-anchoring, an integrator relying on the replay window can silently miss the events that arrived while the stream was down — the gap the anchor exists to close.

### Not introduced by current work
issues.title: Go SDK: a resilient watch sometimes never re-anchors after a reconnect (TestE2EWatchSetLoaderRebuildsFromTruthOnReconnect)

The AssumeUTXO background catch-up connector stopped for the life of the process on its first failed connect, and its three conditions reached `getwarnings` only.

**Retry.** A failed connect is now retried the way the IBD connector retries one, and the two share their constants and retry notice:
- one attempt a second;
- an `assumeutxo.connect_retry` warning on every tenth attempt;
- after 30 attempts, the `assumeutxo_catchup_stalled` alert, while retrying goes on.

Both clear when the block connects. A block that fails validation (`ChainError::is_verdict_on_block`) is not retried. The connector stops and raises the alert with `reason=invalid_block`, and the snapshot stays unvalidated rather than rejected. A handoff I/O failure right after the snapshot-height block connects now goes to the handoff-retry path; before, it ended the loop.

The old ids were undocumented; the upgrade note lists the rename. Each episode has one raise and one clear. A raise before the sink is installed goes to `getwarnings` at once and to the other surfaces when the sink is installed. The Rust and Go SDKs name the new kinds.

issues.body:
Two related gaps found reviewing #554, which fixed the silent-halt half of #545.

## 1. Only one of the three alerting surfaces

The Operator Manual states that a detected condition is reported "at once" on three surfaces — a `status` event on the streaming API, a `getwarnings` entry (which fires `-alertnotify`), and a `satd_alert_active{kind="..."}` gauge — "so they cannot disagree".

The AssumeUTXO warnings added in #554 (`assumeutxo.catchup_halted`, `assumeutxo.handoff_failing`) and the pre-existing `assumeutxo-validation-failed` reach only `getwarnings`. Consequences:

- the alertfile webhook dispatcher fans in over the NodeEvent bus, so it never sees them;
- no `status` event, so a streaming consumer cannot observe them;
- there is **no Prometheus metric at all** for AssumeUTXO background state — `grep 'assumeutxo\|background' node/src/metrics.rs` returns nothing.

An operator running webhooks plus Prometheus and no `-alertnotify`/TUI gets nothing. That is the same alerting hole #535 was about, for a different subsystem.

Worth at least a gauge: background tip height, snapshot height, and attached/rejected state.

## 2. A connect failure kills background validation with zero retries

`bg_catchup_connect_loop`'s `Err` arm returns immediately. The IBD connector, which #554's comment cites as the counterpart, does the opposite: 30 attempts with 1s waits, `connect.retry` every 10th, `connect.persistent_failure` only after giving up, and clears the warning on progress.

So a single transient RocksDB or flat-file write error at height 400001 kills AssumeUTXO validation for the process, where a retry 200ms later would have succeeded. The operator's only remedy is a restart.

#554 added retries for the *handoff* path (`assumeutxo.handoff_failing`) but deliberately left the connect path alone as a larger change. Giving it the same treatment as the IBD connector would close it.

## 3. Undocumented warning ids

`assumeutxo.catchup_halted` and `assumeutxo.handoff_failing`
issues.title: AssumeUTXO background validation has no metric and no status event, and a connect failure never retries

## #506: header rules on a full reindex

A full `-reindex` checked each block's proof of work but none of the header rules `accept_header` applies. `connect_block` checks neither the difficulty nor the checkpoints, and a reorg that later activates a side branch the reindex indexed also goes through `connect_block`. So a block whose `nBits` broke the retarget schedule, or that contradicted a checkpoint, could be connected. That happened at once if its branch claimed the most work, or later through a reorg.

The replay planner now holds every block to the header rules before it descends into it (`check_reindex_header`):

- `check_difficulty`, including testnet4's timewarp rule and the signet schedule from #838

- `time-too-old` against the median time past of the block's own branch, and `bad-version`
- the checkpoint hashes

Deep review of #491 (adversarial test lens) found these. The end-to-end coverage that exists is real — I verified the silent-corruption case asserts on UTXO set contents, not just the tip — but:

1. **`reindex_from_flat_files_tolerates_duplicate_records` passes against the old traversal.** Master's connect loop already ate duplicates (`header_by_hash.remove` then `continue`), so it is not a regression test. It also passes with the new dedup guard deleted. What the guard actually prevents — exponential subtree re-walk, and the production 'three duplicate genesis records' case — is untested (the fixture duplicates blocks 2 and 3, not genesis). The PR body's claim that all four e2e cases fail against the old code was wrong for this one.
2. **`reindex_from_flat_files_does_not_index_side_blocks_above_the_tip` is vacuous.** The losing branch ends below the winning tip, so no side block above the tip exists; deleting the `height <= tip_height` filter would not fail it.
3. **No e2e work-beats-depth coverage.** The unit fixture uses headers with `nonce: 0` that fail `check_proof_of_work`, i.e. a state the production path now discards at scan time. A flat-file fixture with a harder-bits shorter branch would close this and (2) together.
4. **The flat-file fail-open is untested** — a record failing the PoW check is skipped, severing `children` and truncating the plan; the only guard is `plan.path.is_empty()`.
5. **`prefetch::compute_mtp(plan)` is uncovered** — every fixture uses `LockTime::ZERO` with increasing timestamps, so an MTP computed over the wrong branch is unobservable.
6. `plan_reindex_chain_equal_work_keeps_first_seen` cannot distinguish first-seen from lowest-hash (both orderings agree in the fixture).
7. Side-chain `chainwork` is never asserted, and nothing tests that an indexed side branch extended past the tip is actually selected.

issues.body:
`index_reindex_side_chain` validates PoW and nothing else. The justification was that the reorg path validates before connecting — it does not: `reorg_to` connects via `connect::connect_block`, which runs neither `check_proof_of_work` nor `check_difficulty`. Every difficulty-schedule, timestamp and checkpoint rule lives in `accept_header`/`accept_block`, which the reindex bypasses.

So a side entry whose header has wrong `bits` for its retarget window, a garbage timestamp, or a checkpoint violation can be indexed and, if later extended, connected — where the live path would reject it.

Bounded by the PoW check (work cannot be forged, so such a branch cannot *win* selection), so this needs corrupt or hostile flat files. Symmetric with the main-chain reindex path, which has never run `check_difficulty` either — not a regression, but newly relevant now that side branches are retained. The wrong doc claim was corrected in #491 (cedcc432); the gap itself remains.

Found by deep review of #491.
issues.title: reindex: side-chain entries are indexed on a PoW check alone, and the reorg that connects them re-checks nothing

agent_prs.body:
Two 0.7.1 tooling fixes.

**sign-tarballs.sh keeps its working directory across a failed run (#903).** The script downloaded every tarball and SBOM into a mktemp directory and deleted it on exit, failed runs included. A mistyped passphrase or a failed upload meant downloading the whole set again: 431 MB for 0.6.0. The `already_signed` skip could never fire.

- Works in `${SATD_SIGN_DIR:-${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/satd-sign/<tag>}`, mode 0700. It refuses a symlink, a directory owned by another user, one that group or others can write to, and a tag that is not a plain path component.
- `SHA256SUMS` and the `.sha256` files are fetched fresh on every run. A cached tarball or SBOM is kept only if its SHA-256 matches both `SHA256SUMS` and the asset `digest` from the releases API. Anything else is downloaded again.
- An existing `.minisig` is kept only if `minisign -Vm` verifies it against the published key.
- The directory is removed after a successful upload or a `--dry-run`, and kept on failure. The path is printed either way.
- The files to sign and upload come from the release's asset list, not a glob.
- `--images` is unchanged.

A new offline test, `contrib/release/tests/sign-tarballs-test.sh`, puts stub `gh` and `minisign` on PATH. It covers:
- a rerun after a failure downloads no artifact;
- a tampered local file or a replaced asset is downloaded and signed again;

## Problem

`contrib/release/sign-tarballs.sh <tag>` downloads every tarball and SBOM into a fresh `mktemp -d` directory and deletes it on exit (`sign-tarballs.sh:67-68`). The directory goes even when the run fails, for example on a wrong passphrase or a failed upload. Each retry downloads everything again.

The comment above the download (`sign-tarballs.sh:203-208`) says re-downloading is on purpose and cheap: "Tarballs are small; the re-download cost is trivial." That no longer holds. With the debuginfo tarballs, v0.6.0's signed set is 12 files and 431 MB, so a retry after a mistyped passphrase means another 431 MB download before the prompt comes back.

The skip logic for already-signed files (`already_signed`, `sign-tarballs.sh:236-243`) never fires, because a fresh directory never contains a `.minisig`.

## Proposal

Download into a deterministic per-tag directory, keep it across failed runs, and skip any file already there whose hash matches.

- **Directory:** `${SATD_SIGN_DIR:-${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/satd-sign/<tag>}`, created with mode 0700. If it has to live under `/tmp`, the script should refuse a directory it doesn't own or that other users can write to, because a predictable `/tmp` path is easy for another local user to pre-create.
- **Reuse:** every run fetches the small files fresh (`SHA256SUMS` and the `*.sha256` files). A tarball or SBOM already in the directory is kept only if its SHA-256 matches both the fresh `SHA256SUMS` entry and the asset's `digest` from the releases API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/tags/{tag}`, field `assets[].digest`). Anything missing or mismatched is downloaded again. This keeps the property the current comment protects: a file changed on the release after an earlier run is never silently kept.
- **Signatures:** an existing `<file>.minisig` counts as done only if `minisign -Vm` verifies it against the current bytes and the published pubkey. Otherwise it is deleted and the file is signed again. A run that fai

issues.body:
## Context

The `scripts/canary/bdk-canary` harness pins `rustls-webpki 0.101.7`, flagged by Dependabot:
- GHSA-82j2-j2ch-gfr8 (high) — DoS via panic on malformed CRL BIT STRING
- GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh (low) — name constraints accepted for wildcard certs
- GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5 (low) — name constraints for URI names incorrectly accepted

These alerts were **dismissed as tolerable risk** (2026-06-10): the canary is a non-shipped test harness that connects only to a **localhost satd-under-test**, so there is no untrusted TLS peer to supply malformed CRLs/certs — the vulnerable code paths aren't reachable in this context.

## Why it can't be fixed by a simple bump

`rustls-webpki 0.101.7` is pulled by `minreq 2.14.1`, which hard-requires `rustls ^0.21.1` + `rustls-webpki ^0.101.0`. Both consumers cap minreq at the 2.x line:
- `esplora-client 0.12.3` (via `bdk_esplora 0.22`) -> `minreq ^2.11`
- `jsonrpc 0.18.0` (via `bitcoincore-rpc 0.19`) -> `minreq ^2.7`

The next minreq is `3.0.0-rc.1`. Clearing the advisories requires upgrading the BDK 2.x / bitcoincore-rpc 0.19 train (or switching esplora-client to its async/reqwest backend and replacing bitcoincore-rpc's minreq transport).

## Action

Revisit when the BDK / bitcoincore-rpc pins are next advanced; verify `rustls-webpki` resolves to >= 0.103.13 and re-enable the Dependabot alerts.

`ChainState::is_initial_block_download` was only `tip_time < now - maxtipage`. Core's (`ChainstateManager::UpdateIBDStatus`, `CChain::IsTipRecent`) differs in two ways:

issues.body:
`ChainState::is_initial_block_download` (`node/src/chain/state.rs` ~2104) is only `tip_time < now - maxtipage`. Bitcoin Core's `ChainstateManager::UpdateIBDStatus` / `IsInitialBlockDownload` (`src/validation.cpp`) differs in two ways:

1. **Minimum chain work.** Core stays in IBD while the active tip's chainwork is below `-minimumchainwork`, even if the tip is recent. A node fed a short, recent-looking chain with little work leaves IBD in satd but not in Core.
2. **Latch.** Once Core leaves IBD it never re-enters it for the life of the process (`m_cached_finished_ibd`). satd re-evaluates every call, so a node whose tip goes stale (no block for 24 h on signet/testnet, a long mining gap, a stalled peer set) flips back to IBD. Everything gated on IBD then changes behaviour mid-run: `getblocktemplate` -10, fee estimation, tx relay, address-relay and `getblockchaininfo.initialblockdownload`.

## Proposed fix

- Add the minimum-chain-work condition and a process-lifetime latch, as Core does.
- Check each caller that relies on the current re-entering behaviour (stratum's IBD gate, the IBD connector, readiness) and keep anything that really wants "tip is old" on the tip-time predicate under its own name.
- Tests: low-work recent tip stays in IBD; after leaving IBD, mocktime advanced past `maxtipage` keeps `initialblockdownload` false.

agent_prs.body:
Signet `nBits` is checked against the retarget schedule, as Bitcoin Core does (#838).

**The bug.** `check_difficulty` returned `Ok` on signet before looking at `nBits`. That left only the block signature and the hash-meets-its-own-target check. Core runs the normal retarget check on signet, with its own powLimit and no min-difficulty exception, and refuses a mismatch with `bad-diffbits`. `next_bits` already computed signet's value correctly for block templates, so the check now uses it: the early return is gone.

**Test:** `test_signet_any_bits_accepted` pinned the old behaviour. It is replaced by `signet_bits_follow_the_retarget_schedule`.
- **Retarget:** the real boundary at signet height 290304. The period runs from 288288 (time 1769157340) to 290303 (time 1770338984), and the bits go `1d157c9b` → `1d14fd7a`. The real bits pass. The parent's bits, an arbitrary value and the powLimit are refused with `BadDifficulty`.
- **Mid-period:** a block must carry its parent's bits.
- **Perturbation:** with the early return put back, the test fails.

**Live check:** a fresh signet node on this branch synced headers from genesis to the network tip, 329,044, the height a synced signet node reported at the same time. No header was refused, so the default signet's whole chain passes the check.

**Custom signets.** One whose blocks don't follow the standard schedule, such as one run by a modified bitcoind with a shorter block interval, stops syncing. Core refuses it too. The 0.7.1 upgrade notes say so.

Fixes #838

On signet, `check_difficulty` (`node/src/validation/pow.rs`) returns `Ok` for any `nBits`, and `check_proof_of_work` trusts the header's own bits. `test_signet_any_bits_accepted` pins the behaviour. Two test races. Both tests passed on rerun every time they failed.

- **#794: `webhooks::a_hook_that_was_down_resumes_at_the_live_head`.**
  - **The race:** the test counted missed-span attempts before the reload and compared after it, so a retry already in flight at the reload failed it.
  - **The fix:** `Received` now records its arrival time, which is the sharper option the issue suggests. The test fails only for a missed-span attempt that arrives more than 2 s after the reload, watched over a 12 s window. A generation that carried its queue would retry within that window: the backoff is 1, 2, 4, 8 s (`satd-alert/src/retry.rs`), so the next retry is due a few seconds after the reload. The old check gave a 3 s window.
- **`test_esplora_address_txs_mempool_visibility`** (no issue; it failed once in CI on 2026-11-01 with `/txs/mempool must contain the unconfirmed spend; got []`).
  - **The race:** the address index adds a mempool transaction when it receives the mempool's `Enter` event (`node/src/index/address/mempool.rs`, `mempool_index_task`), which can come after `sendrawtransaction` returns. The test read `/txs/mempool` straight away.
  - **The fix:** it polls with `poll_until_json` until the entry appears.

Both pass locally.

Sparrow batches against satd's Electrum server (#1069).

**Why Sparrow didn't batch.** Sparrow decides from the `server.version` name whether to batch, in `ElectrumServer.getServerCapability`. A lowercased name containing `electrumx` gets batching, `blockchain.scripthash.unsubscribe` and `server.features`. A few other servers are matched by prefix and version. satd's default, `satd-electrs-compatible/<ver>`, matched none, so Sparrow sent one request per script hash.

**New default name:** `satd-electrs-electrumx-compatible/<ver>`. Checked against each client's current source:

issues.body:
satd's Electrum server answers JSON-RPC batches correctly (`electrum-proto/src/dispatch.rs:68-81`, `server.rs:559-580`, capped by `-electrummaxbatchrequests`). Sparrow, however, decides whether to batch from the `server.version` name (`ElectrumServer.getServerCapability`): it batches only for names containing `electrumx`, `electrs/` >= 0.9.0, `fulcrum` >= 1.6.0, `frigate`, `cormorant`, or `mempool-electrs` >= 3.1.0. satd's default name, `satd-electrs-compatible/<ver>`, matches none of those, so Sparrow falls back to one request per scripthash. Nothing breaks, but wallet scans and refreshes are much slower than they need to be.

The manual also claims Sparrow batches its whole gap-limit window (`docs/manual/src/electrum.md:45`, `config-reference.md:334`). Under the default name that is not true.

## Constraint

`electrum.md:274-279` documents why the name must not *start* with `electrs`: BlueWallet disables batching on that prefix. And Cake Wallet only probes silent-payment tweaks when the name contains `electrs`. A new default has to satisfy all three wallets at once (for example a name that contains `electrumx` and `electrs` but starts with neither), which needs checking against each wallet's current matching code.

## Proposed fix

- Pick a default `electrumservername` that Sparrow recognises as batch-capable without tripping BlueWallet's prefix check or losing Cake Wallet's tweak probe; document each wallet's rule next to it.
- Correct the manual's Sparrow statement either way.
- Test: a unit test over the documented matching rules of each wallet against the default name.

agent_prs.body:
Storage fixes for 0.7.1, from #547 and #551.

**#547**
1. **Block reads waited behind each stored block's fsync.** `write_block_durable` held the flat-file mutex across `sync_all`, and every block read (`getblock`, Esplora, Electrum, the events watch path, the index backfills) takes that mutex. The record is still written under the lock. Then `FlatFileManager::sync_handle` hands back a clone of the append file's descriptor, the lock is dropped, the clone is fsynced, and `mark_synced` clears `dirty` only if no record was appended after the handle was taken. A clone of the descriptor syncs the same inode, so the record is on disk before the caller commits the index entry pointing at it. If the file rotates in the meantime, the rotation has synced it already.
2. **Rotation could append past the cap.** After a rotation, `resync_append_pos` may land in a populated file, as after a pruning gap, but the size check was not run again. It is now a loop: the write rotates until the record fits.
3. **Already fixed:** the re-fetch map is keyed by `(hash, peer)`, so two concurrent `getblockfrompeer` calls no longer overwrite each other's registration.

issues.body:
Found during the deep review of #541.

#541 makes `check_block` take `(network, height)` and gates the BIP 141 witness
rules on `height >= activation_heights(network).segwit`. That gate only bites
on **mainnet (481824)** and **testnet3 (834624)**.

Every integration test, every regtest E2E, and the static `feature_block`
matrix run on regtest/signet/testnet4, where segwit is active from height 0. So
`segwit_active` is unconditionally `true` in all of them, and **a call site
passing a wrong height — `0`, an off-by-one, the parent's height instead of the
block's — is undetectable by the entire suite.**

The only tests that exercise the gate are the two `SEGWIT_ON`/`SEGWIT_OFF` unit
tests in `validation/block.rs`, and they call `check_block` directly, never
through a call site.

A reviewer enumerated all ten call sites and confirmed each currently passes
the height of the block being checked (`parent.height + 1`, a plan index, or a
BFS-derived height). The riskiest one — `repair_block_data`, which took
`entry.height` from the index it exists to repair — was changed in #537 to
derive the height from the block's own parent link and cross-check the two. So
this is a coverage gap, not a known defect.

Specifically untested call sites: `prefetch.rs` (nothing calls `prefetch_block`
in any test) and `index_reindex_side_chain`.

Options: a test per height-bearing call site pinned at a mainnet boundary
(needs a mainnet-shaped fixture chain, which is the expensive part), or a debug
assertion that the height passed matches the block's position in the index.

agent_prs.body:
Storage fixes for 0.7.1, from #547 and #551.

**#547**
1. **Block reads waited behind each stored block's fsync.** `write_block_durable` held the flat-file mutex across `sync_all`, and every block read (`getblock`, Esplora, Electrum, the events watch path, the index backfills) takes that mutex. The record is still written under the lock. Then `FlatFileManager::sync_handle` hands back a clone of the append file's descriptor, the lock is dropped, the clone is fsynced, and `mark_synced` clears `dirty` only if no record was appended after the handle was taken. A clone of the descriptor syncs the same inode, so the record is on disk before the caller commits the index entry pointing at it. If the file rotates in the meantime, the rotation has synced it already.
2. **Rotation could append past the cap.** After a rotation, `resync_append_pos` may land in a populated file, as after a pruning gap, but the size check was not run again. It is now a loop: the write rotates until the record fits.
3. **Already fixed:** the re-fetch map is keyed by `(hash, peer)`, so two concurrent `getblockfrompeer` calls no longer overwrite each other's registration.
4. **A re-fetched block leaked an IBD slot.** `handle_refetched_block` returns before `handle_block_ibd`, so `block_received` never ran for it. It now runs once the block is readable (`Repaired` or `AlreadyPresent`), not on a failed repair.
5. `block_serving_peer_ids`' doc now says its `NODE_NETWORK` + `NODE_WITNESS` rule applies only when the caller named no peer.

**#551:** `check_block` gates the witness rules on the height it is given, and every test runs where segwit is active from height 0, so a call site passing a wrong height passes the whole suite.

issues.body:
A grab-bag from the second-pass deep review of #537. None blocks that PR; all
are small and independently fixable.

**1. The flat-file mutex is held across the per-block fsync.**
`write_block_durable` holds `flat_files.lock()` across both `write_block` and
`sync_all`. `get_block` takes the same mutex, and it backs `getblock`, Esplora,
Electrum, the events watch path and the SP/address backfills. On network or
spinning storage a 10–50 ms fsync per block now serializes every read-surface
block fetch behind it. `connect_stored_block` deliberately uses the mutex-free
`read_block_direct` to dodge this; the read APIs cannot. Separable from — and
cheaper than — #539's amortization: syncing a cloned handle outside the guard
would do it.

**2. Rotation can append past the 128 MiB cap.** After rotation,
`resync_append_pos` may set `current_pos` to a populated file's length (the
pruning-gap case its comment describes), but the
`current_pos + record_size > MAX_FILE_SIZE` condition is not re-evaluated, so
the record is appended past the cap. Self-correcting (the next write rotates
again) and not corrupting. Wants a loop or a second check.

**3. Two concurrent `getblockfrompeer` calls for the same hash race their
registrations.** B's `insert` overwrites A's, then A's `send_to_peer` failure
path does `remove(&hash)` and deletes B's live registration. Operator-only,
self-healing by re-running.

**4. A consumed refetch leaks an IBD in-flight slot.** `handle_refetched_block`
returns before `handle_block_ibd`, so `scheduler.block_received(id, height)` is
skipped and that peer's slot leaks until timeout. Only reachable if a refetch is
armed during IBD.

**5. `block_serving_peer_ids`' doc reads as if its NODE_NETWORK + NODE_WITNESS
rule is global.** `request_block_from_peer` requires only NODE_WITNESS for an
explicitly named peer. That is the right behaviour (Core checks neither) — just
the comment that misleads.
issues.title: Flat-file and refetch rough edges found reviewing #537

Four HTTP-surface hardening issues for 0.7.1.

## #823: write timeout
`http_serve::WriteDeadline` wraps every accepted socket, under TLS, and fails a write (or flush or shutdown) that has stayed `Pending` for the budget. The clock runs only while a write is stuck and restarts on any progress, so a slow reader and an idle SSE or WebSocket stream are not cut off. Budgets:
- JSON-RPC (plain and TLS): `-rpcservertimeout`, as libevent's write timeout does in Core. With `-rpcservertimeout=0` the fixed `WRITE_STALL_TIMEOUT` (60 s) applies.
- Esplora and streamws: `WRITE_STALL_TIMEOUT` (60 s).

## #822: shutdown of SSE and upgraded WebSockets
- `serve_http_listener` wraps every response whose content type is `text/event-stream` in `EndAtShutdown`, which ends the body when the listener's shutdown fires. Covers streamws `/sse` and all Esplora SSE routes.
- streamws `ws_conn` has a shutdown arm that sends `1001 Going Away`, then ends the socket.

## #825: warning budgets
- "TLS handshake timed out" is budgeted per listener on the shared HTTP loop (Esplora TLS) and on JSON-RPC TLS, and per function (one listener each) on Electrum, MCP and events gRPC TLS.
- "accept error" is budgeted per listener on the shared HTTP loop, both JSON-RPC loops, metrics plain and TLS, Electrum, MCP and Stratum. Electrum, Stratum and the plain metrics loop now back off 50 ms after a failed accept, as the others did. Before, they spun.
- Stratum: each of the V1, V1-TLS and V2 listeners has its own at-capacity and accept-error budget, and the line names the listener.

## #826
1. The method filters (warmup, read-only, capability) now run before `NamedParamsLayer`, as Core's `-rpcwhitelist` check does. `ActiveCommandsLayer` stays innermost. The filters read only the method name and gate batches entry by entry.
2. `-esplorarequesttimeout=0` gives the Esplora TLS handshake 30 s (the option's default) instead of zero.
3. `serve_http_connection` clamps the header

issues.body:
A handful of small inconsistencies in the HTTP surfaces, none urgent:

1. **Parameter validation runs before the capability check.** `NamedParamsLayer` sits outside `CapabilityFilter`, so a token without `rpc:submit` calling `sendrawtransaction` with an unknown named parameter gets `-8 Unknown named parameter` instead of `-32004`. Nothing sensitive leaks, but a caller that may not use a method should get the capability error first.
2. **`-esplorarequesttimeout=0` also zeroes the Esplora TLS handshake budget**, so TLS on Esplora cannot complete. The docs describe `0` only as leaving idle connections open.
3. **Very large timeouts overflow `Instant`.** An `-esplorarequesttimeout` or `-rpcservertimeout` above about 9.2e18 seconds makes hyper compute `now + header_read_timeout`, which panics each connection task (the process survives; the listener serves nothing). Clamp the timeouts the way the connection caps are clamped.
4. **The plain metrics listener has no header timeout and no socket cap.** It runs `http1::Builder` without a timer, so a silent socket is held forever. It is loopback by default.
issues.title: http surfaces: capability-check ordering, zero and huge timeouts, metrics listener limits

Most accept loops now rate-limit their refusal warnings (first five a minute, then a suppressed count). A few log lines are still unbudgeted or share a budget they should not:

issues.body:
On shutdown, the HTTP listeners stop accepting and close idle keep-alive connections, but some long-lived connections stay open until the process exits:

- upgraded `streamws` `/ws` sockets: the per-connection loop in `events/src/ws.rs` (`ws_conn`) has no shutdown arm;
- SSE streams on `streamws` and on Esplora: hyper's `graceful_shutdown` waits for the in-flight response to finish, and an SSE response never does.

They are reaped when the process exits, so this is about a clean drain (clients get no close frame or end-of-stream) rather than a leak. The existing test `shutdown_closes_idle_connections` covers idle connections only.

**Possible fix:** give the WebSocket loop and the SSE body streams the listener's shutdown signal, and end them with a close frame / final event.

issues.body:
The HTTP listeners (JSON-RPC, Esplora, `streamws`) bound how long a connection may idle *between* requests, but nothing bounds a write. A client that sends a request for a large response, or opens an SSE stream or WebSocket, and then stops reading keeps its socket, and its slot under the listener's socket cap, for as long as the kernel send buffer and the server-side write wait allow — indefinitely.

With the socket caps (100 per JSON-RPC listener, `-esploramaxsockets` / `--streamws-max-sockets` default 1024), a client that can reach a listener can fill it this way.

**Possible fix:** a write/progress timeout on the connection IO (a wrapper that fails a write pending longer than N seconds), with a longer budget for streaming responses.
issues.title: http listeners: no write timeout, so a client that stops reading keeps its socket slot

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #875.

## Problem

During IBD every arriving block was stored on the P2P task (`handle_block_ibd` → `store_block` → `commit_block_store`), and `commit_block_store` takes `accept_lock`. The IBD connector holds that lock for a whole connect, script verification included. A block arriving during a long connect parked the P2P task on the mutex: no other peer's messages, no new block requests, no ping replies. When the connect let go, the stall check could drop peers whose deliveries were still queued behind it.

## Fix

The issue offered two directions. This takes the second, moving the store off the P2P task. The first, shrinking the connector's critical section, would mean verifying scripts outside the lock that orders every chain mutator, which is a consensus-path change of its own.

- **`net::ibd_store`**: a queue to a new `ibd-store` thread. `handle_block_ibd` keeps its cheap checks (non-canonical sub-snapshot block, unrequested block above the window) on the P2P task, then queues the block and returns. The queue is bounded at 128 MiB of block bytes. Past that a block is stored inline, as before, so a store that cannot keep up costs what it did and never unbounded memory. An empty queue takes any block.
- **Scheduler**: a delivery is now recorded in two steps. `block_arrived` runs on the P2P task: it credits the holder's liveness, with the same hash and holder checks as `block_received`, and marks the height arrived. An arrived height stays in flight and keeps its peer's slot, so the download window still bounds what is queued. It is no longer owed: `take_stalled_peer` and `release_stale_inflight` skip it, `release_height` (notfound) ignores it, and `peer_disconnected` leaves it in flight for its store to settle rather than asking another peer for it again. `block_received` settles it once stored. On a failed store, `block_store_failed` makes it owed again under the clocks that kept running, which is where it stood before this change.

issues.body:
During initial block download, block download and all peer message handling stop for as long as the connector spends on one block. On a block of large transactions that is tens of seconds.

## Cause

`PeerManager::run` handles peer messages on one task. A `block` message during IBD follows `handle_message` → `handle_block` → `handle_block_ibd` (`node/src/net/manager.rs:5191`) → `ChainState::store_block` → `commit_block_store`. That last step takes `accept_lock` (`node/src/chain/state.rs:4732`) to re-check the block's status and write its index batch.

The IBD connector holds the same lock for its whole connect, script verification included. `connect_preprocessed_block` takes it at `state.rs:4201` and `connect_stored_block` at `state.rs:5011`, and both hold it until they return. While the connector is inside a block, the next block message parks the P2P task on a blocking mutex, inside a tokio worker thread. Nothing else on that task runs: no other peer's messages, no new block requests, no ping replies.

Both acquisitions are documented as uncontended during IBD. `commit_block_store` says it "runs on the single P2P block thread, which does not otherwise hold the lock, so the acquisition is uncontended on the normal IBD path". `connect_stored_block` says it is "uncontended in steady-state IBD". Neither accounts for the other.

## Observed

On a pruned signet node in IBD from height 226,579, block 227,466 takes the connector more than 20 seconds (#874). Stack dumps taken during that connect showed the P2P loop's thread in `store_block`, waiting on `accept_lock`. Before #872 this also held shutdown open: the runtime's drop waited for that worker, and a node stayed up for as long as 171 seconds after logging `satd stopped`. #872 bounded the runtime shutdown, which ended the linger, but the stall during IBD remains.

The lock in `commit_block_store` is needed: it orders the status re-check against connects (#861) and makes the above-tip `height_hash` test

## Why

Under the default `-consensus=rust-shadow` (and `cpp`) the authoritative script engine is Bitcoin Core's C++ interpreter, reached until now through `libbitcoinconsensus`. With the default `-consensus=rust-shadow`, libbitcoinconsensus is the authoritative script engine, and the IBD prefetch workers verify with it as well. `ConsensusVerifier::verify_transaction` (`node/src/validation/script.rs:336-383`) calls `bitcoinconsensus::verify_with_flags` once per input, passing the whole serialized transaction each time.

In the vendored source (`bitcoinconsensus-0.106.0+26.0`, `src/script/bitcoinconsensus.cpp:86-118`), each of those calls:

- deserializes the full transaction (`CTransaction tx(deserialize, stream)`), which also computes its txid and wtxid;
- re-serializes it to check the length (`GetSerializeSize`);
- copies every spent output into a new vector;
- builds a new `PrecomputedTransactionData`, which for any witness spend hashes all prevouts, sequences and outputs again (`interpreter.cpp:1398-1447`).

A transaction with n inputs therefore costs n passes over the whole transaction, so the cost is quadratic in the input count. Core's own validation does this work once per transaction. Every pass also allocates. On the static musl build all threads share one malloc lock, so the prefetch workers verifying in parallel spend much of their time waiting on each other.

The Rust engine (`RustVerifier`) shares one `SighashCache` across a transaction's inputs and does not have this cost.

Signet block 227,466 has 228 transactions and 3,373 inputs, and its largest transaction is 160,545 bytes. On a pruned signet node in IBD (static musl release build), the connector spends more than 20 seconds on this block. Stack dumps taken during it showed the prefetch workers inside `verify_script` with `txToLen=160545`, waiting on musl's `__malloc_lock`. The connector holds `accept_lock` throughout, which also stalls the P2P loop (#875).

## Directions

issues.body:
## Problem

satd has no `.onion` fixed seeds for testnet4 or testnet3, and only a handful for signet and mainnet. A node started with `-onlynet=onion` on testnet4 has no address to dial: DNS seeds are clearnet, and `fixed_seeds_for_network` returns an empty list.

`node/src/net/dns.rs` at b3c79dc7 (v0.7.0):

```rust
fn onion_seeds_for_network(network: Network) -> &'static [(&'static str, u16)] {
    match network {
        Network::Bitcoin => MAINNET_ONION_SEEDS,
        Network::Signet => SIGNET_ONION_SEEDS,
        _ => &[],
    }
}
```

## Counts

Onion entries per network, satd v0.7.0 vs Bitcoin Core v31.1. Core's numbers count the `.onion` lines in `contrib/seeds/nodes_<net>.txt`, the input to `chainparamsseeds.h` (`vFixedSeeds`, `src/kernel/chainparams.cpp:161`, `:282`, `:395`, `:443`).

| network | satd | Core |
|---|---|---|
| mainnet | 20 | 512 |
| testnet3 | 0 | 69 |
| testnet4 | 0 | 78 |
| signet | 2 | 67 |

## Effect

- On testnet4 and testnet3, a Tor-only node (`-onlynet=onion` with `-proxy`) cannot bootstrap unless the operator adds `-seednode`/`-addnode` onion addresses by hand.
- On signet, the node bootstraps only if one of the two seeds is up.
- On mainnet, the 20-entry list churns faster than a 512-entry one, so a fresh Tor-only node is more likely to find every seed dead.

## Fix

Import the onion entries from Core's seed files for each network, and have `onion_seeds_for_network` cover testnet3 and testnet4. Keep the existing liveness check (a handshake over Tor with the right network magic) and note the import's source tag in the doc comment.

Related: #1157 (onion addresses are kept outside addrman). Clearnet and other fixed-seed networks (I2P, CJDNS) are out of scope here.

## Cause

`IbdScheduler::new` put every height from the tip to the header tip into `pending` and shuffled it. `extend_target` appended new heights, also shuffled. `assign_blocks_up_to` hands out the 256-height priority zone above the cursor, then pops from that pool. Its only window check was a count: `downloaded + in_flight + assigned >= max_ahead`. Nothing compared a height with the cursor.

`downloaded` drains only as the cursor passes each height. So early on the `max_ahead` slots fill with heights spread evenly over the whole range. After that, each slot that frees up goes to a uniformly random height anywhere up to the header tip. That block is written into the block file being filled at the time, next to the near-tip blocks the priority zone fetches. The issue's own table shows the result:
- every file holds blocks up to the header tip;
- the far share of each file is about `max_ahead / remaining range`;
- the resume scan re-marks those far blocks on restart.

`prune_up_to` deletes a file only once its highest block is below the cut, Core's `nHeightLast` rule, so on a pruned node no file qualified during IBD.

## Fix

1. **The download window is a height range.**
   - The pool is built and extended in height order, with no shuffle.
   - `assign_blocks_up_to` hands nothing out above `connect_cursor + max_ahead`, Core's `nWindowEnd` (`net_processing.cpp`).
   - Heights pushed back to the pool go to its front, in order, so it stays sorted and the first height above the window ends the pass.
   - The priority zone and the count limit are unchanged.

issues.body:
`satd-init` renders `bitcoin.conf` and appends `conf.d/local.conf` last. The stack README says the appended lines win because "satd takes the last value for a repeated key", and a comment in `satd-init` says the same ("appended last so they win where satd takes the last value").

satd resolves a repeated config-file key **first-wins**, as Bitcoin Core does (`Config::from_cli`'s `file_get` takes the first value; Core's `common/settings.cpp`: "Take first assigned value instead of last"). So a `local.conf` line for a single-valued key that `satd-init` already writes is silently ignored. The keys it writes include `port`, `txindex`, `addressindex`, `prune`, `blockfilterindex`, `server`, `rpcport`, the Electrum, Esplora and metrics binds, and, from 0.6.0, `upgradechainstate`.

The README's own example (`dbcache=4000`) works, because `satd-init` does not write `dbcache`. Multi-valued keys such as `rpcallowip` accumulate, so those also work.

**Fix:** either write `local.conf` first (an `includeconf` would not help: an included file's values are merged after the main file's), or correct the README and the comment to say which keys can be overridden and which cannot.
issues.title: Stack: conf.d/local.conf cannot override a single-valued key satd-init already writes

issues.body:
Bitcoin Core's `IsStandardTx` rejects a transaction whose version is below 1 or above `TX_MAX_STANDARD_VERSION` (3) with reject reason `version` (`src/policy/policy.cpp`). satd's mempool standardness check (`check_standardness`, `node/src/mempool/pool.rs` ~2907) checks size, dust, OP_RETURN and scriptPubKey templates but has no version test, and no `version` reject reason exists anywhere in the mempool code. The only version-aware path is TRUC (`version == 3`).

Expected effect: `sendrawtransaction` / `testmempoolaccept` / P2P relay accept a version-0 or version-4+ transaction that Core rejects as non-standard, and satd then relays it to peers that will drop it. Found by code reading; not yet confirmed with a test.

## Proposed fix

- Add the range check to standardness (honouring `-acceptnonstdtxn` on test chains, as Core does), reason `version`.
- Test: `testmempoolaccept` on otherwise-standard txs with versions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and `0xffffffff` (the negative `int32` case), asserting `version` for 0, 4 and `0xffffffff`.
issues.title: mempool: no IsStandardTx version check (Core rejects version < 1 or > 3)

issues.body:
`getblockchaininfo`, `getnetworkinfo` and `getmininginfo` return `"warnings": ""` when the node has no active warnings, and an array of strings when it has some. Bitcoin Core (since v28) always returns an array, `[]` when there are none; the string form is only returned under `-deprecatedrpc=warnings`, and then it holds the last message, not an array.

So the field's JSON type depends on the node's state. A client written against Core that iterates `warnings` breaks on a healthy satd node, and a client written against satd's empty string breaks once a warning appears.

**Where:**
- `node/src/rpc/blockchain.rs` (`getblockchaininfo`)
- `node/src/rpc/mining.rs` (`getmininginfo`)
- `node/src/rpc/network.rs` (`getnetworkinfo`)

Each does:

```rust
"warnings": match warnings {
    v if v.is_empty() => Value::String(String::new()),
    v => Value::Array(v.into_iter().map(Value::String).collect()),
}
```

The code comment calls the empty-string case a deliberate choice, to keep the form Core used before v27/v28.

**Core reference:** `src/node/warnings.cpp`, `GetWarningsForRpc`: an array unless `IsDeprecatedRPCEnabled("warnings")`, then a single string (`""` if none).

**Why this was not changed with the other RPC parity fixes in 0.6.1:** `STABILITY_POLICY.md` puts response field names and types in Tier 1, with a minimum four-release deprecation cycle. Changing `""` to `[]` changes a field's type, so it needs a decision on how to roll it out. Options:

1. Treat it as a Core-compatibility bug (the field already returns an array whenever there is a warning, so clients must already handle the array) and switch to always-array in the next release, with a release-notes entry.
2. Always return an array by default, and accept `-deprecatedrpc=warnings` (today a recognised but unimplemented option) to bring back Core's deprecated single-string form.
3. Keep the current behaviour and record it in `CORE_DIFFERENCES.md`.

issues.body:
## Problem

`getnetworkinfo` always reports ipv4 and ipv6 as `"limited": false, "reachable": true`, whatever `-onlynet` says. The values are hardcoded in `node/src/rpc/network.rs:195` and `:202` (c80998c4). Only the onion entry is computed (`onion_routing_available()`, line 146).

## Observed

On satd 0.7.0, testnet4, with `onlynet=onion`, `proxy=127.0.0.1:9050` and `listenonion=1`:

```
net ipv4  reachable True  proxy 127.0.0.1:9050
net ipv6  reachable True  proxy 127.0.0.1:9050
net onion reachable True  proxy 127.0.0.1:9050
```

All 14 outbound peers were `.onion`, and the node made no clearnet outbound connections. It was behaving correctly, but the RPC told the operator that clearnet was in use.

## Core

Bitcoin Core v31.1 `GetNetworksInfo` (`src/rpc/net.cpp:630-631`):

```cpp
obj.pushKV("limited", !g_reachable_nets.Contains(network));
obj.pushKV("reachable", g_reachable_nets.Contains(network));
```

Under `-onlynet=onion`, Core reports ipv4 and ipv6 as `limited: true, reachable: false`.

## Fix

Read each network's flags from the `PeerManager`'s `reachable` set (`ReachableNets`, `manager.rs:1172`), which already drives outbound selection and gossip filtering, instead of hardcoding them. Add a regression test that sets `-onlynet=onion` and asserts that ipv4 and ipv6 are not reachable.

Related: Core also lists `i2p` and `cjdns` in `networks`, but satd lists only ipv4, ipv6 and onion. This is worth fixing in the same function, but isn't required for this issue.
issues.title: rpc: getnetworkinfo reports ipv4/ipv6 as reachable and not limited under -onlynet=onion

Five small fixes for 0.7.1, one commit.

Fixes #824, fixes #1066, fixes #1152, fixes #1165. Refs #1144: the worker floor is a mitigation, so #1144 should stay open (see below).

## Changes

- **#824, RPC:** the JSON-RPC listener now reads every request body as JSON, whatever its `Content-Type`. Before, `application/json` was added only when the header was missing, so Core's documented `curl` form (`-H 'content-type: text/plain;'`) and plain `curl --data` got `415`. Both HTTP layers (`CoreHttpPrelude`, and the layer that handles `-rpcwhitelist` scopes) now call one helper, `json_request_content_type`.
- **#1066, RPC:** `getrawtransaction`'s not-found text follows the index state:
  - With no index, the advice to use `-txindex` stays.
  - With a complete index: `No such mempool or blockchain transaction`, as in Core.
  - With an incomplete index (turned on after blocks were connected without it; satd never backfills), the text says those blocks are not covered. This stands in for Core's "still being indexed" case.

  The error code stays -5.

## Problem

The `Peer connected` log line (`node/src/net/manager.rs:5938-5944`, c80998c4) prints `handle.info.addr`. For a `.onion` peer that field is a placeholder `SocketAddr` with an unspecified IP, so the log shows `0.0.0.0` instead of the onion host:

```
INFO node::net::manager: Connecting to .onion peer via proxy onion="wkvaxtftpwmmvrptqavx6mwhrcwiecbodtshuenvot3cjgxsycuurcid.onion" id=25
INFO node::net::manager: Peer connected id=25 addr=0.0.0.0:48333 user_agent=/Satoshi:32.1.0(...)/ height=158396
```

The `Connecting to` line names the onion, but once a node has several onion peers the `Peer connected` lines can't be told apart. `getpeerinfo` reports the right address, so only the log is affected.

## Fix

When `onion_host` is set, log it with the port (`<host>.onion:<port>`), as `getpeerinfo` does. Apply the same to `addr_name` peers (connections opened by name through a proxy). Check the other log lines that print `info.addr` for a peer, such as disconnects and misbehaviour, and give them the same treatment.

A WebSocket on the JSON-RPC listener resolved its bearer token once, at the upgrade request. jsonrpsee copies that request's extensions onto every frame, so the resolved `Principal` rode every call for as long as the socket stayed open. Removing the token from the authfile and sending SIGHUP, or letting its `expires` pass, did not stop an open socket from calling what the token had been granted, `sendrawtransaction` included.

## Design

SIGHUP calls `TokenStore::reload`, which reads the file and swaps the whole table atomically behind an `RwLock<Arc<TokenTable>>`. A failed read keeps the last-good table (`satd/src/reload.rs`, the `token_store.reload()` block; `satd-auth/src/store.rs`, `reload`). A lookup by digest against `snapshot()` therefore sees a revocation the moment the swap happens. With a per-frame recheck there is no need to track open sessions, close them from the reload path, or run a timer per token for expiry. Each frame asks the store as it stands, and time is checked on every lookup.

- `satd-auth`: `TokenStore::resolve_digest(&digest, now)` looks a token up by its SHA-256 and checks `expires`. `resolve` now goes through it. `token_digest(token)` is exported.
- `AuthMiddleware`: when a bearer token authenticates a WebSocket upgrade, it puts a `BearerSession` on the request. The session holds the store and the token's digest, which is what the authfile itself stores, never the token. Plain HTTP requests are unchanged, since they are resolved once for the one call they carry.
- `TokenRecheckLayer`, new and outermost on bearer surfaces, ahead of `BatchRateLayer`: for each call, batch and notification that carries a session, it resolves the digest again. The frame's `Principal` is replaced with the token's current one, so a reload that edits the token's capabilities or rate limit reaches open sockets as well. A WebSocket on the JSON-RPC listener resolves its bearer token once, at the upgrade request. jsonrpsee copies that request's extensions onto every frame, so the resolved `Principal` rides every call for as long as the socket stays open.

**Effect:** revoking a token (removing it from the authfile and sending SIGHUP), or letting its `expires` pass, does not stop an already-open WebSocket from calling methods the token was granted, `sendrawtransaction` included. The per-listener socket cap bounds how many such sessions exist, not how long each one lasts.

**Where:** `node/src/rpc/auth.rs` (`AuthMiddleware::call` resolves the principal); `satd-auth/src/store.rs` (`TokenStore::resolve` checks `expires` only at that point).

**Related, same root:** WebSocket frames also skip the `-rpcthreads` / `-rpcworkqueue` admission layer once the socket is upgraded, and they bypass `JsonRpcCompatLayer`, so a JSON-RPC 1.0 or id-less 1.0 frame is refused `-32600` where the same request over HTTP is accepted.

**Possible fixes:** re-check the principal per frame against the store (by token digest), or close WebSocket sessions whose token was removed or expired, on reload and at expiry.

Per-frame rate limiting is handled separately: frames are now charged against the token's `rate_limit` individually.
issues.title: rpc: an open WebSocket outlives its bearer token's revocation and expiry

Every disconnect that goes through `PeerManager::disconnect_by_id` logs

```
INFO node::net::manager: Disconnecting peer on request id=5 addr=61.220.99.181:38333 reason="rpc_request"
```

because the log line in `disconnect_by_id` (`node/src/net/manager.rs`, the `tracing::info!` with `reason = "rpc_request"`) hard-codes the reason. The function has about 25 callers in `manager.rs`, and most are the node's own decisions, not `disconnectnode`. For example, the IBD stall check (#972) logs

```
INFO node::net::manager: IBD: peer is stalling block download, disconnecting peer_id=5 next_timeout_secs=30
INFO node::net::manager: Disconnecting peer on request id=5 addr=61.220.99.181:38333 reason="rpc_request"
```

Seen on a fresh 0.7.0 signet IBD: 8 stall disconnects, each logged as an RPC request. An operator reading the log would think something was calling `disconnectnode`.

The shadow verification queue was bounded only by entry count: `-shadowqueuesize`, default 4,194,304. Each entry holds a serialized transaction and a copy of every prevout it spends. When the shadow engine lags the primary engine, as it does on a host with few cores during IBD, the queue grew to gigabytes and hit the process's memory limit long before the entry cap. The drop path and its WARN never fired.

## Change

- `ShadowVerifier` keeps a shared `AtomicUsize` of queued bytes. `enqueue` charges each item's cost, and the worker that dequeues the item releases it before verifying. The cost is the struct itself, the serialized transaction, the prevout vector and each prevout's script.

issues.body:
## Summary

The shadow verification queue (`-shadowqueuesize`, default 4,194,304) is bounded by entry count, not by bytes. Each entry is a serialized transaction plus a copy of all its prevouts. When the shadow engine can't keep up with the primary engine, as on a host with few cores during IBD, the queue grows until it hits the process's memory limit, long before the entry cap applies. The drop path that exists for a full queue never fires.

## Where

`node/src/validation/script.rs`, unchanged on master:

- `ShadowVerifier::new` creates `crossbeam_channel::bounded::<ShadowWork>(queue_size)`.
- `ShadowWork` holds `tx_bytes: Vec<u8>` and `prev_outputs: Vec<TxOut>`.
- `enqueue` uses `try_send` and drops only on `TrySendError::Full`.

At a few hundred bytes to several KB per entry, 4M entries comes to gigabytes, far more than a small host or a `-dbcache=300` budget allows for.

## Observed

At e084339d, during signet IBD on a 1-vCPU host with the default `-consensus=rust-shadow` and `-shadowworkers` (4), under `MemoryMax=1500M`:

- The unit's cgroup sat at its limit (`memory.current` 1499M of 1500M) and `memory.events max` reached 144,054. Process RSS was about 950 MB with `-dbcache=300`, and the host was 626 MB into swap.
- No shadow-drop WARN was logged in five hours, so the queue never reached its entry cap. Everything enqueued stayed in memory.
- Block connection slowed steadily: write-cache flushes went from several a minute to about one every 13 minutes.
- Restarting with `-consensus=rust` (single engine) dropped CPU pressure from 99.6% to about 44% straight away.

I didn't measure queue depth directly. The memory attribution rests on the facts above, not on a heap profile.

## Suggested direction

- Bound the queue by bytes, e.g. a shared `AtomicUsize` charged on enqueue and credited when a worker finishes, with a default derived from `-dbcache` or a fixed cap of a few hundred MB. Keep dropping and counting when it's full, as `try_send` does now.
- Report queue
issues.title: Shadow verification queue is bounded by entry count, not bytes; fills memory when the shadow engine lags

## Summary

On a host with one CPU, satd's core tokio runtime gets a single worker thread, and during IBD that worker spends minutes at a time blocked on a futex. Everything on the core runtime stops with it: the JSON-RPC listener and P2P. RPC is still accepted at the TCP level, but no request is read or answered, not even an unauthenticated one.

## Where

`satd/src/main.rs` builds the core runtime with tokio's default worker count:

```rust
let runtime = tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
    .enable_all()
    .build()
```

The default is `available_parallelism()`, so 1 on a 1-vCPU machine. The API runtime (`-apithreads`, default 2) is separate and sized explicitly; the core runtime is not.

## Observed

Seen at e084339d during signet IBD on a 1-vCPU, 3 GB host. satd ran with `-dbcache=300 -prune=6000 -maxconnections=16 -listen=0` and the default `-consensus=rust-shadow`, under a systemd unit with `Nice=15`, `CPUWeight=20` and `MemoryMax=1500M`.

- **RPC:** `getblockcount` and `getblockchaininfo` got no reply within 180 s. While a request was pending, the server side of the connection showed `ESTAB Recv-Q 302`: the connection had been accepted, but its bytes were never read. - **Threads** (from `/proc/<pid>/task/*/stat` and `syscall`, sampled six times over 12 s):
  - the one `tokio-rt-worker` and the main thread were in `futex` (202) every time;

`testmempoolaccept` is meant to answer "would `sendrawtransaction` accept this?". With a policy ruleset that holds an `allow` rule, admission records a failure in the exemptable standardness set and forgives it when the verdict is `Allow`. `test_prechecks` returned the same failure before the policy dry run ran, so `testmempoolaccept` refused, for example, a two-dust transaction that `sendrawtransaction` accepted under `allow mine when tx.source == rpc`.

issues.body:
With a policy ruleset that contains an `allow` rule, admission defers a failure in the exemptable standardness set (`check_standardness`, `pre_check_ephemeral`, and after #998 Core's input and witness standardness) and forgives it when the transaction's verdict is `Allow`. `testmempoolaccept` doesn't. `Mempool::test_accept` returns the standardness error directly, before the policy dry run (`node/src/mempool/pool.rs`, the `check_standardness` and `pre_check_ephemeral` calls in `test_accept`). Its comment says "Standardness is not re-litigated here ... deferred-standardness forgiveness is moot".

So with, for example,

```
version 1
allow mine when tx.source == rpc
```

a transaction with two dust outputs, or one that spends a non-standard output, is accepted by `sendrawtransaction` and refused by `testmempoolaccept` with the standardness reason. `testmempoolaccept` is meant to answer "would `sendrawtransaction` accept this?".

Expected: `test_accept` records standardness failures the way `accept_transaction_unexpired` does (`deferred_nonstd`), runs the policy dry run, and forgives them on an `Allow` verdict. A test should submit one transaction through both RPCs under an `allow` rule and assert they agree.

issues.body:
## What happens

When `getrawtransaction` doesn't find a txid and no block hash was given, satd always returns:

```
-5 No such mempool transaction. Use -txindex or provide a block hash to enable blockchain transaction queries. Use gettransaction for wallet transactions.
```

It returns this text even when `-txindex` is on and the transaction index has already been searched (`node/src/rpc/rawtx.rs:198`, after the `has_txindex()` lookup at `:165`). An operator who has enabled the index is told to enable it.

## Expected

Core picks one of three messages (`src/rpc/rawtransaction.cpp`, `getrawtransaction`), each followed by `. Use gettransaction for wallet transactions.`:

| Condition | Message |
|---|---|
| no txindex | `No such mempool transaction. Use -txindex or provide a block hash to enable blockchain transaction queries` |
| txindex on, still syncing | `No such mempool transaction. Blockchain transactions are still in the process of being indexed` |
| txindex on and synced | `No such mempool or blockchain transaction` |

The error code is -5 in every case, as satd already returns. Only the text is wrong. The "still syncing" case can use the same notion of synced that `getindexinfo` reports for `txindex` (`node/src/rpc/indexes.rs`).

## Also

When a block hash is given and that block has been pruned, satd says "Block not available (pruned data)" where Core says "Block not available". This is minor; fix it in the same pass only if no test or client relies on the longer text.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #1153. On `release/0.7.x`, for 0.7.1; it will be forward-ported to `master`.

## Cause

The Stratum V1 canary failed twice in step 4 with "cpuminer found no block on the filled mempool": run 40986464128 (#1146) and run 41244381441 (#1166). The `minerd.log` in both artifacts shows the same thing. After the fill, cpuminer got the new job (`Stratum requested work restart` right after the resume) and hashed at its full rate for the whole ten minutes without finding a share:

| run | miner rate after the resume | shares in 600 s |
|---|---|---|
| 40986464128 | 22.6 MH/s | 0 |
| 41244381441 | 26.5 MH/s | 0 |

satd's log agrees: the miner stayed connected at difficulty 1, and no submit or error line follows the resume. Nothing was stuck and no work was lost. The run was unlucky.

satd's V1 share difficulty is at least 1, so a share, which on regtest is also a block, takes about 2^32 hashes. That is about three minutes at these rates, not the one minute the script's header assumed. The wait is exponential, so a ten-minute allowance comes up empty about one time in 25 (e^-3.3). The canary waits twice per run, in step 2 and step 4. That matches two failures in roughly 25 runs.

## Change

- `BLOCK_WAIT_SECS`, default 1500 s, is used for both waits. That is about eight average blocks, so an unlucky wait now fails about one time in 4,000. A typical run takes as long as before.
- The job's `timeout-minutes` goes from 20 to 60 to fit two worst-case waits.
- Each wait logs how long it took and cpuminer's hash rate.
- A wait that ends empty prints cpuminer's rate, its last log lines and satd's Stratum counters. A future failure will then show whether it was luck or a broken job.

CI-only: no satd code, no changelog entry.
