issues.body:
The Stratum V1 canary (`scripts/canary/stratum-v1-smoke.sh`) failed once in step 4, "A full block":

```
ok: cpuminer found block 251 and satd counted it
ok: a new tip reached cpuminer as new work
ok: Bitcoin Core accepted all 1 Stratum-found blocks and is at satd's tip
filling the mempool from Core's wallet...
ok: satd's mempool holds 150 transactions, 1178998 bytes
cpuminer found no block on the filled mempool
```

Run: https://github.com/epochbtc/satd/actions/runs/40986464128/job/123843546999 (PR #1146, a version-only change). The rerun passed, and the job had passed in the previous 20 runs that were not skipped or cancelled.

The step pauses cpuminer (`kill -STOP`), fills the mempool, mines one block with `generateblock` so the next job is built from the full mempool, then resumes the miner (`kill -CONT`) and waits 600 s for a Stratum-found block above that height. On regtest cpuminer found the earlier block in about 40 s, so no block in 10 minutes is very unlikely to be luck. satd's log shows the miner still connected for the whole wait (it disconnects only at teardown, `reason="end of stream"`), and no found-block, share or error line after the resume.

Possible causes to check: the job built after the `generateblock` tip never reached the miner, or reached it while stopped and was not re-sent; or the full-mempool job is one cpuminer cannot hash (for example a merkle branch or coinbase it rejects). The canary log artifact keeps satd's log only; capturing cpuminer's output and satd's `mining.notify` sends in this step would tell which.

Five small fixes for 0.7.1, one commit.

Fixes #824, fixes #1066, fixes #1152, fixes #1165. Refs #1144: the worker floor is a mitigation, so #1144 should stay open (see below).

## Changes

- **#824, RPC:** the JSON-RPC listener now reads every request body as JSON, whatever its `Content-Type`. Before, `application/json` was added only when the header was missing, so Core's documented `curl` form (`-H 'content-type: text/plain;'`) and plain `curl --data` got `415`. Both HTTP layers (`CoreHttpPrelude`, and the layer that handles `-rpcwhitelist` scopes) now call one helper, `json_request_content_type`.
- **#1066, RPC:** `getrawtransaction`'s not-found text follows the index state:
  - With no index, the advice to use `-txindex` stays.
  - With a complete index: `No such mempool or blockchain transaction`, as in Core.
  - With an incomplete index (turned on after blocks were connected without it; satd never backfills), the text says those blocks are not covered. This stands in for Core's "still being indexed" case.

  The error code stays -5.
- **#1152, P2P log:** `disconnect_by_id` logged `Disconnecting peer on request reason="rpc_request"` for all of its roughly 25 internal callers. `disconnectnode` now goes through `disconnect_on_request` and logs `reason="rpc_request"`. The node's own disconnects log `reason="internal"`, next to the line their caller already writes. Logging only.
- **#1165, P2P log:** `Peer connected`, `Peer disconnected` and the IBD silent-peer warning use `addr_string()`, which `getpeerinfo` also uses. Onion peers now show `<host>.onion:<port>` instead of `0.0.0.0:<port>`.
- **#1144, runtime:** the core tokio runtime gets `max(available_parallelism, 2)` workers.

Release docs: `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` is now bound for 0.7.1 and points at a new `docs/release-notes/0.7.1-pre.md`. `0.8.0-pre.md` is unchanged. This assumes 0.7.1 is cut from master, which holds no 0.8.0-only work yet.

issues.body:
Bitcoin Core's own RPC help examples call the server with:

    curl --user myusername --data-binary '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "curltest", "method": "getblockcount", "params": []}' -H 'content-type: text/plain;' http://127.0.0.1:8332/

satd answers that request `415 Unsupported Media Type` ("Content-Type: application/json is required"). `CoreHttpPrelude` in `node/src/rpc/compat.rs` only supplies a content type when the header is absent, so an explicit `text/plain` reaches jsonrpsee's check.

Core ignores the request content type. For compatibility satd should accept `text/plain` (and probably any content type) on the JSON-RPC listener, as it already does when the header is missing.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1142.

Moves `bitcoin` from 0.32.9 to 0.32.102, the latest non-yanked 0.32.x. 0.32.10 reverts 0.32.9's `CompactSize` range check (rust-bitcoin #6182), which refused addrv2 entries with high service bits. The same releases also tightened the P2P decoders beyond what Core accepts, so this PR adds `net::payload`, which reads every message payload the way Core's handlers do. Both transports use it: v1 frames, v2 short IDs, and v2 long form.

### Audit against Core

| Change in rust-bitcoin | Core | Divergence | Done here |
|---|---|---|---|
| #6140: a v1 message with bytes after its last field is refused | No handler checks that the payload is used up. `version` reads its later fields only `if (!vRecv.empty())` (`net_processing.cpp:3626-3643`) | **Yes**, new. A `version` or `verack` with a tail would stall the handshake | Trailing bytes are ignored on every known message |
| (0.32.9 already) `version` must carry every field through `relay` | Needs only version, services, time and addrMe. Later fields are optional, defaulting to nonce 1, `""`, start height -1, relay true | **Yes**. A testnet4 peer running `/Gocoin:1.11.1pre/` ends its `version` after the start height. satd skipped it ("IO error"), so the handshake never completed | Core's optional-field read. A user agent over 256 bytes is refused (`LIMITED_STRING`); one that is not UTF-8 is read lossily, where rust-bitcoin refused it |
| #6525: a `sendcmpct` flag byte other than 0/1 is refused (both transports) | `bool` is any byte, with non-zero meaning true (`serialize.h:279`) | **Yes**, new | Non-zero is true |
| #6142: a `feefilter` outside 0..=MAX_MONEY is refused (v1) | Reads the `CAmount` and ignores a value outside `MoneyRange`, keeping the previous filter (`net_processing.cpp:5035-5045`) | Same outcome on v1. Over v2, though (the `bip324` crate does no range check), satd clamped a negative value to 0 and applied a value above MAX_MONEY | Decoded whole. `set_peer_fee_filter` ignores an out-of-range value

issues.body:
satd decodes P2P messages with rust-bitcoin's decoders, and several of them refuse messages Bitcoin Core accepts. Some of this is in the `bitcoin` 0.32.9 we ship, and the move to 0.32.102 (needed to drop 0.32.9's `CompactSize` range check) adds more.

**In 0.32.9 today**

- `version` must carry every field through `relay`. Core needs only version, services, time and the receiver's address, and reads each later field only if bytes remain (`net_processing.cpp:3626-3643`), defaulting relay to true. A testnet4 peer running `/Gocoin:1.11.1pre/` ends its `version` after the start height. satd skips the message ("IO error"), the handshake never completes, and the peer's later messages are refused as "non-version message before version handshake".
- A `version` user agent that is not UTF-8 is refused. Core reads any bytes, up to 256 (`LIMITED_STRING`), and sanitizes them.
- `feefilter`: a negative value is clamped to 0 and a value above `MAX_MONEY` is applied. Core ignores a value outside `MoneyRange` and keeps the previous filter (`net_processing.cpp:5035-5045`).
- Over v2, a long-form `ping`, `tx`, `inv` and so on is read as an unknown message. Core goes by the message type's name.

**Added by 0.32.10 and later**

- rust-bitcoin#6140: a v1 message with bytes left after its last field is refused. No Core handler checks that the payload is used up. A `version` or `verack` with trailing bytes would stall the handshake.
- rust-bitcoin#6525: a `sendcmpct` whose flag byte is not 0 or 1 is refused, on both transports. Core reads the `bool` as any byte, with non-zero meaning true (`serialize.h:279`).
- rust-bitcoin#6142: an out-of-range `feefilter` is refused over v1. Core reads the message and ignores the value, which comes to the same thing once the handler checks the range.

**Changes in 0.32.10+ that bring us closer to Core**

- #6136: a message type with an embedded NUL is no longer read as the type its leading bytes spell (`pi\0ng` was read as `ping`). Core drops such a mes

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #1139.

Each header in a `headers` message is followed by a transaction count. Core reads it as a CompactSize and ignores it (`src/net_processing.cpp:4747`, "ignore tx count; assume it is 0"). rust-bitcoin's `HeaderDeserializationWrapper`, and the `bip324` crate's copy of it for v2, read one byte and refuse the whole message when it is non-zero ("Headers message should not contain transactions"). A multi-byte CompactSize (`fd ...`) would also misalign them. Peers on testnet4 send such messages, and every header in them was lost.

This follows #1136 (`addrv2`):

- `net::headers` decodes the payload as Core's loop does: a CompactSize count, then for each header 80 bytes and a CompactSize that is read and dropped. Both CompactSizes go through rust-bitcoin's `VarInt` decoder. That decoder is Core's `ReadCompactSize` with the range check, so non-canonical encodings, values above `MAX_SIZE` and truncated payloads are refused, as Core refuses them.
- v1: `recv_message` checks the frame checksum and hands the `headers` command to `net::headers` before rust-bitcoin sees it. The `addrv2` interception and this one now share a single branch.
- v2: `decode_message` handles short id 13 and the long form `headers`.
- The decoder does not cap the count. The handler's `MAX_HEADERS_RESULTS` check (more than 2000 is misbehaviour) is unchanged, and so is the existing test for it.

## Tests

- `net::headers` unit tests use hand-built bytes: tx counts `01`, `fc`, `fd 00 01` and `fe 00 00 01 00`, in either entry. They also cover rust-bitcoin's own zero-count encoding, 2001 headers still decoding, non-canonical and over-`MAX_SIZE` counts, truncation in a header, in a multi-byte tx count and in a short entry list, and the v1 checksum.
- v1 transport: `a_headers_with_nonzero_tx_counts_is_read`, `a_bad_headers_frame_is_skipped`.
- v2 transport: `headers_with_nonzero_tx_counts_decode` (short id and long form, plus an encoder round-trip) and `a_v2_headers_with_a_nonzero_tx_count_arrives`.

issues.body:
In a `headers` message each 80-byte header is followed by a transaction count. Core reads it as a CompactSize and ignores the value:

```cpp
// src/net_processing.cpp:4747
ReadCompactSize(vRecv); // ignore tx count; assume it is 0.
```

satd decodes `headers` with rust-bitcoin 0.32's `HeaderDeserializationWrapper` (v1, `p2p/message.rs`) and, on BIP324 v2 connections, with the `bip324` 0.10 crate's copy of it (`serde.rs`). Both read the tx count as a single byte and refuse the whole message if it is non-zero:

```
Headers message should not contain transactions
```

Peers on testnet4 send such messages. A node on testnet4 running current master logged `Skipping unparseable message cmd=headers` 31-56 times in a 4-minute run, so those header announcements are lost (since #1136 the peer is kept; before it, a v2 peer was dropped).

A multi-byte CompactSize tx count (`fd ...`) would also misalign rust-bitcoin's reader, since it reads only the first byte.

Expected: read the tx count as Core does (a CompactSize, canonical and range-checked, value ignored), over v1 and v2 (short id 13 and the long form). The existing `MAX_HEADERS_RESULTS` handling stays as it is.

Fixes #1131

## What

satd checked its checkpoints only as a hash match at each checkpoint height, so a peer could fork from genesis or any early block and have every early-difficulty header it mined written to the block index. This adds Core v29's rule from `ContextualCheckBlockHeader` ("Don't accept any forks from the main chain prior to last checkpoint"):

- A new header whose height is below the highest checkpoint already in the block index (Core's `BlockManager::GetLastCheckpoint`, header-only entries included) is refused as `bad-fork-prior-to-checkpoint` and not stored. It runs where Core runs it: after the difficulty check, before the time and version rules.
- Only after the already-known short-circuit, so main-chain headers sent again are skipped as before. A fresh node is unaffected until its header sync reaches a checkpoint.

- Only when checkpoints are enforced (`-checkpoints`, default on). Mainnet and the default signet carry checkpoints; testnet4, regtest and a custom signet have none.

Fixes #1119 (the header-height part; see "Not in this PR").

## Problem

`headers_tip_height` was a `fetch_max` high-water mark over every accepted header (`commit_accepted_headers_locked`), so a peer that forks from genesis at minimum difficulty and sends a chain taller than the real one raised it. Once it was more than 24 above the tip, `is_ibd` turned true (relayed transactions dropped, announced ones not fetched, compact blocks not served), `getblockchaininfo.headers` reported the attacker's height, readiness failed on header lag, and the locator and verification progress started from the inflated height.

## Change

`headers_tip_height` is now the height of `best_header`, the most-work header, as Core's `m_best_header->nHeight` (`src/rpc/blockchain.cpp`, `getblockchaininfo`):

- it is written only in `update_best_header` (under the pointer's write lock) and in `recalculate_best_header` (`invalidateblock` / `reconsiderblock` / a failed connect), never as a high-water mark;
- startup seeds it from the best header's height (the scan that already seeds `best_header`), not from a probe of the height rows;
- a heavier-but-shorter switch takes it down to the new best header's height;
- snapshot activation moves `best_header` with it (`refresh_best_header_to_tip`) instead of raising the height alone;
- `repair_header_rows_above_tip` used the high-water mark as the ceiling for stale rows; it now walks the contiguous rows above the best header instead.

Every reader (`is_ibd` via the manager's mirror, `getblockchaininfo`, readiness, the locator, verification progress, the IBD scheduler's target) is unchanged and now reads the most-work height.

## Not in this PR

Low-work headers are still stored in the block index. Core keeps them out with an anti-DoS work threshold plus `HeadersSyncState` presync/redownload; adding the threshold alone would refuse the real chain during a fresh IBD, where every early batch is below `nMinimumChainWork`. That is a follow-up.

## What happens

Header acceptance (`accept_header` and `accept_headers` in `node/src/chain/state.rs`) checks the proof of work, the difficulty bits, and the contextual time and version rules. It does not check whether the chain those headers build has a meaningful amount of work. Every accepted header is stored. `commit_accepted_headers_locked` then raises `headers_tip_height` to the header's height with `fetch_max` (`state.rs:2766`), whether or not the header moved `best_header`.

So a peer can fork from genesis, or from any early block, and send headers at or near minimum difficulty. Each such header on mainnet takes about 2^32 hashes, so a chain taller than the real one costs roughly 4×10^15 hashes: seconds to minutes on one current ASIC. Checkpoints do not stop it, because they are checked only when a block is stored or accepted (`state.rs:5237`, `:7959`), not when a header is.

Once that chain is more than 24 blocks taller than the tip, everything that reads `headers_tip_height` treats the node as far behind:

- `is_ibd` (`node/src/net/manager.rs:4494-4502`) returns true. The node then:
  - drops relayed transactions (`:9657`);
  - stops fetching announced ones (`:6405`);
  - stops serving compact blocks (`:10983`).
- `getblockchaininfo` reports the attacker's height as `headers` (`node/src/rpc/blockchain.rs:253, 624`).
- Readiness fails on header lag (`node/src/metrics.rs:785-787`).
- A `-restoreopreturns` pass waits for a tip that is behind the best header (`node/src/chain/state_strip.rs:616`).
- Verification progress and the getheaders locator start from the inflated height (`state.rs:3128`, `node/src/net/sync.rs:17`).

The fake headers stay in the block index for good. A restart clears the inflated height, since startup seeds it from the best-header rows only (`state.rs:890-908`), but the next header from the same peer raises it again.

Fixes #896.

## Problem

`gettxoutsetinfo` accepted `hash_type`, `hash_or_height` and `use_index` and ignored all three: `gettxoutsetinfo none 154000` answered with the tip's stats, and `gettxoutsetinfo muhash` with no `muhash`, in replies that look like answers.

## Change

satd keeps no per-height UTXO stats and no UTXO-set hash, so the handler now reads the arguments and refuses what it cannot honour, following Core's `gettxoutsetinfo` (`src/rpc/blockchain.cpp`):

- `ParseHashType` first: an unknown `hash_type` is `-8 '<x>' is not a valid hash_type`.
- `hash_or_height` is parsed as Core's `ParseHashOrHeight` (negative height, height above the tip, `ParseHashV` length/hex errors, `-5 Block not found`, `JSON integer out of range`, the `get_str` type error).
- A block that is not the tip gets Core's error for a node without coinstatsindex: `-8 Querying specific block heights requires coinstatsindex`. The tip, named by height or hash, is still answered, after Core's two named-block checks (`hash_serialized_3 hash type cannot be queried for a specific block`, `Cannot set use_index to false when querying for a specific block`). If a block connects between the check and the read, the reply's `bestblock` no longer matches and the call is refused with the same error rather than answered for the new tip.
- An explicit `muhash` or `hash_serialized_3` is refused by name (-8). An omitted `hash_type` or `"none"` answers exactly as before, so plain callers (the TUI, the MCP tool) are unaffected.
- Mistyped `hash_type` / `use_index` now get Core's type error through `Args::check`.

issues.body:
Split from #892, which keeps the `bogosize` fix and the documentation for 0.6.x.

`gettxoutsetinfo` accepts `hash_type`, `hash_or_height` and `use_index` but ignores them, so every call answers for the tip. For example, `gettxoutsetinfo none 154000` returns the stats at the tip (154963 in the #892 example), and `gettxoutsetinfo muhash` returns no `muhash`. A caller asking for a historical height gets the tip's numbers in a reply that looks like an answer.

`node/src/rpc/indexes.rs:126` already notes that the arguments are ignored, and `getindexinfo` reports `coinstatsindex` as never synced so a client that polls the index first stops there. A client that calls `gettxoutsetinfo` directly gets no such protection.

## Change

Until satd keeps per-height UTXO stats, refuse by name what it cannot honour. This is the pattern `CORE_DIFFERENCES.md`'s "Optional RPC arguments satd does not yet act on" table already uses:

- refuse a `hash_or_height` that does not name the tip;
- refuse an explicitly supplied `hash_type` of `muhash` or `hash_serialized_3`;
- keep today's reply when `hash_type` is omitted or `"none"`, so plain `gettxoutsetinfo` calls are unaffected;
- add the method to the table.

## Why 0.7.0 and not a patch release

Calls that return a (wrong) answer today would start returning an error. `STABILITY_POLICY.md` treats that as a validation tightening (§2) and keeps the permissive behaviour as the default (§4), so it belongs in a minor release with a release-notes entry, not in 0.6.x.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #1120.

**Stacked on #1127** (`fix/addrman-tried-group-cap`); both PRs touch `AddrEntry::is_terrible`. Merge order: #1129, then #1127, then this one, retargeted to `master` before #1127 merges.

## Problem

The address book is keyed by `SocketAddr` and cannot hold onion peers, so onions learned from `addrv2` go on `connect_peer_addrs`, capped at `MAX_ONION_CONNECT_ADDRS` (512). That list was first come, first kept. One outbound peer that answered `getaddr` with 512 onions filled it on its first message, and every onion gossiped after that was refused until a restart. The only removal was `addnode … remove`. For an `onlynet=onion` node this list is the whole outbound candidate set apart from the seeds.

## Change

This is the smaller fix that #1120 suggests. Moving onions into the address book is out of scope.

- Each learned onion gets a record (`onion_candidates`) with Core's `AddrInfo` fields that `IsTerrible` reads: last seen, last success, last try, failed attempts. The record also holds the onion's **source**: the network group of the clearnet peer that announced it, or the announcing onion peer's own host. The reconnect loop's onion dials update the record (`note_onion_dial`, called from `spawn_redial`).
- **Per-source share:** one source holds at most `MAX_ONION_ADDRS_PER_SOURCE` = 64 (an eighth of the list), as Core bounds a source group to `ADDRMAN_NEW_BUCKETS_PER_SOURCE_GROUP` of its new buckets (`src/addrman.h:25`). Seeds count against no source.
- **Eviction:** when the list is full, a new onion takes the place of a learned one that is terrible (Core's `IsTerrible`, `src/addrman.cpp:49-70`, now a shared free function in `addrman.rs`). The dropped onion must not be connected or being dialled, and must not be a peer the operator named. Its backoff state goes with it. This mirrors `AddSingle` overwriting a terrible entry (`src/addrman.cpp:581`). If nothing is terrible, the new onion is refused as before.

## What happens

The address book is keyed by `SocketAddr` and cannot hold `.onion` peers. Onion addresses learned from `addrv2` go into a separate in-memory list instead, `connect_peer_addrs`, capped at `MAX_ONION_CONNECT_ADDRS` (512) (`node/src/net/manager.rs:83-88`).

## What happens

With `-proxy` set, satd doesn't query its DNS seeds. To avoid resolving names locally, it bootstraps from compiled-in `.onion` seeds only (`node/src/net/dns.rs`, `resolve_seeds_with`). Its fixed seeds are `.onion` too.

So a proxied node whose `-onlynet` leaves out onion (for example `proxy=…` with `onlynet=ipv4`) has no built-in way to find peers. A fresh node like that needs `-seednode` or `-addnode`. Since #992, satd warns about this at startup, and it's listed in CORE_DIFFERENCES.md.

## Expected

Core still seeds through the proxy. `ThreadDNSAddressSeed` adds each seed hostname as an address-fetch connection (`AddAddrFetch`), which `-proxy` dials by name, so the proxy resolves it. The node gets addresses on any reachable network, without a local DNS lookup. satd should do the same: open a short-lived connection to each seed name through the SOCKS5 proxy, send `getaddr`, and keep the answers on reachable networks. ## What happens

An Electrum connection may hold at most `DEFAULT_MAX_SUBS_PER_CONN` (1000) scripthash subscriptions (`electrum-proto/src/config.rs:30-36`). The 1001st `blockchain.scripthash.subscribe` gets error code 3, `subscription cap reached (1000)` (`electrum-proto/src/subscribe.rs:163-165`, `electrum-proto/src/error.rs:152-155`).

A desktop wallet subscribes, on one connection and for every loaded wallet:
- every address it has ever used;
- plus the gap-limit window, on both the receive and change chains.

A wallet with a few hundred transactions of history, or a few accounts open together, passes 1000. Its sync then fails partway through, and the user sees no reason why. The doc comment says 1000 "clears realistic wallets", and it does not.

## Why the obvious fix is not enough

The server-wide registry, `-addrindexsubscriptions`, defaults to 10,000 (`node-index/src/config.rs:12`). Every Electrum connection and every Esplora SSE stream share it. With today's defaults, 10 full connections exhaust it (`electrum-proto/src/config.rs:159-176`, test `the_defaults_let_ten_connections_fill_the_registry`).

Raising only the per-connection default, to 10,000 say, would let one wallet take the whole registry, and every other client would be refused. The two defaults have to move together.

Both values can be configured, and the manual explains how to size them (`docs/manual/src/electrum.md:246-262`). But a node with default settings should serve a normal wallet without tuning.

1. Measure what one subscription costs: a registry entry plus a spawned forwarding task (`subscribe.rs:167-178`). Pick the defaults from that measurement rather than a guess.
2. Raise `DEFAULT_MAX_SUBS_PER_CONN` to cover a large single-user wallet, on the order of 10,000.

## Problem

`-alertnotify` was installed late in startup, after the chain had loaded and any `-reindex` had run, and `NodeWarnings::record` fires the hook only when an id first becomes active. A warning raised before the install, such as `reindex.halted` or `reindex.short`, showed in `getwarnings` but never ran the command.

Core has no such window. `AlertNotify` (`src/node/kernel_notifications.cpp:30`) reads `-alertnotify` from `gArgs`, and `KernelNotifications::warningSet` (`:80-85`) calls it whenever `Warnings::Set` inserts a new warning (`src/node/warnings.cpp:29-34`). issues.body:
`-alertnotify` is wired up after the startup reindex has already run, and it does not catch up on warnings that are already active. A warning recorded during a `-reindex` shows up in `getwarnings`, but its `-alertnotify` command never runs.

## Where

- `satd/src/main.rs:1513` runs `reindex_from_flat_files` for `-reindex`.
- `satd/src/main.rs:1851` installs the notifier: `chain_state.warnings().set_alert_notifier(alert_tx)`.
- `node/src/warnings.rs:177` (`set_alert_notifier`) only stores the sender. `record` fires the hook only the first time an id becomes active, so a warning that became active before the sender was installed never fires.

The two warnings a reindex can raise are both affected:

- `reindex.halted`: a block cannot be replayed from the block files, and the chain above it will be re-fetched from peers.
- `reindex.short` (#504, #882): the block files end below the tip the node had before the reindex.

Both mean the node is about to sync part of the chain from peers instead of from its own files. That is the case an operator running an unattended reindex wants to hear about.

The comment above the `reindex.halted` record (`node/src/chain/state.rs`, in `reindex_from_flat_files`) says the warning "reaches `getwarnings`/`-alertnotify`". Only the first half is true.

## Fix

One of these:

- Have `set_alert_notifier` fire once for every warning already active when it is installed. This also covers any other warning recorded earlier in startup.
- Install the notifier before the reindex runs.

Either way, a test should record a warning, install the notifier afterwards, and assert the command runs.

## How it was found

While fixing #504. The first draft of the `reindex.short` docs said it reached `-alertnotify`; tracing the startup order showed it cannot, and the claim was taken out before #882 merged.

`submitpackage` accepted a parent below the relay floor or the rolling minimum fee only when it was a zero-fee parent with one ephemeral dust output. Any other below-floor parent was refused even when its child paid for both. That rules out Lightning's force close once mempool fees rise past a commitment's signed feerate. Closes #973, with #1011 (persistent key) and #1015 (onion `-externalip`).

## What was wrong

Tor removes an `ADD_ONION` service when the control connection that added it closes. satd connected to the control port once, at startup. A Tor that was not up yet, or that restarted later, left the node without a hidden service until satd was restarted. The node also kept advertising the dead address in `addr`, `getaddr` replies and `getnetworkinfo.localaddresses`: `advertised_onion` had no code path that cleared it.

## The fix

`node::net::tor::HiddenService` holds the control connection in a task, as Core's `TorController` does (`src/torcontrol.cpp`):

- **When the connection closes**, the address is withdrawn (Core's `disconnected_cb` → `RemoveLocal`). The task waits 1 s, then 1.5× longer each time up to 600 s (Core's `RECONNECT_TIMEOUT_START/EXP/MAX`). It then reconnects and adds the service again with the saved key, so the service comes back at the same address.
- **An onion `-externalip`** is advertised while the node's own service is down, and replaced by the node's own service while that is up.
- **Unlike Core**, a failed authentication or `ADD_ONION` is retried on the same backoff. Core stays connected and gives up. The backoff resets only once the service is up, so a persistent auth failure costs one attempt every 10 minutes.

The first attempt still runs inline at startup.

## Tests

issues.body:
## What happens

With `-listenonion=1`, satd creates its hidden service with `ADD_ONION NEW:ED25519-V3 ... Flags=DiscardPK` (`node/src/net/tor.rs:252`). Several things follow:

- **The onion address changes on every restart.** Tor never returns the private key, so the next start creates a new service. Peers that learned the old address keep gossiping a dead one, and an operator can't publish a stable address for their node. Core saves the key to `onion_v3_private_key` in the datadir and reuses it (`src/torcontrol.cpp`).
- **The control connection is made once, at startup** (`satd/src/main.rs:2836-2890`). If Tor isn't up yet, or restarts later, satd logs the failure and never retries. Core's `TorController` reconnects with backoff and re-adds the service.
- **`advertised_onion` is never cleared** (`node/src/net/manager.rs:1659-1665` is the only writer). After Tor restarts and the service is gone, satd keeps advertising the old address in `addr` / `getaddr` replies and in `getnetworkinfo.localaddresses`.
- **`externalip=<x>.onion` is a startup error** (`satd/src/config.rs:2392-2395`). That breaks Core's documented manual hidden-service setup, where the operator configures the service in `torrc` and tells the node its address with `-externalip`.

## Expected

Match Core: persist the key in the datadir with mode 0600 and reuse it; reconnect to the control port with backoff and re-add the service; withdraw the advertised address while the service is down; accept an onion `-externalip`.

Fixes #976.

## What was missing

satd never warned when blocks signalled a soft fork it didn't know about. Core does, in `Chainstate::UpdateTip` (`validation.cpp:2902-2913`), outside IBD. The check is `CheckUnknownActivations`: a BIP 9 machine for each of the 29 version bits (`WarningBitsConditionChecker`, `versionbits.cpp:299-345`), with:
- start 0 and no timeout,
- the retarget interval as the period (2016 blocks, 144 on regtest),
- a threshold of 90% on mainnet and 75% on test chains.

A block counts towards a bit when all of these hold:
- it is a version-bits block and sets the bit,
- it is at or above `MinBIP9WarningHeight` (711648 on mainnet, 2013984 on testnet3, 0 elsewhere),
- `ComputeBlockVersion` would not have set that bit itself.

A locked-in bit goes into the UpdateTip log line. An active bit sets "Unknown new rules activated (versionbit N)".

## Fix

- **`versionbits::UnknownBitsMonitor`** runs that machine for all 29 bits in one walk per period.
  - States are cached by period end, as Core's `m_warning_caches` keeps them. The first check walks about 120 periods on mainnet; after that a check reads only the tip's own period.
  - The expected-version mask is `testdummy`'s bit while it is started or locked in, computed per `testdummy` window, since that window (144 on regtest) differs from the warning period.
- **`PeerManager::check_unknown_versionbits`** runs the monitor on `spawn_blocking`, one run at a time, outside IBD. It runs when the tip moves, and every 10 s, which catches a same-height reorg.
  - An active bit is recorded in `NodeWarnings` under `versionbits.unknown.<bit>`. That puts it in the `warnings` of `getblockchaininfo`, `getmininginfo` and `getnetworkinfo`, and fires `-alertnotify` once.
  - A locked-in bit is logged once, with Core's message.
  - The warning clears if a reorg takes the activation away.
- `ChainState` implements `BlockView`.

## What was wrong

DNS and fixed seeds were tried once, at startup, and only when the address book had nothing reachable (or with `-forcednsseed`). A node back on a stale `peers.dat` skipped seeding entirely. If every address in the book was dead, it stayed at zero outbound peers until a restart.

The new `node::net::seeding` runs both seed sources in the background, as Core's `ThreadDNSAddressSeed` and the fixed-seed fallback in `ThreadOpenConnections` do (`src/net.cpp`).

- Added at once when DNS seeding is off and no `-seednode` or `-addnode` is set.

## What happens

DNS seeds and fixed seeds are queried once, at startup, and only when the address book is empty (or with `-forcednsseed`) (`satd/src/main.rs:4518-4567`). Nothing else calls `resolve_seeds*` or `fixed_seeds_for_network`.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #972.

## What was wrong

`IbdScheduler::detect_stalls` handled a peer that stopped delivering its assigned blocks by calling `peer_disconnected` on it. The peer stayed connected, which had several effects:
- Nothing marked it ineligible, so the same tick's `assign_all_peers` could hand it the heights it had just failed to deliver.
- Blocks it was still sending arrived unrequested.
- `peer_disconnected` erased the peer's per-height cooldowns, which are the record meant to keep it away from those heights.

Separately, a height handed to another peer kept the first request's `in_flight_at`. So the 15 s near-cursor timeout could release the height from a peer that had only just been asked, and charge that peer a failure.

## Fix

- **Disconnect the stalling peer**, as Core does ("Peer is stalling block download", net_processing.cpp:6095-6107).
  - `take_stalled_peer` returns the longest-idle peer past the stall timeout, takes its blocks back, and doubles the timeout. The cap is Core's `BLOCK_STALLING_TIMEOUT_MAX` (64 s).
  - The IBD tick takes peers until none is left and disconnects each with `disconnect_by_id`. Each later peer is judged against the doubled timeout, so a node whose own link is slow drops one peer rather than all of them.
  - `connect_cursor_advanced` takes 15% off the timeout, down to the existing 15 s floor, as Core's `BlockConnected` does (net_processing.cpp:2074-2082).
  - `detect_stalls` is removed; its two tests now use `take_stalled_peer`.
- **Time each holder from its own request.**
  - A new `requested_at` records when the current holder was asked; every hand-off resets it.
  - The holder's timeouts (15 s near the cursor, 60 s elsewhere) run on `requested_at`.
  - The 60 s guard still runs on the height's first request (`in_flight_at`), so a height no peer delivers is still released however often it moves.
  - Only the holder's own timeout records a failure against it.

## Tests

Each test below fails with its piece of the fix reverted:
agent_prs.title: net: disconnect a peer stalling initial block download (#972)

issues.body:
## What happens

`IbdScheduler::detect_stalls` (`node/src/net/ibd.rs:426-443`) handles a peer whose assigned blocks have stopped arriving by calling `peer_disconnected` on it, but the peer is still connected. That has three side effects:

1. Its slots are removed and its heights go to the front of `pending`, but nothing marks the peer as ineligible. On the same 2 s tick, `assign_all_peers` (`node/src/net/manager.rs`, called from the IBD tick) filters only on `Connected`, so it can hand the stalled peer a fresh set of heights, possibly the same ones it just failed to deliver.
2. Blocks the peer was still sending arrive as unrequested. The peer's real queue can exceed the 16-block limit, and the same block may be downloaded twice.
3. `peer_disconnected` also clears the peer's entries in `height_peer_cooldown` (`ibd.rs:415-420`). That table exists to keep a peer away from heights it failed on. A stall erases exactly the history it should record.

`in_flight_at` is kept across hand-offs on purpose (doc comment at `ibd.rs:398-404`). After a stall, the next holder inherits the old timestamp and can be released by the near-cursor timeout almost immediately, so a healthy peer can be penalized for the stalled peer's delay.

## Expected

Core's equivalent (`net_processing.cpp`, the block-download stall timeout) disconnects the stalling peer. satd should either do the same, or keep the peer connected but out of the assignment pass and keep its cooldowns. A height handed to a new peer should get a fresh `in_flight_at`. The 60 s `release_stale_inflight` guard the comment describes should key on the height's first request, not on the current holder's.

## Notes

This is a sync-speed and bandwidth problem, not a correctness one: IBD still completes. Found by code reading at ec66331c. A regtest test with a peer that accepts getdata and never answers should show the reassignment.
issues.title: IBD: a stalled peer is treated as disconnected, keeps its connection, and can be reassigned work on the same tick

Fixes #977.

## What was wrong

`invalidate_block` marked the block and its descendants `Invalid`, then ran a single reorg from the tip to the best valid candidate. When that candidate was a competing branch and reconnecting it failed, `abort_reorg` restored the pre-reorg tip, which was a block just marked `Invalid`. The node stayed on it and refused every block extending the real best chain until a restart ran `reconcile_invalid_tip`. The retry path is gated on `best_header_beats_active_tip`, which this state defeats.

## Fix

Core's `InvalidateBlock` first disconnects down to the invalidated block's parent, then calls `ActivateBestChain`. satd now does the same:
- When the block is on the active chain, a truncating `reorg_to(parent)` runs first. It reconnects nothing.
- Then `activate_best_chain` runs. If it fails on the competing branch, `abort_reorg` returns to the parent. The failing block's subtree is marked invalid, as before, when the failure is a verdict on the block.
- A truncation failure is mapped to the same partial-success error as an activation failure, since the marks are durable either way.

issues.body:
## What happens

`invalidateblock` marks the block and its descendants invalid (`node/src/chain/state.rs`, `mark_subtree_invalid` in `invalidate_block`) and then activates the best valid chain. If that activation is a reorg onto a competing branch and reconnecting the branch fails, `reorg_to` calls `abort_reorg` (`state.rs:9671-9686`), which restores the old tip. That old tip is a block that was just marked invalid.

The node is then left with an active tip it has itself marked `Invalid`. The retry path is gated on `best_header_beats_active_tip`, which this state defeats, so the node doesn't move. Every block that extends the real best valid chain is refused until a restart, when `reconcile_invalid_tip` fixes the tip.

The existing test (`state.rs` around line 12218) checks the RPC's error text but not where the tip ends up.

## Expected

Core's `InvalidateBlock` disconnects one block at a time down to the invalidated block's parent before it looks for another candidate. If `ActivateBestChain` then fails on the competing branch, the node still stands on a valid tip (the parent) and the failed branch is marked invalid. satd should fall back the same way: when the reconnect fails, end on the invalidated block's parent, not on the pre-invalidation tip.

Found by code reading at ec66331c. A regtest test should build a competing branch with an invalid block, invalidate the active tip, and assert the tip and `getchaintips` afterwards.

The shutdown watch already stopped the JSON-RPC listeners accepting new connections (each listener has a bridge on it, and open keep-alive connections close gracefully). ## What happens

At shutdown, satd stops the JSON-RPC server last (`satd/src/main.rs:5010`). That happens after the chainstate flush, the clean-shutdown marker, the mempool dump, the peers.dat dump and the banlist flush (`main.rs:4892-5008`).

During that window the RPC server still accepts requests. A `sendrawtransaction` admitted after the mempool dump is lost. A `setban` after the banlist flush is answered as accepted but isn't flushed. Reads may see state that is in the middle of being written.

`readiness()` (`node/src/metrics.rs`) failed only when the connector had given up or the tip trailed the best header by more than six blocks. A node that has lost every peer hears of no new headers, so it showed no lag and `/readyz` kept answering 200 while its tip aged.

- `NotReady::TipStall`: "no block has connected for longer than -alerttipstallseconds";
- `NotReady::PeerFloor`: "fewer connected peers than -alertpeerfloor".

## What happens

`readiness()` (`node/src/metrics.rs:684-711`), which backs `/readyz`, fails in two cases only: the connector has given up (`CONNECT_PERSISTENT_FAILURE`), or the header tip is more than `READY_LAG_BLOCKS` ahead of the chain tip.

A node that has lost every peer passes both checks. It has no new headers, so it shows no lag. `/readyz` keeps answering 200 while the tip gets hours old, and a load balancer or orchestrator keeps sending it traffic: wallets get stale balances and fee estimates.

Each `getblocktemplate` transaction now carries two fields from Core (`src/rpc/mining.cpp`, `getblocktemplate`):

`getblocktemplate` emits each transaction with `data`, `txid`, `fee`, `sigops` and `weight` (`node/src/rpc/mining.rs:255-268`). Core also emits:

- `hash`: the transaction's wtxid (`src/rpc/mining.cpp`, `tx.GetWitnessHash()`).

agent_prs.body:
Closes #975.

`decode_varint` (`node/src/storage/coinview.rs`) ORed each byte's low 7 bits in at `shift`, and failed only once `shift` reached 64. The tenth byte lands at `shift = 63`, where only its lowest bit fits in a `u64`. A terminating tenth byte with any higher value bit set lost those bits in the shift, and the function returned `Some(truncated)`.

It now returns `None` in that case. The coin and undo readers already treat `None` as a corrupt record (`UndoDecodeError::Truncated` in `undo.rs`; `None` from `Coin::decode`). Only satd's own records are decoded this way, so this can't be reached from the network.

**Test**: `varints_fill_a_u64_and_no_more`. It round-trips every boundary value up to `u64::MAX` (which encodes as ten bytes ending in `0x01`). It refuses `ff×9 02` and `ff×9 7f`, an eleventh byte, and a varint that runs off the end. With the check removed, it fails.

issues.body:
## What happens

`decode_varint` (`node/src/storage/coinview.rs:92-106`) ORs each byte's low 7 bits in at `shift` and fails only after `shift` reaches 64. The 10th byte arrives at `shift = 63`. If it terminates (high bit clear) with any of its upper 6 value bits set, those bits are shifted out of the `u64` and silently lost, and the function returns `Some(truncated)` instead of `None`.

This reader only decodes satd's own coin records, so it can't be triggered from the network. But a corrupt record would decode to a wrong amount or height instead of failing, and the storage layer elsewhere fails closed on corruption.

## Expected

Return `None` when the 10th byte has any bit above bit 0 set (or more generally, when `byte & 0x7F` has bits that don't fit at the current shift). Add a unit test with a 10-byte input whose last byte is `0x02`.

## What

Closes #544, and covers the IBD half of it too.

- **Steady state.** The block processor's `Err(e)` arm logged `Block rejected` and charged no one. A peer could re-serve the same invalid block on every request cycle.
- **IBD.** A block is stored on arrival and judged only when the connector reaches it. A block that failed then was marked invalid, but by that point the sender was unknown, so it was never charged.

issues.body:
Found during the deep review of #541.

`block_tx` carries only the `Block` — the `PeerId` is dropped at the channel
boundary. So the normal-mode block processor's error arm is:

```rust
Err(e) => tracing::warn!(%hash, "Block rejected: {}", e)
```

No ban score, no attribution, no metric. A peer feeding invalid or
witness-mutated blocks can re-serve the same forgery on every
`request_missing_blocks` cycle indefinitely, and the only evidence is repeated
warn lines with no indication of where they came from.

It cannot poison the index — nothing is persisted on a `check_block` failure —
and an honest peer's copy still lands, so this is bandwidth and CPU waste
rather than a stall. But it is invisible, and it is the one place where satd
has strictly less peer accounting than the IBD path right next to it (which
does penalize, score 10 of 100).

Fix is to carry the `PeerId` alongside the block through the processing
channel and penalize on `ChainError::Validation`, matching what the IBD arm
already does.

## Problem

**#894.** satd's automatic dial pass (`dial_automatic_peers`, `node/src/net/manager.rs`) walked `learned_addrs` in order and skipped a candidate only if it was excluded by `-connect`, already connected or being dialled, banned, or backing off. The network group (`group_fn` in `addrman.rs`, replaced by `-asmap`) was used for address-book bucketing only. Addresses learned together often sit in one /16, so several outbound slots could go to one operator's nodes. Core collects the group of every manual, full-relay and block-relay-only outbound peer on IPv4/IPv6 (`src/net.cpp:2654-2690`, v31.1) and skips any candidate in a group already present, feelers excepted (`src/net.cpp:2829`).

The group is the address book's (`AddrMan::group_key`), so `-asmap` groups by ASN. Inbound peers, feelers

satd opens automatic outbound connections without Core's rule that no two of them share a network group: the /16 for IPv4, the /32 for most IPv6, or the ASN under `-asmap`. Without it, one operator holding addresses in a single /16 can fill several of a node's outbound slots. Making that expensive is the point of the rule, since filling the outbound slots is the precondition for an eclipse attack.

## Evidence

- On a synced testnet4 node, 11 of its 23 outbound full-relay peers were in a single /24. They disconnected within 8 ms of each other because the remote side closed them, and the node dropped from 23 peers to 12 at once.

Fixes #922

## Problem

`ChainState::accept_block` stores a block whose parent is not the tip as `DataStored`. When no chain can be activated yet (the parent's block has not arrived), it returned `BlockAcceptance::Stored` without touching the best header. The stored-tail drain connects stored blocks along the best-header chain (`next_block_to_connect` reads the height rows above the tip), so a block that reached the node as a block, never as a header, was not on that chain. Once its parent arrived and connected through the normal path, nothing reached the child: it stayed `valid-headers` in `getchaintips`, and `getblockchaininfo.headers` did not count it, until another block or header moved the best-header chain past it.

Bitcoin Core indexes the header of every block it accepts: `AcceptBlock` calls `AcceptBlockHeader` (`src/validation.cpp:4307`), whose `BlockManager::AddToBlockIndex` (`src/validation.cpp:4232`) raises `m_best_header` to any entry with more work (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:249`). `ReceivedBlockTransactions` parks a block whose parent lacks data in `m_blocks_unlinked` and makes it a candidate once that data arrives (`src/validation.cpp:3790-3823`), so `ActivateBestChain` connects it.

## Fix

The stored path of `accept_block` now commits the block's index entry through the header path, `commit_accepted_headers_locked` (the body of `commit_accepted_headers`, split out for a caller that already holds `accept_lock`). A stored block with more work than the current best header becomes the best header, `headers` counts it, and the height rows above the tip are re-derived along it exactly as for a header from `submitheader` or a peer. Once the parent connects, the existing stored-tail drain connects the child. A stored block with no more work than the best header leaves it alone (first seen wins, as for headers). A stored child that fails to connect is marked invalid by the drain and the header tip moves back off it (#957).

## Problem

`dump_mempool` wrote `mempool.dat` in the pool's hash-map order (`get_all_entries()`), and `load_mempool` re-admitted the records sorted by entry `time` only, which has one-second resolution, keeping file order on a tie. - `DumpMempool` takes `pool.infoAll()` (`src/node/mempool_persist.cpp:169`) and writes it as is (`:196`).

issues.body:
## Summary

A clean restart loses most of the mempool. `load_mempool` re-admits `mempool.dat` records in `time` order, but `time` has one-second resolution, and ties keep file order. `dump_mempool` writes `get_all_entries()` in map order, which is not parent-first. So a child that shares its parent's second is often tried before the parent. It fails with `missing-inputs`, and every descendant behind it fails too.

Each restart makes this worse. Re-admission gives the txs it accepts a fresh `time`, so thousands of them end up in the same few seconds. On the next restart, most parent/child pairs are ties.

## Evidence

On a synced mainnet node (0.6.0), over two consecutive clean restarts:

| restart | persisted | re-admitted | skipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 46,711 | 15,825 | 30,886 (66%) |
| 2 | 36,121 | 13,799 | 22,322 (62%) |

After restart 2, I parsed the `mempool.dat` it had loaded and ran each record through `testmempoolaccept`:

- 20,030 `missing-inputs`
- 19,871 of those have their parent **in the same file**
- in 14,959 of those, the parent has the **same `time`** as the child
- no case where the parent's `time` is later than the child's

The file has 1,935 distinct timestamps for 36,121 records. The largest same-second group is 1,883 txs, all stamped during restart 1's re-admission.

Nothing in the log shows this, because `load_mempool` discards the error (`Err(_) => stats.skipped += 1`). The only trace is the `skipped=` count.

## Expected

Like Bitcoin Core, a restart should keep everything that is still valid. Core avoids this by writing `mempool.dat` in topological (depth) order.

## Suggested fix

- **Write parents first** in `dump_mempool` (topological / ancestor-count order), and/or have `load_mempool` order ties by in-file parent dependency. A retry pass for `missing-inputs` would also work, but costs more.
- **Keep each tx's original admission time** on reload instead of stamping the reload time, so `time` stays meaningful (and so does mempool exp

Fixes #931.

A full `-reindex` empties the database before it scans the block files. `ChainState::new` then took the empty store for a new datadir: genesis was not in the block index, so it appended the genesis block to the last block file.
- Every reindex left a duplicate genesis record behind, 293 bytes on signet.
- On a datadir switched from Bitcoin Core, the duplicate went into one of Core's files.

Seen on signet: after `--reindex` over a 324,463-block datadir, the last file had grown by exactly one genesis record.

## Change

On an empty store, `ChainState::new` reads the first record of `blk00000.dat`, through the `xor.dat` key. If its payload is the genesis block byte for byte, it indexes genesis there and writes nothing.

- satd and Core both write genesis as the first record of `blk00000.dat`.
- A datadir whose files do not begin with genesis still gets it written: a new datadir, a pruned one, or one without `blk00000.dat`.
- The `-reindex-chainstate` branch (#201), which reuses the position the kept block index records, is unchanged.

Core reaches the same result another way. During `-reindex` it reads genesis from `blk00000.dat` and records the position it finds it at. After reindexing it calls `LoadGenesisBlock` once more as a fallback, which writes nothing when the files held genesis.

The #504 coverage check's comment mentioned the append; it now says the append happens only when the files do not begin with genesis. The check's logic does not depend on the append: without it, a missing file stays a gap, and the check reports the gap.

issues.body:
## What happens

A full `-reindex` empties the database before it scans the block files. `ChainState::new` then opens an empty store and can't tell it apart from a brand-new datadir: genesis is not in the block index, so it writes the genesis block again (`node/src/chain/state.rs`, the `Fresh node: store genesis block` branch). The record goes to the end of the highest-numbered `blk*.dat`, 293 bytes on signet.

So every full reindex adds a duplicate genesis record to a block file it otherwise only reads.

- The rest of the reindex writes nothing to the block files. A reindex that is stopped and continued (#915) does not append it again.
- On a Bitcoin Core blocks directory, the file it writes to is one of Core's. This undercuts the claim that switching from Core leaves Core's block files untouched.

Seen on signet: after `--reindex` over a 324,463-block datadir, the last file had grown by exactly one 293-byte record.

## How Core does it

Core writes genesis only when the block files do not hold it. At startup it calls `LoadGenesisBlock` only once the block files are indexed (`src/node/chainstate.cpp`). During `-reindex`, the import loop reads genesis from `blk00000.dat` and records the position it found it at. After reindexing, `ImportBlocks` calls `LoadGenesisBlock` once more as a fallback, which does nothing when the files held genesis (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp`).

#201 already stops the append for `-reindex-chainstate`, by reusing the genesis position the kept block index records. A full `-reindex` keeps no block index, so it still appends.

## Fix

On an empty store, read the first record of `blk00000.dat`. If its payload is the genesis block byte for byte, index genesis at that position and write nothing. Otherwise append as today, which covers:
- a brand-new datadir;
- a pruned one;
- a blocks directory without `blk00000.dat`.

Both satd and Core write genesis as the first record of `blk00000.dat`. `xor.dat` is honoured by the read.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #916.

A flat-file `-reindex` plans its chain from the block headers alone. Its phase 1 scan still read every `blk*.dat` whole (`std::fs::read`) to get them. On mainnet that is the whole chain, about 700 GB, before the first block connects. Since #915 a continued reindex paid that again on every start.

## Change

- `FlatFileManager::for_each_block_header` walks the same records as `for_each_block`, and ends a file on the same zero-padding and length checks. It reads each record's 8-byte framing and up to 80 header bytes, then seeks to the next record.
- Reads are 4 KiB: a block larger than that costs one read, and smaller blocks share reads. Each read is de-obfuscated at its file offset, so an `xor.dat` blocks dir works as before.
- The reindex scan uses it and logs the `bytes_read`. The plan comes from the same records as before. `check_resumable_prefix` compares the stored entries with the scan's map in memory, so a continued reindex reads no more than a fresh one.
- One behaviour change: a read error partway through a file now ends that file there, with a warning. Before, a failed `fs::read` dropped the whole file without a word.

## Why headers only, not skipping the files below the stored tip

The issue offered both. Skipping the early files still means checking each stored entry against them. The issue proposes doing that by reading the header at each recorded position, which is the same one small read per block the header scan makes. Skipping would also need:
- a fallback for out-of-order blocks and more-work branches in early files;
- a fingerprint of the files kept in the rebuild marker.

The header scan makes the same reads without any of that. Its plan matches a full scan's by construction, and it speeds up a fresh reindex too.

Not measured: the issue's caveat that on a hard drive, one seek per large block may cost about as much as reading the files sequentially.

Follow-up to #906 (PR #915), which continues an interrupted full `-reindex` from the height it had flushed.

## What it does now

A continued run plans the chain the same way a fresh reindex does. Phase 1 scans every block file, and `FlatFileManager::scan_one_file` (`node/src/storage/flatfile.rs:823`) reads each file whole with `std::fs::read` to parse the record headers. Only after that does the resume check run and the connect continue.

On mainnet that means reading all of the block files again, about 700 GB, on every start that continues a reindex:
- On a hard drive at a typical 150 MB/s, that is more than an hour before the first block connects.
- On the SD cards and USB drives app-store boxes use, it takes longer.
- A replay that is stopped several times pays it each time.

A fresh reindex pays it once as well, but the repeat is the problem here.

## What it should do

Either or both of these.

**1. Skip what the interrupted run already indexed.**

The block index holds every block the run connected up to height H, with its header and file position, and the resume already checks those entries against the block files. Reading the files again only matters for blocks above H. The scan could start at the file holding the stored tip, or the lowest file holding a block above it, instead of at `blk00000.dat`.

Open points:
- **Out-of-order blocks.** Blocks are not stored strictly in height order, because parallel download writes some out of order. A block above H can sit in an earlier file. When the plan finds a block above H whose parent has not been scanned, it has to scan back for it, or fall back to a full scan.
- **More-work branches.** The plan picks the most-work branch over every record. A branch that forks below H and has more work can live in an earlier file. The first run's scan already chose against those records, so the resume can trust that choice only if the files have not changed since. One way to know: record in the rebuild marker what the first scan

## The problem

0.6.0 refused every start after an interrupted full `-reindex` except one with `--reindex`, and that start wiped the database and replayed from genesis. A mainnet replay takes days, so every stop, reboot or settings change during one threw the work away. A package that passes `--reindex` once, as StartOS's migration from Bitcoin Core does, was left with a node that would not start.

## The change

You chose this behaviour: **any start that finds an unfinished full reindex continues it, whatever the flags.**

**How it continues.** `resume_reindex_from_flat_files` scans the block files and plans the chain exactly as before. Before connecting anything, `check_resumable_prefix` checks every block the interrupted run stored against the scan:
- the stored tip is the planned block at its height;
- each entry at or below it is `Valid` at its planned height, with the header the files hold, at the file position the scan found;
- each entry's chainwork is the sum of its ancestors' header work.

What the continued replay reads from those entries (parent links, chainwork, the timestamps behind median time past) is then backed by the block files, as in a replay from genesis. It then connects the rest. Nothing is downloaded and no block file is written. The check costs one index read per stored block.

**When it can't continue.** The rebuild marker gains `resumable`. It is set once the wipe has finished and genesis is indexed and flushed durably, which is just before the scan. Three cases run the reindex again from genesis instead, still on any start:
- a marker without the flag: one 0.6.0 wrote, or one written before its wipe had finished;
- a marker at another chainstate schema;
- a stored chain that fails the check. satd exits 1 with `ReindexCannotResume`, having changed nothing, and clears `resumable`; the next start runs from genesis.

issues.body:
Found by Start9's intake review of the StartOS package (https://github.com/Start9-Community/satd-startos/pull/1, "Blocked on", item 1). The package switches a node from Bitcoin Core to satd by keeping Core's block files and running one `--reindex` over them.

## What Start9 saw (0.5.2)

Their setup was a Core-synced signet datadir with `chainstate/` removed, running `satd --chain=signet --reindex`. The replay was killed (SIGKILL) at block 231,797 of 322,806. On restart:
- satd had no record of the 91k blocks still on disk;
- it went back to network IBD from its last flushed tip, downloading about 600 MB in three minutes;
- it wrote the re-downloaded blocks to new `blk00149+.dat` files next to the originals.

On mainnet that means hundreds of gigabytes downloaded and stored twice.

## What 0.6.0 does instead

#848 added a rebuild marker. An interrupted full `-reindex` is now refused on the next start (`satd/src/main.rs:132-145`, "Restart with --reindex to rebuild them from the block files"), so the network fallback and the duplicate block files are gone.

The interruption still costs the whole replay, though:
- **The restart needs `--reindex` again.** A package that passes it once, as Start9's one-shot does, leaves a node that refuses to start until something re-arms the flag.
- **`--reindex` then starts over.** `reindex_from_flat_files` (`node/src/chain/state.rs:5994`) rescans every block file and connects from genesis, even though the chainstate on disk was flushed partway (`DURABLE_FLUSH_EVERY`).

A full mainnet replay takes days, and a long replay is likely to be interrupted (#907 covers SIGTERM during a replay). So on a StartOS or Umbrel box, every stop, reboot or settings change during the replay throws all the work away.

## Expected

An interrupted full `-reindex` continues from where it stopped, from the block files on disk:
- it keeps the chainstate flushed so far;
- it connects the remaining blocks without downloading any;
- it writes no new block files.

## The problem

satd registered its SIGTERM and SIGINT handlers only when startup finished, and the block replays of `-reindex`, `-reindex-chainstate` and `-upgradechainstate` run inside startup. Until then a stop signal had its default effect:

- satd as PID 1 of its PID namespace (a container with no init): the kernel drops the signal, so `docker stop` waits out its grace period and SIGKILLs the replay. This is what Start9 saw.
- Anywhere else: the signal kills the replay at once, part-way through a batch.

Found by Start9's intake review of the StartOS package (https://github.com/Start9-Community/satd-startos/pull/1, "Blocked on", item 2):

> SIGTERM is ignored while connecting blocks. `docker stop` with a 600 s grace period ran the full 600 s and killed it. StartOS sends SIGTERM and kills after the package's `sigtermTimeout`, so any stop, reboot or settings change during the reindex produces #1. Seen on the StartOS box too, on an ordinary sync.

Their "#1" is #906: an interrupted full `-reindex` starts over.

## During a replay

satd has no SIGTERM handler while `-reindex`, `-reindex-chainstate` or `-upgradechainstate` runs:
- **Where the replay runs.** It runs synchronously during startup: `reindex_from_flat_files` at `satd/src/main.rs:1532`, `reindex_chainstate` at `:1563`.
- **Where the handler is registered.** The only SIGTERM handler on that path is registered after both, at `satd/src/main.rs:4415`. The other one, in `fast_start.rs:130`, is local to the snapshot download.

So SIGTERM gets its default disposition for the whole replay, which can mean either of two things:
- **satd is PID 1 of its PID namespace, with no init in front of it.** The kernel drops default-action signals sent to a namespace's init, so SIGTERM is ignored until the supervisor's SIGKILL. That matches the 600 s `docker stop`. The published image puts `tini` in front of satd (`Dockerfile:240`), so this depends on how the container was started; a package that execs `satd` as its entrypoint gets this.
- **Anywhere else.** SIGTERM kills the process at once, mid-batch, the same as SIGKILL.

Neither is a graceful stop. Either way the replay ends unclean and #906 then throws it away.

The handler exists by then, and Start9 still saw the stop run out its timeout on a StartOS box. Not yet explained. It needs a measurement of how long shutdown takes after SIGTERM during IBD, and what it waits on: the connect thread finishing its batch, the final flush of a large `dbcache`,

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #909. For 0.6.1, on `release/0.6`.

The manager loop's maintenance pass is where IBD stall handling lives:
- the release of a height stuck with one peer (15 s at the connect cursor);
- `detect_stalls`;
- the drop of silent peers;
- work for idle peers.

Its cadences count passes ("every 4 ticks (2s)"), so the pass has to run every 500 ms. During initial block download it hardly ran at all.

## Cause

The cause in the issue holds, but it is not the whole story:
- **#781's fast drain sets `drain_only`.** So every run of fast drains ends in a wait for the next tick, and the pass after that tick finds the queue full again.
- **Every drain is slow during IBD.** The manager stores each arriving block itself (`handle_block_ibd` → `store_block`), at one fsync per block (#539). So a drain of 64 blocks takes hundreds of milliseconds on a slow disk.

A first fix that only stopped the fast drain from setting `drain_only` still left maintenance every ~9 drains. On a disk with 9 ms fsyncs that is ~5 s apart, so stall detection, every 4 passes, came round every ~20 s. It made no visible difference on mainnet.

## Change

`DrainPacer` decides after each drain:
- **Maintenance is due** on an interval tick, as before, or once 500 ms have passed since it last started. It then runs after the drain in progress, however full the queue is, at most one drain (64 events) late.

Fixes #900. For 0.6.1, on `release/0.6`.

A block that reached the tip through the stored-tail drain (`connect_stored_tail`) was connected without `ChainEvent::BlockConnected`. Two cases put a block there:
- a block that arrived before its parent;
- the stored tail an IBD batch leaves when it tears down (#582).

Everything that learns of new blocks from chain events missed it:
- `-blocknotify`;
- block announcement to peers;
- Electrum header and scripthash subscriptions;
- Esplora `/blocks/sse`;
- the streaming API and the ZMQ `hashblock` topic.

## Change

**The drain emits the event.** The drain now connects through `ChainState::connect_stored_block_and_report`. After the connect, and before releasing `accept_lock`, that call drops the block's transactions from the mempool and emits `BlockConnected { hash, height }`. `accept_block` does the same, in the same order and under the same lock.

The lock matters for event order. An earlier revision emitted from `connect_stored_tail` after the lock was released. A `submitblock` of the drained block's child could then connect and report in between, and subscribers would hear of the child before its parent (found in review).

`connect_stored_block` still emits nothing, because the IBD connector uses it too and stays quiet, as the issue scopes. `emit_chain_event` stays private.

**`-stopatheight` keeps its explicit check in the drain.** The watcher in `main` now hears of drained blocks, but asynchronously. Without the check, the walk would connect the rest of its batch (up to 24 blocks) before shutdown landed, so it stays and stops the walk at the target.

Both paths now ask for shutdown at the target. The watcher uses `send_if_modified`, so the second request neither logs "-stopatheight reached" again nor wakes shutdown waiters twice.

## Tests

- **`the_stored_tail_drain_reports_each_block_it_connects`** (unit, `node/src/net/manager.rs`): drains a three-block stored tail and asserts exactly one `BlockConnected` per block

agent_prs.body:
Two issues that share a shape: a harness race that will flake other people's PRs, and the test debt the Core-functional wave left behind. Both are about the tests rather than the node, which is why they are one PR.

Closes #695, #673, #703 and #704.

## #695 — the shim must not tee a process that exits

The `bitcoind` shim gives satd a `debug.log` by teeing its stdout from a forked child, while satd itself `execv`s in the parent (the framework reads `/proc/<pid>/fd` for `get_bind_addrs`, so satd has to *be* that process). Nothing synchronises the tee with satd's exit. The framework waits on satd's pid and reads the stdout file straight afterwards: a node that runs for seconds is long drained by then, but a process that writes once and exits can lose the race outright, and the test sees an empty stdout and reports it as a satd defect.

`-h`, `-help`, `-?` and `-version` are the only invocations in the run set that print one thing and exit, which is why `feature_help.py` is the only test that shows it. None of the shim's four jobs apply to them — nothing greps a help dump for a log line — so they now exec straight through with no tee.

The invariant is stated at the fork and in the harness README, because the next print-and-exit invocation added will hit exactly this: **the tee is only safe for a process that outlives the reader's first look.**

`tests/test_shim_bitcoind.sh` pins it, and runs in the existing `Inventory` job. It asserts a print-and-exit invocation leaves *no* `debug.log` behind — which is what proves the tee was skipped, rather than merely having won the race that time — while an ordinary node start still gets one, and `-help-debug` is not mistaken for a print-and-exit flag.

Verified: `feature_help.py` passed 6/6 with the machine deliberately loaded, and the full run set is green (35/35 rows).

Partially addresses #660; closes the mempool half of #671.

Fourth in a four-PR stack, based on #711. **Merge order**: #709 → #710 → #711 → this. The remaining #660 item — the full feerate-diagram comparison — follows in its own PR, which is why this one does not close it.

## Rule 5 counted conflicts, not clusters

Core's Rule 5 bounds how much of the mempool one replacement can force it to re-sort: no more than `MAX_REPLACEMENT_CANDIDATES` — 100 — distinct *clusters* may be directly conflicted (`GetUniqueClusterCount`, `policy/rbf.cpp`). A cluster is a connected component of the spend graph, so a hundred and one transactions that all descend from one parent are one cluster and Core accepts the replacement. satd counted the conflicts themselves and refused it.

The count floods the component in both directions — children through the spend index, parents through each entry's inputs — and short-circuits once the limit is exceeded, because Rule 5 exists precisely to keep that walk bounded.

The descendant walk that follows is bounded too. It runs under the mempool write lock, where an unbounded walk is a stall a peer can ask for; Core relies on the cluster rule for the same bound ("the cluster count limit ensures that we won't do too much work on a single invocation of this function"). The ceiling is derived from Rule 5 — 100 clusters × the cluster size limit — rather than reusing the cluster limit directly, so it cannot refuse a replacement Core would accept.

- **The relay floor.** `sendrawtransaction` gated on the base fee while `testmempoolaccept` gated on the modified fee, so the two disagreed about a prioritised transaction — one of #660's bullets. Core's `CheckFeeRate` takes `ws.m_modified_fees` on both.
- **Eviction.** `entry.fee_rate` is the rate as of admission and no delta ever rewrote it, so a transaction an operator deliberately lifted was evicted as though the lift had not happened.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #660.

Last of the 0.5.2 close-out stack, based on `fix/702-remaining-placeholders` (#720).

## A replacement was compared against the wrong thing

satd compared a replacement's feerate against each conflicting transaction's **own** feerate. That misses what a miner actually sees: a cheap transaction carrying an expensive child is one *chunk*, taken or left together. Beating the parent alone is not beating the chunk, so satd was accepting replacements that made the mempool worse to mine.

Bitcoin Core's rule is `ImprovesFeerateDiagram` — and in v31.1 it is the *only* rule of its kind, run for every replacement (`ReplacementChecks`); the old `PaysMoreThanConflicts` is gone. The mempool the replacement leaves behind must be no worse anywhere and better somewhere, comparing cumulative fee-against-size curves.

The concrete case, and the new regtest test:

- parent: 1,000 sat over ~110 vB (~9 sat/vB), signalling replaceability
- child: 500,000 sat spending the parent → the pair is one chunk at ~2,300 sat/vB
- replacement: conflicts with the parent, pays **505,000 sat — more in total than parent and child combined** — spread over ~90 outputs, so ~170 sat/vB

It clears RBF rules 3 and 4 and is still refused, with Core's `replacement-failed`. Under the old rule its 170 sat/vB beat the parent's 9 and it went straight in.

## What's ported

`node/src/mempool/feefrac.rs` is Core's `util/feefrac.cpp`: `FeeFrac`, `FeeRateCompare`, `CompareChunks`, kept structurally identical so it can be diffed against the original. Two details worth calling out:

- **Comparisons are exact integer cross-products, never divisions.** Dividing to get a feerate first rounds, and a rounded feerate makes the verdict depend on transaction size in a way no policy intends.
- **The arithmetic is widened to `i128`.** A mainnet-scale fee times a block-scale size overflows `i64`, and the release profile has no overflow checks — it would wrap silently into the opposite verdict. There is a test that pi

issues.body:
RBF replacement accepts transactions that make the mempool worse for a miner, and the conflict walk is unbounded.

### Feerate-diagram approximation is not conservative
`node/src/mempool/pool.rs` compares a replacement only against each *direct conflict's own* feerate, never against the CPFP'd chunk that conflict belongs to. A low-feerate parent lifted by a high-feerate child presents as cheap, so a replacement can evict a chunk worth more to a miner than what replaces it. Core's `ImprovesFeerateDiagram` compares chunks.

### Rule 5 counts transactions, not clusters
Core counts distinct clusters against `MAX_REPLACEMENT_CANDIDATES`; satd counts conflicting transactions. Stricter, so not a safety problem, but it rejects replacements Core accepts and the divergence is undocumented.

### The conflict + descendant walk is unbounded
The 100-conflict cap bounds only *direct* conflicts. `max_descendant_count` is declared, defaulted and SIGHUP-reloadable but never read. A small replacement of a pre-built subtree root walks the whole subtree under the mempool write lock and then rejects — so the work is done on behalf of a transaction that never enters.

### Smaller
- `incremental_relay_fee * vsize` can overflow; the parser accepts any bare `u64` where Core caps at `MAX_MONEY`.
- The `prioritisetransaction` delta reaches mining selection but not the relay floor or the eviction sort key. Core uses modified fees for both.
- `testmempoolaccept` and `sendrawtransaction` compute different ancestor feerates, so one can say allowed while the other rejects — the exact disagreement `testmempoolaccept` exists to prevent.
- Deferring `Dust` past the fee check routes non-standard transactions into the orphanage: a dusty transaction with unknown parents returns `MissingInputs`, and the net layer then orphans it and fetches parents. Core never does this.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #661. Closes #670.

Bottom of a four-PR stack; **merge in order**: this → #663 → #662 → #660-bounds.

## Dust thresholds were wrong for every script type

Core's `GetDustThreshold` adds 67 vbytes to spend any witness program — `32 + 4 + 1 + 107/4 + 4` — and 148 for anything else, then rounds the fee **up**. satd added 68 for the three witness types it knew by name, 107 for P2SH, 68 for everything else, and truncated.

| script | satd | Bitcoin Core |
|---|---|---|
| P2PKH | 546 | 546 |
| P2SH | 417 | **540** |
| P2WPKH | 297 | **294** |
| P2WSH / P2TR | 333 | **330** |
| P2A | 333 | **240** |

The 330 row is the one that bites: Lightning anchor outputs are built against it, and a node that calls 330 dust refuses a commitment transaction its peers relay. The P2SH row is a 123-satoshi window in which satd relayed outputs Core drops.

The classification now branches on `IsWitnessProgram` as Core's does, so pay-to-anchor and future witness versions are priced as witness spends. Core's own table is pinned as golden vectors.

## The dust *rules* were wrong too

Core splits them three ways: `IsStandardTx` permits one dust output (`MAX_DUST_OUTPUTS_PER_TX`), `PreCheckEphemeralTx` requires a dusty transaction to pay nothing at all, and `CheckEphemeralSpends` requires a child to sweep it. satd refused *every* dust output on the single-transaction path and enforced the zero-fee rule only inside `submitpackage`, with the strings written out by hand — `MempoolError::EphemeralDustFee` existed but was never constructed.

Both paths now share one `pre_check_ephemeral`, which reads the `prioritisetransaction` delta as well as the base fee (Core's `base_fee != 0 || mod_fee != 0`). It is gated on `require_standard` as Core gates it, and joins the exemptable standardness set an `allow` rule can forgive.

issues.body:
The ephemeral-dust rules introduced alongside `submitpackage` are enforced on one path only, and the dust definition itself diverges from Core.

### Enforced only inside `accept_package`
`sendrawtransaction` and the P2P acceptance path have neither check. The two new error variants are never constructed anywhere — dead code, and a fair signal the policy is half-wired.

### A failed child strands a zero-fee dust parent that we then mine
The dust parent is committed to the mempool before the child is validated, and `assemble_template` has no `blockmintxfee` floor. A child that fails validation leaves the parent behind, and the miner ships it. That is precisely the UTXO-bloat vector ephemeral dust exists to prevent.

### The dust threshold does not match `GetDustThreshold`
`node/src/mempool/policy.rs`: P2TR is 333 sat where Core says **330** — the canonical taproot limit Lightning anchor outputs are built against — and P2SH is 417 where Core says **540**.

### `-dustrelayfee` is ignored
All three dust helpers hardcode the constant rate instead of reading `cfg.dust_relay_fee`, so `-dustrelayfee=0` still triggers ephemeral-dust rules, and `prioritisetransaction` refuses transactions the node does not itself consider dust.
