agent_prs.body:
Closes #806.

## What happened

The nightly block-differential fuzzer reported a satd/Core consensus divergence on the first scheduled run after the transaction-ordinal re-keying (#800–#805) landed:

```
satd_accept=false core_accept=true
block_hex=0000002006226e46111a0b59caaf126043eb5bbf28c34f3a5e332a1fc7b2b73cf188910f...
```

The block is a coinbase-only block sitting directly on regtest genesis. There is nothing wrong with it, and nothing wrong with how satd validates it.

## Why

The harness builds its shared base from `InMemoryStore::new()` — an empty store. That was a fine fixture until `connect_block` began reading the parent's cumulative transaction count to number a block's transactions. That read is deliberately fail-closed: a missing row is storage damage, and guessing zero would mis-key every index row in the block against every other block.

An empty store has no row for genesis, so satd rejected *every* block the fuzzer built, for a storage reason. Core accepted the valid ones. The first structurally valid block the fuzzer produced therefore looked like a consensus divergence.

`fuzz/` is a standalone workspace excluded from the parent, so `cargo test --workspace` and clippy never compile it. CI does compile-check it (`cargo check --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml`), and that passed throughout — this was a semantic gap in a fixture, not a type error.

## The fix

Seed the row a real chainstate holds at genesis, so the base models a chainstate rather than a bare map. Genesis holds exactly one transaction.

Also self-check the fixture at startup. A base missing a row `connect_block` needs makes every iteration look like a divergence, which is exactly how this got filed against consensus when the fault was in the harness two lines above. Failing at startup routes it to the broken-harness bucket, which files nothing against consensus and says what is actually wrong.

Fixes #723. **Independent of #795/#796** — branches off `master`, no stacking.

One 20 MiB constant governed both directions of the JSON-RPC pipeline:

```rust
.max_request_body_size(RPC_MAX_BODY_SIZE as u32)
.max_response_body_size(RPC_MAX_BODY_SIZE as u32)
```

Its own doc comment justifies the number entirely in *request* terms — Core's
functional suite sends `echo` two 8 MiB arguments, which a 10 MiB cap rejects.
A request-shaped budget ended up policing replies.

A reply's size is not set by the caller. `getrawmempool verbose` crosses 20 MiB
at roughly **17,000** mempool transactions, which is an ordinary mainnet
mempool, not a fee-spike condition — past that satd answers `-32008 Response is
too big`, *after* building the reply, where bitcoind answers the call. I
confirmed the Core side from source rather than assuming:
`evhttp_set_max_body_size(http, MAX_SIZE)` (`src/httpserver.cpp:410`) bounds the
request body; `WriteReply` has no cap.

#723 estimates the threshold at ~40,000 transactions from a ~0.5 KB entry. Real
entries measure **1,183 bytes** mean (random sample, n=120, against a synced
mainnet node) — the `depends` and `spentby` arrays carry 64-char txids and CPFP
clusters make them long — so the true threshold is ~17,000. That is the
difference between a latent edge case and a node that has been failing this
call continuously.

## What changes

The request cap is **unchanged** at 20 MiB. That one is the DoS guard: it bounds
what a caller can make the node buffer before it has decided anything.

Replies get their own bound, `RPC_MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE`, at 256 MiB — derived
rather than picked. Verbose mempool JSON measures about 0.76x the mempool's own
serialised bytes, so the default `-maxmempool=300` (286 MiB) tops out near
217 MiB of reply. The guarantee this buys: *a node at its default mempool
ceiling can answer `getrawmempool verbose`*.

Two things I want stated rather than buried:

- A node configured with a larger `-maxmempool` can still outgrow the b

issues.body:
satd caps every JSON-RPC reply at 20 MiB. Bitcoin Core has no reply cap at all. A reply that Core serves in full is answered by satd with jsonrpsee's `-32008 Response is too big`, and the compatibility layer's documented fallback for that case is unreachable.

## Where the cap is

`node/src/rpc/server.rs` builds one `ServerConfig` for every listener with `max_response_body_size(RPC_MAX_BODY_SIZE)`, and `RPC_MAX_BODY_SIZE` is 20 MiB (`node/src/rpc/mod.rs`). jsonrpsee 0.26 enforces it when it serialises the **whole** reply envelope (`MethodResponse::response` writes through a `BoundedWriter`), and again per batch (`BatchResponseBuilder::append`). A reply that does not fit is replaced by an error object:

```
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32008,"message":"Response is too big","data":"Exceeded max limit of 20971520"}}
```

The compatibility layer then maps the unknown code to HTTP 500 (`core_http_status`), so a Core-style client sees a 500 with a JSON-RPC error it has never heard of.

## What hits it

Anything whose result grows with the chain or the mempool rather than with the request:

- `getrawmempool true` — one entry is on the order of half a kilobyte, so a mempool of roughly 40,000 transactions crosses the cap. Mainnet mempools exceed that routinely during fee spikes. Core answers the call; satd answers `-32008`.
- `getblock <hash> 3` on a full block (prevout data on every input), `scantxoutset` over a busy descriptor, and batches of large `getblock` calls, all of which can be pushed past 20 MiB by chain data alone.

## The documented fallback cannot run

`node/src/rpc/compat.rs` (`oversized = resp_bytes.len() > MAX_NORMALIZE_BODY`) forwards a reply over the cap in jsonrpsee's 2.0 shape instead of DOM-parsing it to JSON-RPC 1.0. `MAX_NORMALIZE_BODY` is the same 20 MiB, and jsonrpsee has already replaced any reply larger than that with the error above, so the branch is dead code. The 0.5.2 release notes ("A very large response is no longer DOM-parsed")

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #792.

## What happens

A node following a peer in BIP 152 high-bandwidth mode stops syncing and stays stopped.

```
Starting parallel block download target_height=431 blocks_to_download=95
IBD download: 336/431 stored, 0 in-flight, 95 pending, 1 peers
IBD download: 336/431 stored, 0 in-flight, 95 pending, 1 peers
IBD download: 336/431 stored, 0 in-flight, 95 pending, 1 peers
```

Ninety-five blocks pending, one peer that has every one of them, and nothing is ever requested.

## Why

`assign_peer_work` will not give a peer heights above what the node believes that peer holds, and returns early when that belief is at or below the connect cursor:

```rust
let Ok(max_height) = u32::try_from(peer_height) else { return };
...
if max_height <= scheduler.connect_cursor() {
    return;
}
```

The belief is Bitcoin Core's `UpdateBlockAvailability`, and it was updated in exactly one place — `handle_headers`. A high-bandwidth peer announces new blocks with `cmpctblock` **instead of** `headers`, so `accept_compact_header` was the only thing that saw those announcements, and it recorded nothing. The node learned the headers, raised its target, and kept believing the peer held only what its last `headers` message had said.

With several peers another one eventually carries the download. With one — a regtest pair, or a node with a single upstream — nothing else ever calls `assign_peer_work` and the wedge is permanent.

## Blast radius

This is why CI has been red across unrelated branches since 2026-09-17, including a dependabot lockfile bump:

- `feature_bip68_sequence.py` fails in `activateCSV`, whose `sync_blocks` is exactly this shape — `Block sync timed out`, at 240 s and again at 480 s, because a stall is not cured by a bigger budget.
- The Stratum V2 Job Declaration canary fails with `satd did not sync Core's chain`. Its uploaded node log is the one quoted above.

Master's own canary last ran 2026-09-14, before high-bandwidth relay (#770) landed on 09-16, which is why

File ".../feature_bip68_sequence.py", line 397, in activateCSV
    raise AssertionError("Block sync timed out after {}s:".format(
AssertionError: Block sync timed out after 480s:
```

## It is not the timeout

The budget was 240 s (`SATD_CF_TIMEOUT_FACTOR: 4`) for the first three failures. It was raised to 480 s to test the hypothesis that a slow hosted runner was the cause. It failed again at 480 s.

## It is not the code under test

Two runs of the same job, minutes apart, on branches where one commit range strictly contains the other:

| commit | contains the other | Core functional |
|---|---|---|
| `53c768a5` | — | **failed**, `feature_bip68_sequence.py` 504 s |
| `e77674cd` | yes, plus five more commits | **passed**, whole run set in 2m26s |

The whole run set finishing in 2m26s on one runner while a single test in it stalls past 480 s on another is not a linear difference in machine speed. The same job also fails this way on unrelated branches — a dependabot lockfile bump among them.

## Where to look

The chain is ~432 blocks at that point, so this is inside the window where [#740](https://github.com/epochbtc/satd/issues/740) applies: `assign_peer_work`'s "peer too far behind to be a useful source" test is `peer_height < target_height - 1000`, evaluated in `i64`, which on a chain shorter than 1000 blocks is a condition no peer can fail. The shape — a short regtest chain, a block download that never completes, no progress rather than slow progress — is the same.

Fixes #744.

`verificationprogress` was the tip's timestamp divided by the current time, both counted from 1970, so a node at genesis reported 0.688. `getchainstates` gave the background chainstate a height ratio instead. Both entries, and `getblockchaininfo`, now compute Bitcoin Core's `GuessVerificationProgress`.

## What Core does, and what this ports

From `src/validation.cpp` and `src/kernel/chainparams.cpp` at v31.1, the pinned Core release. The formula is unchanged since v30.

- `ChainTxData` per network, copied exactly: the cumulative transaction count at a time, and the rate after it. A custom signet has none. Regtest has a rate of 0.001 and nothing else.
- Progress is the block's cumulative transaction count over `tx_count + (now - time) * rate`. Past the snapshot count it is over `count + (now - block_time) * rate`, capped at 1.
- A block within two hours of the clock uses `now - (best_header - height) * 600` as its time, so a synced tip is exactly 1, and a header above it drops it below 1.
- 0.0 when the block has no count.

The estimate is a pure function in `node/src/chain/verification_progress.rs`, operation for operation. `ChainState::verification_progress` feeds it from the index and the node clock.

## A difference Core doesn't have

Core's best header is never below its active tip. satd's headers tip can be, for blocks that arrive whole rather than header-first (`submitblock`, a local miner). Using it as is failed the two-hour branch, and a just-mined regtest tip read 0.99999 where Core reads 1. The best header is now the larger of the two.

## Verification

Differential against **bitcoind v31.1** (the release binary, checksum-verified), same chain, same clock:

- Regtest: 150 blocks mined by Core and submitted to satd. With both clocks mocked to the tip plus 0 s, 1 s, 1 h, 7199 s, 7200 s, 7201 s, 1 day, 1 day + 1 s, 1 year and 10 years, plus a clock before the tip, `getblockchaininfo` and `getchainstates` are equal at Core's printed precision.

agent_prs.title: rpc: verificationprogress is Bitcoin Core's GuessVerificationProgress

issues.body:
`getblockchaininfo` and `getchainstates` report `verificationprogress` as the tip's timestamp divided by the current time, both in seconds since 1970 (`node/src/rpc/blockchain.rs`):

```rust
"verificationprogress": if is_ibd { time as f64 / now as f64 } else { 1.0 },
```

So a node at genesis reports **0.688**, and the figure moves under two points per year of blocks. A mainnet block from 2015 reads 0.794, where even time since genesis would give 0.339. Anything that shows the field as a percentage tells a user starting a multi-day sync that it is two-thirds done. The StartOS package's **Blockchain Sync** health check did exactly that.

The background chainstate's entry in `getchainstates` uses a third definition, a height ratio against the snapshot height.

## Core

`ChainstateManager::GuessVerificationProgress` (`src/validation.cpp`, v31.1):

- It counts transactions. The block's cumulative transaction count is divided by an estimate of all transactions to date, which comes from a per-network `ChainTxData` snapshot (count, time, rate) in `src/kernel/chainparams.cpp`.
- A block within two hours of the clock is positioned by its height against the best header (`now - (best_header - height) * 600`) instead of its timestamp. A synced node reads exactly 1, and drops below 1 as soon as a new header arrives.
- It returns 0.0 when the block's transaction count is unset.
- `getchainstates` applies the same function to each chainstate's tip.

satd already keeps cumulative per-block transaction counts (`getchaintxstats` reads them), so the formula can be applied as is.

## Expected

Values equal to Core's for the same chain and clock, on every network. No test asserts the field today.

agent_prs.body:
Two issues that share a shape: a harness race that will flake other people's PRs, and the test debt the Core-functional wave left behind. Both are about the tests rather than the node, which is why they are one PR.

Closes #695, #673, #703 and #704.

## #695 — the shim must not tee a process that exits

The `bitcoind` shim gives satd a `debug.log` by teeing its stdout from a forked child, while satd itself `execv`s in the parent (the framework reads `/proc/<pid>/fd` for `get_bind_addrs`, so satd has to *be* that process). Nothing synchronises the tee with satd's exit. The framework waits on satd's pid and reads the stdout file straight afterwards: a node that runs for seconds is long drained by then, but a process that writes once and exits can lose the race outright, and the test sees an empty stdout and reports it as a satd defect.

`-h`, `-help`, `-?` and `-version` are the only invocations in the run set that print one thing and exit, which is why `feature_help.py` is the only test that shows it. None of the shim's four jobs apply to them — nothing greps a help dump for a log line — so they now exec straight through with no tee.

The invariant is stated at the fork and in the harness README, because the next print-and-exit invocation added will hit exactly this: **the tee is only safe for a process that outlives the reader's first look.**

`tests/test_shim_bitcoind.sh` pins it, and runs in the existing `Inventory` job. It asserts a print-and-exit invocation leaves *no* `debug.log` behind — which is what proves the tee was skipped, rather than merely having won the race that time — while an ordinary node start still gets one, and `-help-debug` is not mistaken for a print-and-exit flag.

Verified: `feature_help.py` passed 6/6 with the machine deliberately loaded, and the full run set is green (35/35 rows).

issues.body:
`feature_help.py` failed once in a local full run and passed 3/3 immediately afterwards on an idle machine. The failing run overlapped with another build on the same box, which is the tell: this is a load-sensitive race in the harness, not a satd defect.

**What fails.** `assert b'Options' in output` (`feature_help.py:42`) — the framework read the node's stdout file and found it empty. `ret_code` had already asserted 0, so satd started, printed its help and exited cleanly.

**Why.** `shims/bitcoind` gives satd a `debug.log` by teeing its stdout, and satd has to end up as *this* process so the framework can read `/proc/<pid>/fd` for `get_bind_addrs`. So the shim forks, hands the child the pipe's read end plus the real stdout, points its own stdout at the write end, and `execv`s satd:

```
parent -> execv(satd)          stdout -> pipe write end
child  -> for line in pipe: log.write(...); sys.stdout.write(line)
```

Nothing synchronises the child with the parent's exit. The framework waits on satd's pid — the parent — then immediately seeks and reads the stdout file. For a long-running node that is harmless: by the time anything reads the file the tee has been draining for seconds. For a process that writes once and exits, `process.wait()` can return before the child has copied a single line, and the test reads an empty file.

`-h` and `-version` are the only invocations in the run set that exit immediately, which is why `feature_help.py` is the only test that shows it. Both are in that one file, and it exercises them twice.

**Fix.** Those invocations need no `debug.log` — nothing greps a help dump. Skipping the tee for them and `execv`ing straight through removes the race for exactly the cases that hit it, and leaves every real node start on the existing path. `-h`, `-help`, `-?` and `-version` are the set.

issues.body:
The desk v2 tab icon is wrong in four ways. One goal fixes all four: the right icon on the first paint.

1. ERPNext, Gameplan, the `/apps` index and Frappe's own desk show the grey Frappe square (`frontend/index.html:21`, `frappe-framework-logo.svg`). Their tabs look the same, although each app declares a `logo` in `add_to_apps_screen`.
2. Desk v2 ignores the site's favicon (Website Settings → Favicon). Desk v1 shows it (`frappe/www/desk.html:33`).
3. CRM shows the Frappe square first, then its own icon: `applyAppFavicon` (`frontend/src/shell/appFavicon.ts`) waits for the boot fetch.
4. The grey square has low contrast on dark tab bars. v1's `frappe-favicon.svg` changes with `prefers-color-scheme`.

## Owner rulings (2026-11-11)

**Order of precedence.** For an app prefix:
1. The app's `brand` favicon (`app_brand(app)["favicon"]`, site data such as FCRM Settings)
2. The app's `logo` from `add_to_apps_screen`. Skip this step for `frappe`: its logo is the grey framework square, so Frappe's own desk falls through like v1's `/desk`.
3. The Website Settings favicon
4. `/assets/frappe/images/frappe-favicon.svg` (adapts to dark mode)

For the `/apps` index: steps 3 and 4.

**Set on the server.** `ShellPage` writes the resolved href into the document's `<link rel="icon">` for each prefix, so the icon is right before any JS runs. Remove `applyAppFavicon`, its call in `main.ts` and the `app_favicon` boot key, unless something else reads them. The document still does not vary by user, so `no_cache` and the per-process mtime memo (#42111) stay. Do the replace on the memoized bytes per request (or memo per prefix). Escape the href for an HTML attribute. Change the static default in `index.html` to `frappe-favicon.svg`.

issues.body:
In a desk v2 tab that was opened before a `bench build`, Cmd+K and the rail's Search button do nothing. No feedback is shown.

## Cause
- The palette loads on demand: `AppShell.vue` uses `defineAsyncComponent(() => Promise.all([import("./ShellPalette.vue"), appActsPending()]))`.
- `bench build` swaps the whole `frappe/public/frontend` directory and deletes the previous build (`frappe/bundler.py` `swap_shell_assets`). A tab loaded before the build still holds the old hashed chunk names, so its first `import("./ShellPalette.vue")` returns 404.
- Console: `TypeError: Failed to fetch dynamically imported module: .../ShellPalette-<hash>.js`. Ctrl+K (three times) and a click on the rail's Search never open the palette.
- The same failure applies to every lazy chunk the shell fetches after load: dialogs, standing windows, settings panes. Pages already handle it (`frontend/src/pages/list/renderer.ts` gives an async route component an `errorComponent` with a full reload).

## Fix
One shell-wide handler: when a lazy chunk fails to load because the build changed, show one persistent toast "A new version is available" with a "Reload" action. No auto-reload, so unsaved form edits are not lost.

## Known minor gap (out of scope)
About 200 ms after a full reload, Cmd+K is not bound yet (`PaletteKey` loads lazily).

Fixes #44699

**Cause:** in `_export_query`, both the `selected_items` and the `visible_names` branches assigned `form_params["filters"] = {"name": ("in", ...)}`, replacing every filter the report view had sent. Filters on child table fields were lost, so the export contained every child row of the chosen documents instead of only the rows matching the filter.

Both branches use it. The ordering done by `_reorder_by_visible_names` is unchanged.

**Test:** `test_export_query_keeps_child_table_filters` exports a User Group with three members as a non-admin user, filters on one child row (`User Group Member.user`) and checks that only that member is exported, for both `selected_items` and `visible_names`.

**Testing:** ran `frappe.tests.test_reportview` on a MariaDB 11.8 site: the new test fails on `develop` (all three members are exported) and passes with the fix. The only remaining error in the module is `test_export_report_via_email`, which needs a default outgoing Email Account and errors the same way without this change.

agent_prs.title: fix: keep report view filters when exporting selected or visible rows

issues.body:
## Description of the issue
Since #40854 (released in v16.50.0, exports in earlier versions were correct), the Report View export sends `visible_names` (the primary keys of the rows on screen) whenever "Export all rows" is not ticked. `_export_query` then **replaces** all filters with them:

    if visible_names:
        form_params["filters"] = {"name": ("in", visible_names)}

With child-table columns and a filter on a child-table field, this drops the child filter. The query then returns **every** child row of the visible parents, and `_reorder_by_visible_names` picks one of them per occurrence. So parent columns are correct, but every child-table column in the export holds a different child row's data than the one shown on screen.

`selected_items` has the same issue: it also overwrites `form_params["filters"]`.

#44452 changes the reorder so it keeps several rows per parent, but the filters are still replaced. A visible parent therefore still gets an arbitrary child row (`order_by` is set to `None`), not the one that matched the filter.
## Context information (for bug reports)

**Output of `bench version`**
```
erpnext 16.51.0 version-16 (fd97695)
frappe 16.52.0 version-16 (4515014)
```

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Create a Sales Invoice with three items in this order: an item from group `Services`, an item from group `Products`, another item from group `Services`.
   (Which child row ends up in the export depends on the order: up to 16.52 it's the last one, with #44452 the first one. With the `Products` item in the middle, both are wrong.)
2. Open Sales Invoice in Report View.
3. Pick Columns › section "Items (Sales Invoice Item)": add `Item` (fieldname `item_code`).
4. Add the filter `Item Group (Items)` = `Products`. The table shows one row per invoice, each with its `Products` item.
5. Menu › Export › Excel. The dialog shows no "Export all rows" option, because all rows are loaded.

### Observed result
The ID and the other Sales Invoice columns match
issues.title: Report View export ignores filters on child-table fields (`visible_names` replaces all filters)

Remember each saved-view lookup per session user, doctype and key, so a return visit to `/view/<key>` paints at once instead of blanking for one round-trip.

- `useSavedView` keeps the last `find` answer in module scope (cleared when the session user changes). A mount whose answer is remembered sets `view` synchronously and looks it up again behind the page.
- A changed answer replaces it; a refusal clears the entry and shows as before; a view not yet remembered still shows the empty frame.
- `List.vue` keys the page on the view's type and layer too, so a changed type or layer mounts the page again instead of leaving a stale `view`.
- No frontend code renames or deletes a Doctype View (only settings save/reset and favourites), so no writer needs to forget an answer; the background lookup corrects any other change.
- Cost: no new request or surface. A return visit still sends the same `find`, now off the critical path. The cache key is user + doctype + key; the permission check stays on `find`, which still answers each visit.

Owner report 2026-11-10: "When I go to notes it reloads first time which is fine then I go to tasks and again come back to notes the flicker exists the skeleton is not visible but flicker is there".

Cause (diagnosed): since crm 9bbe7020f, FCRM Note opens its app view `notes` (Cards), so the address is `/apps/crm/fcrm-note/view/notes`. On each visit `useSavedView` (`frontend/src/list/savedView.ts:29-52`) sets `view` to `null` and calls `frappe.desk.doctype.doctype_view.api.find` again. While it runs, `List.vue:9` renders an empty `PageFrame` (`opened` is null, `List.vue:47`). The rows then paint from the shared cache at once, so the only gap is the lookup's round-trip. Walk on desk.localhost:8000: the Tasks page leaves at 61 ms, `find` answers at 94 ms, Notes mounts at 140 ms. With `find` held 1.5 s, the page is blank except the rail at 500 ms. Tasks shows no gap, because its address names no view.

This applies to every list address that names a view (`/view/<key>`), not only Notes.

Expected: a return visit to a view the person opened before in this session paints at once from the remembered lookup, and the lookup runs again in the background. A changed answer replaces it; a refusal shows as it does today. Another session user starts with nothing remembered. Add a test that fails today: the second mount of `useSavedView` for the same doctype and key has `view` set synchronously.

issues.body:
Phase 2 of the settings dialog clean-up: make the shipped `Settings Dialog` files readable and give each name one meaning. It comes after phase 1, so the new checks guard the patch.

- **Native JSON in the exported files.** `fields`, `bindings`, `settings`, `anchors` and `roles` are Code fields, so each file holds JSON as a string inside JSON. Export them as native JSON, either with the `JSON` fieldtype (check how it exports first) or by writing parsed values in `export_settings_dialog`. Import must read both shapes during the change.
- **A `kind` Select (`Generated` / `Component`) on Settings Block.** Today the kind is inferred from which fields are filled. `validate_binding_shape` then checks against `kind`.
- **Rename the component block's `fields` to `saves_fields`.** It is the fields the component saves and owns. On a generated block, `fields` stays the fields it shows.
- **Rename `settings` to `search_entries`.** It holds a component's search entries.
- **Make `roles` a Table MultiSelect of `Role`**, which gives link validation.
- **A patch that rewrites the shipped files** in frappe and in frappe/crm (`crm.json`, `crm-frappe.json`), plus the CRM change on its desk-v2 branch.
- **Update `frontend/CONTEXT.md`** ("Settings Pane and Settings Block").

agent_prs.body:
Adds the creator to `_seen` when a record is inserted on a Track Seen DocType.

- `Document.insert` calls the new `add_creator_to_seen` after `db_insert` (non-Single only). It adds `frappe.session.user` to `_seen`, keeps a value set before the insert, and sets `doc._seen` in memory.
- `db_insert` does not write `_seen`, and `_validate` clears optional fields on a new doc. So the value set before the insert is read before `_validate` runs, then written with one `UPDATE` (`update_modified=False`). This also makes the `_seen` that `frappe/email/receive.py` sets for a Communication survive the insert; it was dropped before.
- A preset `_seen` that is not a JSON list of strings is ignored. A skipped duplicate insert (`ignore_if_duplicate`) leaves the existing row's `_seen` alone.
- Virtual DocTypes (Activity Log has `track_seen`) are skipped: they have no table to update.
- No change to `reset_seen` (the save rule) or `add_seen` (the read rule). Desk v1's list now shows your own new records as seen (accepted in #46873).
- Surface: no new read, no cache key, no new permission check. Cold-load cost: none. An insert on a Track Seen DocType gains at most one `UPDATE`.

No UI change.

How tested:
- New tests in `frappe/tests/test_document.py` (as `test@example.com`, not Administrator): an insert puts the user in `_seen` (in memory and in the DB); a preset `_seen` keeps its users and gains the creator; a malformed preset is ignored; a skipped duplicate keeps the existing row's `_seen`; a DocType without `track_seen` is untouched.
- `bench --site desk.localhost` via `unittest` (5 new tests: OK) and `~/wt/ui-test/server-tests.sh` on `frappe.tests.test_document` (96 tests, new ones pass; the one error, `test_save_after_insert_on_a_whole_second`, is a missing `freezegun`). `test_email_account` and `test_communication` show the same errors as on `upstream/desk-v2` (no default outgoing email account, no `freezegun`).

Part of #46871 (Desk v2 — Track Seen). Graduated from [Grilling: which records count as unseen](https://github.com/frappe/frappe/issues/46873). The rulings are in its resolution comment.

## Question

Build ruling 2 of #46873: on a DocType with `track_seen`, an insert puts the creator in `_seen`.

Scope:

- The value is written with the insert, or right after it in the same request, and the in-memory doc holds it too.

- Desk v1's list then shows your own new records as seen. This is accepted.
- No change to `reset_seen` (the save rule) or `add_seen` (the read rule).

The surface: no new read, no cache key and no new permission check. Cold-load cost: none. An insert on a Track Seen DocType gains at most one `UPDATE`.

issues.body:
Part of #46871 (Desk v2 — Track Seen). Follows #46875 (PR #46880, merged as `a34c3c27a4`). It amends ruling 2 of [Grilling: which records count as unseen](https://github.com/frappe/frappe/issues/46873), on the owner's ruling of 2026-11-10.

## Question

On insert, a Track Seen record's `_seen` holds only its creator. A value the caller sends is ignored.

Why: `add_creator_to_seen` (`frappe/model/document.py`) keeps a preset `_seen`, and `create_doc` (`frappe/api/v2.py`) passes the request body into the doc. So any user can create a record through REST with `_seen` naming other users, and the record never looks unseen to them. Before #46880, `_validate` cleared a preset. The only server preset, in `frappe/email/receive.py`, is reset by its own `save()` anyway (#46881, out of scope).

Scope:
- `add_creator_to_seen` writes `[frappe.session.user]`. Remove the preset handling, its `preset_seen` argument and the read before `_validate` in `insert`. Keep the `ignore_if_duplicate` guard and the virtual and Single skips.
- Tests: drop the two preset tests. Add one that shows a preset `_seen` sent to an insert is replaced by the creator alone. Run the tests as a normal user.

The surface: no new read, no cache key and no new permission check. Cold-load cost: none.

Done when: a PR is merged on `desk-v2`, and the tests pass on desk.localhost and on `~/wt/ui-test/server-tests.sh`.

agent_prs.body:
Opening a record wiped the list row's `_seen`, `_assign`, `_user_tags` and `_liked_by` from the shared cache, and never added the reader to `_seen`.

- A record read and a save keep those four columns from the entry they replace (`as_dict` never returns them); a part in the same reply refreshes `_assign` and `_user_tags`, and a save leaves `_seen` unchanged.

Part of #46871 (Desk v2 — Track Seen). Graduated from [Grilling: how the list learns that a row is seen](https://github.com/frappe/frappe/issues/46874). The rulings are in its resolution comment.

## Question

Build rulings 2 and 3 of #46874 in the shared cache (`ui/src/cache/`): opening a record marks its cached list row seen, and a record read or a save no longer wipes the list-only columns.

Scope:
- **Test first.** A vitest shows that a record read (`recordRead`) and a save (`documentWrite` → `replaceDoc`) wipe `_assign`, `_user_tags`, `_liked_by` and `_seen` that a list read put on the entry. `doc.as_dict()` never returns these columns, so the record reply leaves them out. If the test shows they survive today, say how, and keep only the `seen` write-back.
- **Keep the list-only columns.** The record read and the save carry `frappe.model.optional_fields` (`_user_tags`, `_assign`, `_liked_by`, `_seen`) over from the entry the reply replaces, the way `applyRow` keeps the fields a newer row leaves out. A part written in the same reply wins: `assignments` → `_assign`, `tags` → `_user_tags`.
- **The `seen` write-back.** Add a `PART_FIELDS` entry `seen` → `_seen`, in the server's JSON form (`pythonJsonList`). When the record read's envelope holds `seen`, write it onto the cached doc. The entry's `parts` still never hold `seen`.
- After a save, the row's `_seen` is carried forward unchanged (ruling 3).
- No session set, no refetch, no timing guard.

The surface: no new read, no new cache key, no new permission check. Cold-load cost: none.

Done when: a PR is merged on `desk-v2`, with vitests for the four columns surviving a record read and a save, and for `_seen` gaining the reader from the `seen` part. A list row that read `_seen` without the reader holds it after `loadRecord` lands.

## Overview

The runner re-dumps YAML that another parser reads back: the patched sandbox values (Helm), the sanitized compose file and dumped `ComposeConfig` (k8s_sandbox's converter, PyYAML) and the approval config (Inspect, PyYAML). ruamel's safe dumper writes YAML 1.2 and leaves strings bare that those parsers misread: a `?` inside a list (a URL with a query string) makes the file unparseable, so every sample fails at `helm install`; `off`/`yes` are read as booleans; and Helm reads `0o17` as the number 15. This quotes every string in those four files.

Closes #2693

## Approach

Set `default_style = '"'` on the dumper at each of the four sites. Every string is written double-quoted, so no parser has to guess its type; numbers, booleans and null are written with explicit tags (`!!int "17"`), which Helm and PyYAML both read back as their types. Writing YAML 1.1 instead (an earlier commit here) fixed `?` and `off`/`yes` but made Helm read `"0o17"` as 15, because Helm's parser mixes 1.1 and 1.2 rules; block style alone fixed only the `?` case. The compose file is still loaded as before; only its re-dump changes. The existing `test_patch_sandbox_environments` matched the values file's text (`kubernetes.io/arch: amd64`), which quoting changes, so it now checks the parsed value.

| `test_patched_values_render_through_helm_as_written` | `helm template` | fails | fails (`0o17` → 15) | passes |

agent_prs.title: fix(runner): quote strings in sandbox yaml so helm reads them as written

issues.body:
The runner re-dumps each sample's sandbox values in flow style, and Helm cannot parse the result when a list holds a string with `:` or `?`, such as a URL. Every sample of such an environment then fails at `helm install`:

```
Helm install failed. ... Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: failed to parse /tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX: error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: line N: did not find expected ',' or ']'
```

## Cause

`hawk/hawk/runner/run_eval_set.py` writes the patched values with `ruamel.yaml.YAML(typ="safe")` (the `yaml.dump(sandbox_config.model_dump(...))` into a `NamedTemporaryFile`, around line 1510). That dumper emits leaf lists in flow style and drops quotes it considers unnecessary, so

```yaml
command: [wget, -q, -O, /dev/null, "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health?probe=1"]
```

comes out as

```yaml
command: [wget, -q, -O, /dev/null, http://127.0.0.1:8080/health?probe=1]
```

which is valid for ruamel but not for Helm's YAML parser: inside a flow sequence it reads the unquoted `:` / `?` as mapping indicators. The values file the environment author wrote parses fine; only the re-dumped copy fails.

## Reproduction

`values.yaml`:

```yaml
services:
  default:
    image: busybox
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command: [wget, -q, -O, /dev/null, "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health?probe=1"]
```

```python
import ruamel.yaml  # 0.19.1

yaml = ruamel.yaml.YAML(typ="safe")
data = yaml.load(open("values.yaml"))
with open("redumped.yaml", "w") as f:
    yaml.dump(data, f)
```

`helm template t <any chart> -f redumped.yaml` (Helm 3.16.4):

```
Error: failed to parse redumped.yaml: error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: line 5: did not find expected ',' or ']'
```

## Overview

Require code access as well as model access to launch runs or read their outputs. Code access is checked the way model access already is: against groups each row carries, not by re-deriving the decision on every read. Closes #976.

## Approach

Each run's `code_policy` row records the code groups a reader needs, and every eval, job and scan row of that run carries a copy in `code_groups`. Existing triggers on main rewrite those copies in the same transaction as any policy change: rule edits, launches, imports and the #2081 backfill. Checks compare the copy with the caller's groups, as model checks compare `model_groups`:

- **Warehouse RLS:** the code check joins main's permissive `*_model_access` policy on eval, job and scan, as #976 specified. Services (`rls_bypass`, through main's bypass policy, and the API writer) pass; other roles need every group in the row's copy. There is no per-row function, and the API keeps main's index plans.
- **API reads:** listings compare the copies on the rows they already read. Single-run reads use `code_policy_has_read_access`. Two exceptions, API only: the native owner may read through their own incomplete inventory, and Hawk admins pass `__unresolved__` (missing, incomplete or pending inventories) so they can see runs that need repair; repair tooling is follow-up (PLT-1173). Admins still need named groups.
- **Writers** (launch, resume, import, approvals) use `code_policy_has_write_access`, with no exceptions. It ignores scan results not linked to a sample (normally because the sample isn't imported yet), so an online-scanning eval set or a scan can resume before its import finishes. Every source and the scan's own code are still checked.
- **Keeping copies authoritative:** deleting a policy marks its rows and dependent scans unresolved. Truncating or moving a policy is refused. Every policy keeps a positive revision. The late-result linker locks the samples it links and their source policies until commit.

issues.body:
Parent: HWK-25. Turns the feature on: applies `code_groups` at every point access is decided, reusing the model-access path. **You may see or run a thing only if you hold every group it requires — its** `code_groups` **and its** `model_groups`**.**

### Enforcement points

* **DB row-level security** — extend the existing `eval` / `scan` / `job` policies so a row is visible only when the caller's roles cover `code_groups` as well as `model_groups`. Governs direct warehouse readers.
* **Submission gate** — both the eval-set and scan create paths gate on code beside the existing model check, *before* the config is persisted. Resolve the exact dependency set the runner will install (`get_runner_dependencies_*`, incl. `model_roles`) and **refuse** if any source is unclassifiable or names a repo the caller can't hold. (Scans are code too, and are ungated today.) This is how "can't run X" is met.
* **Listing / endpoints** — extend the endpoint-gaps subset check with the code dimension. An eval-set is visible only if the caller can see every run in it (the union of all runs' groups).
* **Log reader (S3)** — serve a log only if the caller holds every group in its `.code-groups.json` (+ `.models.json`); no per-group tags. Resolve the caller's groups from the identity store (not the login token) and widen the group-prefix filter to include `code-access-`. **Fail closed on empty/unknown groups** (today it fails open).
* **Fail closed on doubt** — an unparseable URL or an errored rules/registry lookup → refuse. A successful "no rule matched" falls through to the no-rule behavior (the rules issue), not an error.

### No feature flag / non-breaking

With no rules, every repo is public, so each check is a safe no-op until the first rule exists — enforcement needs no feature flag.

### Scope

* **In:** RLS predicate extension; the submission gate on both create paths; the code dimension on listing/endpoints (builds on the endpoint-gaps issue); the log-reader `.code-groups.json` che

issues.body:
Parent: HWK-25. A one-time, **opt-in** migration that populates `repo` + `code` from **stored** eval-set / scan configs (`.config.yaml`), so the registry reflects history — not just new submissions (the passive-resolution issue).

### How

Reuse the passive-resolution resolve → normalize → upsert path over stored configs. Nothing new about the data model; this just replays it over the archive.

### Non-breaking & optional

* **Optional:** not a prerequisite. A deployment that never runs it keeps working; its registry is simply less complete (and everything stays public until rules exist anyway).
* **Non-fatal:** an unparseable / refused historical source is **skipped and logged**, never aborts the migration. "Skipped" = no `repo`/`code` row (so nothing is silently mis-attributed).
* **Reconcile step:** at the end, surface the skipped stragglers so an admin can fix the data manually or ship a follow-up parser fix. Migration-only, not a product feature.

### Idempotent

Re-runnable: upsert by identity (`(repo_id, subdirectory, registry_name, item_type)`), so re-running after a partial failure or a re-parse converges — no duplicates, no drift.

### Scope

* **In:** the one-time migration/command; reuse of the passive-resolution resolve/normalize/upsert; skip + log + end-of-run reconcile for unparseable history.
* **Out:** the normalizer, live per-submission recording, rules + `code_group` resolution, enforcement. (When rules later land, the rules API's idempotent apply recomputes `code_groups` across historical runs too.)

issues.body:
Parent: METR/hawk#632. **Security-critical.** Converts any declared package source into **one canonical identity** — a `git` repo identity (host+org+repo) or a `package_index` identity — or **fails closed**. A URL that parses but normalizes *wrong* yields the wrong `repo_id` = wrong access boundary = leak, so this is its own reviewed, fuzz-tested unit.

### Principles

* Registration and lookup use the **same** canonical form (a repo always matches its own rule).
* **Fail closed:** unparseable/unrecognized → refuse, never public. (A URL that parses but matches no rule isn't the normalizer's call — that's the no-rule behavior in the rules issue.)
* If two URLs point to the same repo, they normalize to the same string **or** one fails to parse.

### Must neutralize (from the adversarial review)

* **Same-repo aliases:** scheme (`git+https`, `git+ssh`, scp-style `git@host:org/repo`, `ssh://`), `.git` suffix, trailing slash, case, embedded credentials, explicit port, percent-encoding, dot-segments → one identity.
* **Host identity:** exact host match (no suffix matching); case / trailing-dot / port normalized; credentials from after the last `@`; IDN / homograph handling; self-hosted GitLab (variable subgroup depth) needs an explicit repo-boundary rule.
* **Sub-repo forms:** `@ref`, `#subdirectory=`, `/tree/<ref>/…`, `/blob/…` collapse to the repo identity (`ref`/`subdirectory` captured as metadata for the `code` row — recorded by the registry issue).
* **Non-degenerate identity:** host, org, repo all non-empty after normalization.
* **Matching discipline:** segment-boundary prefix (`org/hawk` ≠ `org/hawk-secret`); longest-match; errors fail closed.

### Source classification (fail closed) — incl. PyPI

Every declared source is *positively* classified as exactly one of:

* **git repo** (`git+https/ssh/http/file`, bare `….git`, scp-style, `name @ <git-url>`) → normalized `git` repo identity.
* **bare PyPI package** (bare PEP 508 name) → the shared public `pypi.org` `pack

issues.body:
### Problem

`hawk list evals` prints only the first 100 evals of an eval set, with no note and exit 0, though its help says "List all evaluations in an eval set". It asks `/meta/evals` for one page (`page=1&limit=100`) and ignores the `total` the API returns.

Walking the pages isn't enough on its own: `/meta/evals` sorts only by `created_at`, which Inspect stamps to the second, so evals of one run share a few timestamps and move between pages. On our deployment, reading the 120 evals below 50 at a time returned only 115 different ones.

### Steps to reproduce

Any eval set with more than 100 evals shows it: many tasks × models (say 26 × 4), retried tasks (each attempt is an eval), or an imported folder of logs. To make one in two minutes, with no sandbox or provider key:

1. Save this as `many.py` and run `python many.py` where `inspect-ai` is installed. It writes 120 small logs to `logs/`.

```python
from inspect_ai import Task, eval
from inspect_ai.dataset import Sample
from inspect_ai.scorer import includes

eval([Task(name=f"t{i:03d}", dataset=[Sample(input="Say hello", target="hello")], scorer=includes()) for i in range(120)], model="mockllm/model", log_dir="logs")
```

2. `hawk import logs/ --name many --yes`. It prints `Imported as <id>`
3. `hawk download <id> --list` lists 120 `.eval` files.
4. `hawk list evals <id>`

**Expected:** 120 evals, or a note that the list is cut.

**Actual:** 100 evals and exit 0. Nothing says 20 are missing.

### Fix options

- Walk the pages in the client, as `hawk list jobs` does since #2702, and sort `/meta/evals` by `created_at, pk` (an index for that exists).
- Ask for 500 rows, the API's maximum, in one request: no API change, but the list still stops at 500.
- Print "showing 100 of N" from `total`: honest, but the list stays incomplete.

**Impact:** looks like 3/5 for now. It only affects stacks upgrading from 3.x to 4.0.0, a workaround exists (below), and no data is lost.<sup>1</sup>

## Problem

3.x gives the main database account (`postgres`) an extra role. With Aurora's newer login rule, an account with that role can't log in with a password. When upgrading to 4.0.0, the deploy's database login step (`rds-db-users`) uses that password, so it's refused and the upgrade stops.<sup>2</sup> The fix for this is in #2101, but its manual step isn't in the upgrade notes.<sup>3</sup>

## Workaround

From #2101's description:<sup>4</sup>

1. Connect to the database as `inspect_admin` with an IAM token from inside the stack's VPC.<sup>5</sup>
2. Run `REVOKE "inspect_admin" FROM postgres;`
3. Check that `SELECT pg_has_role('postgres', 'rds_iam', 'MEMBER');` returns false.
4. Re-run `pulumi up` from 4.0.0.
5. Run the check from step 3 again.

## Possible fixes

1. Add a short section to `docs/infrastructure/upgrading.md` under 4.0.0, for example `### Master user locked out of the Data API (#2101)`.<sup>6</sup>

## Overview

Observability backends that read the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (token dashboards, cost views, agent-trace UIs) can't use the runner's `model.usage` and `tool` spans without a custom mapping, because those spans only carry `inspect.*` names. This PR adds the standard GenAI attribute names next to the existing ones. Every `inspect.*` attribute stays.

Closes #2240

## Approach

- **`model.usage`** gains `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`.
- **`tool`** gains `gen_ai.operation.name` (`execute_tool`), `gen_ai.tool.name` and `gen_ai.tool.call.id`. The call id is set only when the call has one, the same rule as `inspect.tool.id`.

Model names, tool arguments and tool results still stay off spans, and no other GenAI attributes are added. The `inspect.*` names stay because the GenAI conventions are still in development.

**`gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` is not a straight copy of `inspect.usage.input_tokens`.** In inspect, `ModelUsage.input_tokens` is "Input tokens charged at full rate (excludes cached tokens)", and the OpenAI provider subtracts cache reads and writes from `prompt_tokens`. The GenAI convention says `input_tokens` should include cached tokens. A straight copy would therefore undercount every cached call, and agent evals are mostly cache reads. The GenAI value is `input_tokens + cache_read + cache_write`. `output_tokens` is a straight copy.

The names are plain string literals, like the `inspect.*` ones beside them. `opentelemetry-semantic-conventions` isn't a dependency, and adding it just for constants isn't worth it.

The tracing docs table lists the new names. It also adds `inspect.tool.id`, which the table never listed.

## Risks

- **Two input-token values on one span.** `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `inspect.usage.input_tokens` differ whenever a call hits the cache. That is intended and documented, but anyone comparing the two should expect it.
- **Unstable conventions.** If the GenAI conventions rename these a

Lets a Hawk deployment serve Amazon Bedrock models from its own AWS account, with Middleman signing requests as its ECS task role and no Bedrock key stored. Closes #1184.

Bedrock now speaks Anthropic's Messages API and OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs natively, so a Bedrock lab is a row on Middleman's existing Anthropic and OpenAI routes, and runners use Inspect's stock `anthropic/` and `openai-api/` providers. This replaces the earlier OpenAI-to-Converse translator.

## Approach

- A lab with the new `credential_kind: aws_sigv4` has a Bedrock Runtime `base_url`. Instead of attaching a key, Middleman SigV4-signs the exact request bytes with its ambient AWS credentials, off the event loop. Model access, usage, errors and the traffic log are the existing route's.
- Signed requests still pass the key-host allowlist (as `AWS_SIGV4`), and the signer only signs `bedrock-runtime.<region>.amazonaws.com` hosts.
- Bedrock labs skip Anthropic accounts and priority routing, and drop the top-level automatic `cache_control` that Inspect's own Bedrock client omits. Bedrock has no `count_tokens`, so Middleman answers it with a 404 marked `x-middleman-unsupported: count_tokens`. Bedrock's 403s, which name the AWS account and task role, become a generic error.
- Model and lab writes refuse a Bedrock model that records a provider other than `amazon` or an ARN as its upstream name. The viewer's lab form can set up an Anthropic lab on Bedrock, and Bedrock's OpenAI-compatible usage, which bills as `amazon`, is priced like OpenAI's.
- `hawk:middlemanBedrockModelArns` attaches a size-checked managed policy that invokes only the listed inference profiles (their backing models only through them) and in-region foundation models, plus the `project/default` resource the Responses API invokes, and allows `AWS_SIGV4` to each listed region's host. A migration adds the credential kind.

Alternatives: the earlier translator and a native-Converse prototype were both built on

## Issue 1970: root cause

Every red perf run since October failed on one case, `stripControlMarkers on repeated block opening tags without a close` in `packages/core/src/pathological-input.perf.test.ts` (309 to 1317 ms against 200 ms, 26 of the last 30 pushes to main). The threshold was right; the code was slow:

- `MARKER_ATTRS` in `packages/core/src/context/marker-parsing.ts` let an unquoted attribute run scan up to 4000 characters, across the next `<<`, before it failed. 8000 unclosed `<<plan ` tags cost 8000 x 4000 steps, twice. Local measure: 106 ms at 8000 tags, 229 ms at 16000; a CI runner is 3 to 7 times slower.
- The unquoted run now stops at a `<<` (quoted values are unchanged). Local: 0.3 ms at 8000, 0.6 ms at 16000.
- That exposed a second, quadratic regex: `CONTROL_PARTIAL_TAIL_RE` rescanned to a trailing `>` from every `<` (342 ms at 8000 tags plus one close, 1636 ms at 16000). A match can never contain `>`, so it now runs only after the last `>`: 0.3 ms. The perf file gains that case.
- No threshold changed. `perf.yml` dispatched on this branch: perf tests green (core 87, desktop 25, db 4).
- Other perf reds in the window: `store.stream-tick` 2.46 ms vs 2 once, `hostile-input` envelope once (local max 9 ms vs 200). Single runner spikes, not changed.

agent_prs.body:
## Root cause

The wipe dropped tables one by one and never views, so `live_agents` (m156) survived reading a dropped `agents` table.
The replayed chain then died at m015's `ALTER TABLE sessions_new RENAME TO sessions`, because a rename re-checks every view.
m001 to m014 had already committed, so every later boot failed at m015 again.

## Fixes

- **Atomic wipe.** `db_wipe` first stops running turns, summaries, planners, scripts and terminals. Then it empties the file in one step with SQLite's reset (`SQLITE_DBCONFIG_RESET_DATABASE` plus `VACUUM`), and the chain replays on an empty schema.
- **Heal on launch.** `db::open` finishes a half-done wipe only when a view reads a missing table and `schema_version`, `sessions` or `agents` is missing. First it checkpoints the WAL and copies the file to `data.db.pre-reset-<ts>.bak`. If the copy fails, nothing is reset. Any other migration failure keeps today's error screen.

Fixes #1895

## Tests

- `dropping_tables_one_by_one_strands_the_view_that_blocks_a_table_rebuild`: reproduces the exact #1895 error.
- `a_reset_leaves_an_empty_schema_the_chain_can_replay_on`: tables, FKs, index, trigger and view are all gone, WAL and FKs are back on, and a second connection sees the empty schema.
- `opening_a_half_wiped_database_finishes_the_wipe`: the reporter's state (schema_version 1..14, `agents` missing, `live_agents` present) boots on an empty schema.
- `a_reset_on_open_keeps_a_complete_copy_first`: `data.db.pre-reset-<ts>.bak` exists and holds the pre-reset rows.
- `a_broken_view_on_a_complete_schema_is_not_reset`: no reset and no backup.
- `opening_a_healthy_database_keeps_its_data`.
- Full `cargo test` for the desktop crate, `@goodboy/db` vitest (including `rust-sql-schema`), knip and `check:tauri-commands` all pass.

agent_prs.body:
## What

An agent may now mount a second project on its own, the deferral says which limit it hit and stops instructing the agent to end its turn, and a deferred proposal reaches the conversation that asked for it instead of living only in the Activity timeline. The deferral also stopped rendering as a red failure.

Closes #1714

## The gate

`materializationGate` returns a discriminated decision instead of a string. Inputs: prior mount count `P` snapshotted at batch entry, named-by-goal `N`, immediate count `I` of successful new mounts already made in this batch.

| `P` | `N` | `I` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| any | either | 2 or more | Defer, cause `batch` |
| any | yes | 0 or 1 | Allow |
| 0 | no | 0 or 1 | Allow |
| 1 | no | 0 | Allow |
| 1 | no | 1 | Defer, cause `scope` |
| 2 or more | no | 0 or 1 | Defer, cause `scope` |

The behaviour change is the third and fourth rows: a session with zero or one mount now gains one unnamed project without asking. Goal matching is unchanged. An already-mounted project returns the existing mount and consumes no allowance; a failed mount consumes none either, since the immediate count now increments only after `materializeProject` resolves. `P` is snapshotted rather than derived from the mutating mounts array, batches are serialised per session, and the live mount count is rechecked before an unnamed mount commits, so two parallel batches cannot both claim the last slot. A table-driven test covers every row, both cap boundaries, all four goal-name sources, the already-mounted short circuit, the concurrent-claim recheck, and non-integer inputs.

## Both deferral strings, verbatim

Scope limit:

> Mount deferred for {projectName}: adding an unnamed project beyond this session's two-project allowance requires approval. A mount suggestion is available in this session's projects section or the requesting agent's conversation.

Batch limit:

> Mount deferred for {projectName}: this request has already mounted two projects

issues.body:
## Goal

Modernize the receipt LayoutLM stack so the normal Python training/inference environment can move to **Python 3.14 + current PyTorch**, while preserving the existing Core ML exporter and adding an **experimental Apple Core AI `.aimodel` export/runtime path** for Swift on macOS 27 / Xcode 27.

Do **not** replace the working Core ML path yet. Core AI should land alongside it behind an explicit opt-in until conversion + numerical + Swift runtime parity are proven.

## Why now

As of 2026-09-17:

- PyTorch supports Python 3.14 on macOS.
- Hugging Face Transformers/LayoutLM can run on current Python/PyTorch; LayoutLM itself is no longer the primary blocker.
- Apple released Core AI / `coreai-torch`, which converts `torch.export.ExportedProgram` into Core AI assets for Swift/on-device execution.
- The current Apple Core AI converter stack still has a Python-version mismatch: `coreai-torch` supports modern PyTorch, but the binary `coreai-core` dependency currently does not provide Python 3.14 support, so Core AI export should remain in an isolated Python 3.13 environment for now.
- Existing `coremltools 9.0` compatibility is also tied to the older PyTorch range, so the legacy Core ML exporter should stay isolated instead of constraining the whole package.

References:
- https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/

agent_prs.body:
Closes #102

## Summary
`SecretScan` already walked a local function's body as part of the enclosing body, but it never bound the local function's parameters. So `k: Secret<u64>` was a public, unknown name inside the body, and calls to the local function skipped the call rule. Now the scan treats a local function the way it treats a top-level one, at the place it is declared:

- `Enter(Declaration(Function f))` → `open_local`: opens a scope that binds `f`'s params. Their keys are `LOCAL + body*256 + i`, built from `parameter_facts`, the code `scan_body` now shares. Params written `Secret` are marked secret, and their `ParamFacts` (secret/escapes) apply to the store rule. `param_facts` now looks params up by key instead of by index.
- `Leave(Declaration)` → `close_local`: applies the result rule (`SecretScan.result`, pulled out of `report_secrets`), closes the scope, then binds the name, after the body as sema does, and records it in `functions`.
- `call` checks `local_callee` first. A call that names a local function goes through `public_parameters`, the same call rule as a declared callee. Its result is secret only if its `ret` is written `Secret`.

**About the `zen:secret` marker:** a local function has no C symbol (it is inlined where it is called, `gen_lower_core.inline_local`), so it can't get its own marker or `Func.secrets` record. Lowering is unchanged. A secret reaches a local function's `Secret` parameter from its declaring function, and the local's code is inlined into that function's C. That function carries the marker, so tools/ct audits the inlined code. I checked this by hand: `mix = (key: Secret<u64>, n: u64) Secret<u64> { f = (k: Secret<u64>, m: u64) Secret<u64> { k.bit_xor(m) } f(key, n) }` emits `zu_f..mix..(uint64_t zu_l3key, uint64_t zu_l1n) /* zen:secret zu_l3key */`.

- `must-fail/sema/secret_local_function_branch`: a local function's Secret parameter picks a match arm (the issue's case).

issues.body:
Found by the independent reviewer of the #67/#68/#71 jit integration. It is also on main, so it isn't caused by that branch.

**Problem:** sema never applies the Secret discipline to local functions. A local function with a `Secret<T>` parameter that branches on the secret compiles with no diagnostic on asm, the jit and C. C emits no `zen:secret` marker for it, so tools/ct never sees it either.

```zen
main = () {
    f = (k: Secret<u64>, n: u64) u64 { (k == 3).match({ true => 1, false => n }) }
    ...
}
```

The same body as a top-level function is rejected with `a secret value cannot choose a branch ... (k is secret)`. `docs/DESIGN.md:2541-2546` doesn't list local functions as untracked. The backend `IrFeature.Secrets` refusal can't catch this either, because a local function never gets a `secrets` record.

**Done when:** local functions get the same Secret checks and `secrets` record as top-level functions, and a must-fail corpus test covers the branch-on-secret case above.

## Summary

Fixes #59. Lowering no longer solves types itself. It reads the types sema publishes, and when a fact is missing it reports `unsupported: an expression sema published no type for` instead of guessing one. Delivered as one PR: once real gaps were told apart from legitimately open lambda/recovery types, the gap list was small.

**How the gaps were found.** A temporary strict probe (not committed) made lowering report every place sema's fact was missing or disagreed with lowering's own answer. It was run over the whole compiler (`./zen build src --entry zen/zen.zen --backend js`) and the corpus. Turning the fallbacks off and running `make jscheck` exposed more. Every gap was fixed in sema:

| gap | fix (sema) |
|---|---|
| a generic enum payload published `T`, not its instance type (`Box<i32>.Full` → `T`) | `sema_case`: `subst(variant_payload(v), inst_of_named(n))` |
| constant / default members' bodies were never checked, so they had no memo | `sema_decl.member_body`: `Const(k) => c.const_body(k, mi)` |
| a bound member settled at a call (e.g. `Alloc.realloc<T>`) left the supplying impl member's own type variables unbound (~870 probe reports) | `sema_call.bind_suppliers` binds them into `CheckedCall.inst` |
| `arena.create<T>()`: an implementor that leaves out an optional hook (`create`, `free`) reached nothing, so the call was silently `Unknown` | `sema_supply.keep_reachable` keeps bodyless `Hook` members |
| `same<U: Eq>(5000000000, 705032704)`: the instance typed `U` as i32, which truncated the literal (noted in 28b18700) | `sema_call.widen_literal_params`: a parameter settled only by literals is i32 unless a literal argument doesn't fit, then i64 (`Inst.rebind`) |

**Deleted from lowering:** `local_type`, `function_result`, `method_result`, `settle_params`, `unify`, `settle_range`, `range_elem`/`range_bound`/`impl_range_elem`, and the local solving in `solved_type`. `type_of` is now `recorded_type(id)` (the instance memo) or else `check.expr_memo`, and

issues.body:
Lowering (`src/gen/gen_lower*.zen`) still carries its own type inference as a fallback for when sema hasn't published a type: `local_type`, `function_result`, `method_result`, `settle_params`, `unify`, `settle_range`, and the related `type_from_ast` / local solving.

Sema is supposed to be the only source of types; lowering should read sema's published facts (including the per-instance tables from #30) and report a disagreement or missing fact instead of solving types itself.

Steps:
1. Make lowering read sema's published instance tables first everywhere, and report (not paper over) any place where they're missing or disagree with lowering's own answer.
2. Fill the sema gaps that report shows (known: bound defaults; others from strict probes).
3. Delete the fallbacks listed above.
4. Add an archcheck rule that lowering cannot import sema's inference helpers, so they can't come back.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #6028

## What

When `vercel()` wakes a stopped core and the wake takes longer than the 10 s handshake timeout, the backend's reconnects give up while they are still waiting for it. `WakingSocket.close()` reported each of them as `unreached`, a connection "that never reached the core", and the count outlived the wake. Once a new session was up, the count already met the #5517 recycle threshold (2 in 20 s). So the first connection to the woken core that didn't open in time (a busy core, slow to say hello) made the instance **stop the session it had just woken** and wake it again. That paid another full wake. Every warm instance keeps its own count and does the same, so the core can be stopped over and over while it is coming back. A fresh instance has no count, which is why a redeploy recovered at once.

Two changes in `vercel-store.ts`:

- **Only connections made to a session count.** A `WakingSocket` given up while it was still waiting for the wake (no origin yet, no socket opened) never tried the core, so it no longer reports `unreached`.
- **Counts belong to a session.** A wake that brings up a new session (a different `startedAt`) starts the `unreached` count afresh. A wake that finds the same session keeps it, so #5517's case still recycles: a core that answers `/health` but that no connection reaches.

## Root cause analysis (the issue's questions)

- **Is the link stuck terminal?** No. The issue's stack (`new Error` in `applyLinkStatus`) is the `backoff` + `outagePublished` path. The link keeps retrying, as the link machine intends.
- **Is a cached failure replayed?** Yes, by design. During a published outage, reads that aren't held through outages rethrow the one `serverTransportError`, hence the identical stack and the ~0.3 s rejections. It clears when a retry is admitted.
- **Is the store's connect path bypassed?** No. Every retry goes through `WakingSocket` → `ensure()`. The retries never succeeded because of the recycle loop above.
- **`remote()`**

## Summary

With the `vercel()` store on `2.0.0-alpha.65`, the core Sandbox stopped briefly. After that, warm backend instances never reconnected. The first query failed with `the server did not answer the connection within 10 s` (`websocket_silent`, `retry: "later"`). Every later `db.all` / `db.one` in the same instance then rejected within about 0.3 s with the same error, for as long as I watched (5+ minutes). That kept happening after `vercel sandbox ls` showed the core `running` again. Only fresh instances recovered: a redeploy of the same build fixed it at once.

agent_prs.body:
#5927 item 4, R3b. Builds on R10 (#5977, #5987, merged). A server that refuses a credential now says why in a typed field instead of only in its message. Before, every client found the reason by searching the message text for words like "expired", and `wire.rs` says that text isn't part of compatibility. This is a **wire change**, gated by a feature bit.

### Encoding: `wire-error-reason-v1`
- `FEATURE_TYPED_ERROR_REASON = 1 << 14`. A **client** offers it in its Hello. The server decides by what the client offered, not by negotiation, so it can name the reason before its own hello too. It never advertises the bit, so negotiated features (and everything above the carrier) are unchanged.
- `WireErrorReason`, postcard enum tags pinned: `expired=0, missing=1, invalid=2, disabled=3, revoked=4, reauthenticate=5`. Append-only.
- Bytes: the existing `WireFrame::Error` frame (tag 1) with its body (code, retry, message) **followed by the reason tag**. The message is length-prefixed, so the extra byte is unambiguous.
  - **Why not a new frame tag:** after its hello, a server's frames are told apart from sync messages by their first byte, and every tag past 1 is a sync message's (tag 8 is `Rows`; I tried it first and the browser/server tests caught the collision).
- Fixture: `crates/jazz/layers/protocol/fixtures/wire_reasoned_error_v1.json`, one row per reason with `reasoned_hex` (bit offered) and `plain_hex` (not offered, identical to today's bytes). Rust encodes and decodes it; TS decodes it.
- Rust: `encode_error_frame_for_client(error, client_features)`; `decode_frame_with_error_reason` for a client that offered the bit. **`decode_frame` stays strict**, so `INV-WIRE-1` (no trailing bytes) holds for every receiver that didn't offer it. `WireError.reason` is `#[serde(skip)]`, so the plain `Error` encoding is byte-for-byte unchanged.
- SPEC 8 §8.1.1 gains "Typed error reasons" with the compatibility write-up below.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #5565

## What
`vercel()`'s core region is now explicit, following the `namespace` precedent ([#5391](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/pull/5391)):

- **`region` is required.** `vercel()` without it throws at call time (so `next dev` reports it too) with the fix to copy: `vercel({ namespace, region: "iad1" })` keeps existing cores where earlier versions created them. It is not taken from `VERCEL_REGION` or the project's settings. Errors link [Vercel's Sandbox regions page](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/concepts/regions) and don't list regions themselves.
- **Region mismatch on an existing core throws** instead of being silently ignored. `@vercel/sandbox` exposes `sandbox.region` (the configured region) and `drive.region` since 3.9.0, our minimum peer version. The store checks the Sandbox it finds before resuming it (a resume starts its server), and again for one that is already running. When it provisions, it checks the Drive `Drive.getOrCreate` returns, which covers a Drive left behind by a deleted Sandbox. The error names the core's actual region, says moving isn't supported yet (#5441), and gives `region: "<actual>"` to copy. Nothing is created in the new region.
- **A once-per-process warning** fires when `VERCEL_REGION` differs from the core's region, naming both regions and the per-request round trip. It uses a `globalThis` symbol, like the Blob store warning, so separately bundled routes don't repeat it.
- **`s3()`'s bucket-region check uses the configured region** (it used to fall back to `iad1`), and its warning now goes through the injected `warn`.

## Tests
- `vercel-namespace.test.ts`:
  - missing or invalid region throws, with the copyable fix and the docs link
  - `refuseRegionMove`
  - the warning fires once per process, even across module copies
  - names stay independent of region
- `vercel-store.integration.test.ts`: the fake now tracks Sandbox and Drive regions.
  - a new core is created in the configured region
  - an existing iad1 core
agent_prs.title: vercel(): make the core region explicit (required region, error on region change)

issues.body:
`vercel()` currently defaults the core's Sandbox region to `iad1` (`packages/jazz-tools/src/backend/vercel-store.ts`). The region is fixed when the Sandbox and its Drive are created, so this is a lasting decision that today is made implicitly.

## Proposal
- **`region` becomes required** on `vercel()`, like `namespace`. Leaving it out throws at call time with a copyable fix (`region: "iad1"` keeps today's location, so existing cores stay where they are).
- **No default from the invoking function's region** (`VERCEL_REGION`): the first cold request would pick the region, and multi-region / failover projects could get different core regions per deploy or branch.
- **No default from the project's region**: not visible to the function at runtime, ambiguous with several regions, and still an implicit first-creation choice.

## Also, regardless of the default
- **Region change on an existing core is silently ignored today**: the existing Sandbox is looked up by name only, and `region` only applies when creating. Detect a mismatch between the existing core's region and the configured one and throw an explicit "moving a core to another region isn't supported yet" error (moving needs a data copy, see #5441).
- **Once-per-process warning** when `VERCEL_REGION` differs from the core's region, naming both and the per-request cross-region round trip.
- `s3()`'s fallback region (currently `options.region ?? "iad1"`) follows the explicit region.

## Done when
- Tests for: missing region error, mismatch error on an existing core, the warning, unchanged names/regions for existing cores with `region: "iad1"`.
- Docs: Vercel page options table and every `vercel()` snippet in docs, examples, create-jazz templates and the agent quickstart updated; changeset with migration text.

`allowedTo.*` inside an `exists` was accepted by the TS DSL (types and runtime) and by the `jazz.permissions.json` reader, then refused by the engine when the schema compiled at load:

issues.body:
## Problem

A rule can't say "this row's value appears in a row of another table **that the reader may read**." `allowedTo.read(...)` inside `exists` gets past the TypeScript types and the DSL, but the engine refuses it when the app files are loaded:

```ts
// synthetic schema: profiles{accountId}, groups{ownerId}, members{groupId, accountId, group: rel(groups)}
profiles: {
  read: (p) => exists.members({ accountId: p.accountId }, (m) => allowedTo.read(m.group)),
},
```

```
core schema policies do not support Inherits { operation: Select, via_column: "groupId", max_depth: None } yet
```

`allowedTo.read(...)` on the found row's `id` inside `exists.groups(...)` is refused the same way. An `exists` nested inside another `exists` can't refer to the outer row either ("a condition of an `exists` inside another `exists` names only its own row's columns").

Verified on main at 30dbb67.

## Also: the error names the wrong rule

The rule is on `profiles`, but the error path is `$.members.policies…`.

## Workaround today

Copy the other table's read rule into this one, using `.hop` and relation queries. That works, but the two rules have to be kept in sync by hand.

## Proposed

1. **Short term:** reject `allowedTo.*` inside `exists` in the types and in `generate`, with a clear "not supported yet" error that points to the workaround. Fix the error path.
2. **Decision:** whether to support `allowedTo` inside `exists` in the engine.
issues.title: Policies: allowedTo.* inside exists is refused at load (not supported yet)

agent_prs.body:
Fixes [#4808](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/issues/4808). The browser SharedWorker now keeps its upstream link as one latched value per context (`BrowserWorkerLinkFate`: link state and status, the runtime's current upstream failure, and the auth refusal) and sends it as a `link-fate` message to each tab when the tab is admitted and again whenever it changes. This replaces the one-off `remote-link`, `transport-error`, `auth-failure` and `auth-restored` events. The failure comes straight from the worker runtime (new `NativeRuntimeAdapter.upstreamFailure()`), so it clears exactly when the worker's own does. The tab's follower applies a fate the same way whether it arrived at admission or later: the failure fails Global/Remote waits and remote subscriptions (an `AuthorityChangedError` stays typed through the relay), the link status follows the worker's, and the auth error clears when the worker's clears, including when a new worker connection has none. Writes are not rejected, so they still upload if the app recovers (e.g. `deleteClientStorage()`).

Why: before, only tabs admitted at the moment of the failure heard it. A tab opened or reloaded after an AuthorityChanged refusal showed `offline/authority-changed` but its `wait({tier: "global"})`/`waitForSync` waited forever, and a stale `authState.error` could outlive a reconnect, which `stopPastRefusal` reads to tell a refused sign-out from an outage. The React Native relay already has no such gap: its foreground polls the relay's latched `upstreamFailure`/`authRejection` on every tick, so nothing changes there. The docs caveat about multi-tab `authority-changed` is removed.

Risk: low–medium. It's a worker↔tab protocol change, but tab and worker ship in the same bundle. One behaviour shifts slightly: a tab now drops a relayed failure when the worker's runtime does (for example when an explicit reconnect starts a new attempt), not only when the link reaches `connected`. issues.body:
Follow-up to #4803 (typed `AuthorityChanged` for a recreated server store).

**Scenario.** A browser app runs its local-first store in a SharedWorker, and its tabs relay through that worker. The server's store is recreated, so it has a new namespace, and the worker reconnects. The worker's upstream link is refused with `AuthorityChanged`. With #4803, the worker's own `Global` waits fail and its sync status becomes `offline / authority-changed`.

**Problem.** Nothing passes that refusal on to the tabs. A tab's own `authority_changed()` stays `None`, so a tab's `wait({tier: "global"})` and `waitForSync` can wait forever, which is the stuck state #4803 fixes for clients that hold the server link themselves. #4803's changeset and docs say the tab path is unverified.

**Why it isn't a quick fix.** The worker can't simply answer the tabs' pending commits with `Outcome::Refused`. That would reject those writes permanently, and the design keeps them so they can upload if the old server comes back or the app resets storage. The refusal needs its own protocol message, or state that doesn't end the link, from the worker to its tabs, and that state must not reject the commits.

**Expected.** A tab's `Global` waits fail fast with `AuthorityChangedError`, and the tab's sync status shows `offline / authority-changed`. Local writes and reads keep working. Test this with a worker plus at least two tabs.
issues.title: A browser tab's global waits don't fail when its SharedWorker's link is refused as AuthorityChanged

issues.body:
`jazz-tools validate` and the dev server accept relation policies that `deploy` then refuses. Found in #5927 (R8).

**Repro:** in `jazz.permissions.json`:
```json
{ "docs": { "read": "exists (from shares where shares.userId = session.user limit 1)" } }
```
- `npx jazz-tools validate`: passes. The expression parser accepts `limit`, `offset`, `order by`, `distinct on` and `param.…` ([`artifact/expr.rs:1352-1410`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/crates/jazz/src/tools/deployment/artifact/expr.rs#L1352-L1410), [`:1724`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/crates/jazz/src/tools/deployment/artifact/expr.rs#L1724)).
- `npx jazz-tools deploy`: refused with "relation policies do not support Distinct, OrderBy, Offset or Limit".

Duplicate or NUL union labels and query parameters behave the same way.

**Why**
- `validate` ([`dev/schema-validation.ts:9`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/packages/jazz-tools/src/dev/schema-validation.ts#L9-L18)) runs `validate_deployable_schema` → [`check_deployable_policies`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/crates/jazz/layers/model/src/model/public_schema_convert.rs#L127-L153), which only refuses nested outer-row references.
- The relation checks live in [`jazz-server/src/server/permissions_validation.rs:13`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/crates/jazz-server/src/server/permissions_validation.rs#L13), and only publish runs them ([`catalogue/deployment.rs:101`](https://github.com/garden-co/jazz/blob/6ab0dd60982fae66220150197358298a0eb4e73f/crates/jazz-server/src/server/catalogue/deployment.rs#L101)).

**Fix:** move `validate_permissions_relations` into the model crate and call it from `check_deployable_policies`; better still, have the expression parser refuse these shapes. No ABI change.
