On macOS, `shutdown(SHUT_RD)` does not wake a blocked `accept`, so an acceptor thread stayed blocked until a peer connected, and its listener kept the port until then.

## Change

On non-Linux platforms the listener is non-blocking, and the acceptor waits in `wait_for_connection`, which polls with a 100 ms timeout and checks `shutdown_flag`. Linux keeps its blocking `accept4`, so the accept path connect benchmarks measure does not change.

The issue proposed a per-runtime wake pipe. The flag already exists and already ends an acceptor waiting for queue room (#745), so polling it needs no new descriptor.

An idle macOS listener now makes 10 `poll` calls a second, and each accepted connection costs one more `poll`. That is calculated, not measured, and the mio backend does not need to be optimal.

issues.body:
On macOS (and other non-Linux targets), an acceptor thread does not exit at shutdown until one more peer connects.

## What happens

Each pool-mode listener has an acceptor thread that blocks in `accept` (`accept_nonblock` in `ringline/src/acceptor.rs`). Shutdown wakes it with `shutdown(fd, SHUT_RD)` on the listening socket. On Linux that makes a blocked, or later, `accept4` fail with `EINVAL`, so the acceptor exits at once. On macOS it does not: the acceptor stays blocked in `accept` until a peer connects. `accept_nonblock`'s doc already notes this ("on non-Linux platforms the wake is best-effort").

Since #557 the acceptor accepts on its own duplicate of the listener fd and closes it when it exits. That fixes a fd-reuse race, but it means that on macOS the listening socket stays open until the acceptor thread exits, which can be indefinitely on a quiet port. Before, the socket was also kept alive by the blocked `accept`'s file reference, so this is not new, but it is now explicit.

## Proposed fix

On non-Linux targets only, make the acceptor's wait interruptible:

- Put the acceptor's copy of the listening socket in non-blocking mode.
- `poll` it together with a per-runtime shutdown wake fd (a pipe; `RuntimeShutdown` in `worker.rs` already owns a per-runtime pipe for task-panic notification and could own this one too).
- On the wake fd becoming readable, exit; on the socket becoming readable, `accept` until `EAGAIN`.
- `RuntimeShutdown::shutdown` writes to the wake pipe alongside `shutdown(SHUT_RD)`.

Keep Linux on the current blocking `accept4` + `shutdown(SHUT_RD)` path, so the accept path that connect-rate benchmarks measure is unchanged.

## Testing

`acceptor::tests::an_acceptor_never_accepts_on_a_reused_fd_number` is Linux-only because it relies on the acceptor exiting after `shutdown(SHUT_RD)`; with this fix it can run on macOS too. A test that shuts down an idle runtime and requires every acceptor thread to exit within a bound would cover the fix directly

## Change

The error kind changes at run time with no compiler error, so it is listed under `### Changed`. A caller matching `Other` or the old text falls through. issues.body:
`ringline::spawn()` returns `Option`/`Err` with no way for an operator to see
that the standalone task slab is the reason, and nothing in
`ringline/src/metrics.rs` counts it. The failure is therefore invisible unless
the caller happens to log every occurrence itself.

That is how #478 stayed hidden. The slab leaked a slot per completed task, so a
server spawning one task per unit of work exhausted it and then failed every
subsequent spawn for the life of the process — and the only reason anyone
noticed was that the caller logged a warning per failed spawn and someone read
the log. A caller with a reasonable inline fallback just gets slower:

- `spawn()` returning `None` looks exactly like backpressure, which is a
  legitimate transient. There is no signal that distinguishes "the slab is
  permanently full" from "try again shortly".
- The consequence lands somewhere unrelated to the spawn. In our case each
  fallback did a multi-megabyte write inline on the event loop, so the symptom
  was a p99 an order of magnitude above p90, with nothing in it pointing at
  task spawning.
- `standalone_task_capacity` defaults to 256, which a task-per-work-item caller
  passes in seconds, so this is reachable without a leak at all.

## Suggestion

There is already a counter group for exactly this: `ringline/pool`, described
as "Pool exhaustion counters", alongside `send_exhausted` and
`timer_exhausted`. A `standalone_tasks_exhausted` slot in that group would have
made this a dashboard line rather than an investigation.

Two smaller things that would each have shortened it independently:

- A rate-limited `warn!` the first time the slab is found empty, naming
  `standalone_task_capacity`. Exhausting a fixed-size slab is worth one line.
- A distinct error rather than a bare `None`, so a caller can tell "full" from
  other causes and decide whether to retry or fall back.

Happy to send a PR for the counter if the group has a spare slot and the naming
looks right.
issues.title: No signal when the standalone task slab is exhausted

The acceptor closed a connection when every worker's accept queue was full. By then the handshake was done, so the peer saw a successful connect followed by EOF or a reset. #658 measured 1,955 of 10,000 connections lost this way on one worker.

## Change

With every live worker full, `send_when_room` holds the connection and blocks in `crossbeam_channel::Select`, which wakes on room or a worker's exit. Later connections stay in the kernel's listen queue. The wait checks `shutdown_flag` every 100 ms, so a held connection does not keep the port until the workers exit.

`ConfigBuilder::backlog` now defaults to 65535 instead of 1024. The kernel uses the smaller of that and `net.core.somaxconn`.

## For the reviewer

**Behaviour change under a wedged runtime.** Closing was a fast failure. A runtime whose workers stop taking connections now accepts connects that then get no reply, and the client waits for its own timeout. A TCP-connect health check no longer sees the problem. `accept_queue_full` replaces `accept_backlog_dropped` and counts each wait plus each 100 ms of it, so a wait that does not end shows as 10 per second. There is no knob that restores prompt failure. The issue listed this as an option and did not decide it, so this is the decision to check.

The counter name changes, and it was not in any release, so this is not a `!:` change. No consumer in this repo or `experiments/` uses the old name.

The tokio arms of `ringline-bench` and `ringline-benchmarks` get the same 65535 backlog so connect-burst comparisons stay fair.

- `accept_queue_full.rs`: 100 connections against a capacity-1 queue with the worker blocked. All served on both backends. With close-on-full restored, connection 1 gets a reset.

- nextest: 1505 passed on io_urin

`run_acceptor` (`ringline/src/acceptor.rs:171-224`) calls `accept4` and then calls `try_send` on each live worker's channel in turn. If every channel is full, it drops the `AcceptedConn`, which closes the socket, and increments `ACCEPT_BACKLOG_DROPPED`.

Fixes #742. On io_uring all of a worker's UDP sockets shared one provided ring, and a queued datagram holds a buffer until it is read. A socket with no reader could take every buffer, which had two effects:

- The worker's other UDP sockets stopped receiving, as the issue describes.
- The worker spun. Each multishot rearm on the empty ring returned `ENOBUFS` at once, measured at 1.0 s of CPU per second and about 985,000 `ENOBUFS` per second. On io_uring every UDP socket on a worker shares one provided-buffer ring, and a queued datagram holds its buffer until the socket's task reads it. A socket with no reader can therefore take every buffer and stop the worker's other UDP sockets receiving.

Found reviewing #741. The reproduction used two sockets on one worker, socket 0 unconsumed and socket 1 echoing:

| Datagrams flooded to socket 0 | Sibling replies |
|---|---|
| 127 | 4/4 |
| 128 and up, tested to 400 | 0/4 |
| 2000, with a consumer on socket 0 (control) | 4/4 |
| 400 on mio | 4/4 |

The ring has 128 buffers by default, and the receive queue capacity is clamped to that. Setting `udp_recv_queue_capacity(16)` let the sibling keep receiving. The behaviour predates #741: `on_udp_bind` returning `None` gives the same result. A stalled consumer should have the same effect, from reading the code, and `let (tx, _) = udp.split()` for a send-only task reaches it more easily.

Options:
- Discard datagrams for a socket whose receive half was dropped.
- Cap each socket's queue below the ring size, so that one socket cannot take every buffer. This also covers a stalled consumer.

The behaviour is documented on `UdpSocket`.

No task owned a connection opened through `DriverCtx::connect`, `connect_unix`, `connect_with_timeout`, `connect_tls` or `connect_tls_with_timeout`, so the runtime closed it once it was established. They were deprecated by #580. 0.7.0 is the breaking release, and it keeps one way to open a connection, so they are removed here.

**What a caller can no longer do**
- Start a connect from `DriverCtx` and get a `ConnToken` back synchronously. Spawn a task from `on_tick` or `on_notify` and call `ringline::connect`; `token()` on the connection handle gives the token after establishment.
- Each such task takes a `standalone_task_capacity` slot (default 256 per worker), and `spawn` returns `Err` when none is free.
- On the mio backend in 0.6.x, `connect`, `connect_tls` and their timeout forms left the connection open, so code that relied on that must change. Those users saw no deprecation warning, because the deprecation is unreleased. `connect_unix` returned an error on mio, and `ringline::connect_unix` still does.

issues.body:
`DriverCtx::connect`, `connect_unix`, `connect_with_timeout`, `connect_tls` and `connect_tls_with_timeout` (reachable from `on_tick` / `on_notify`) return a `ConnToken` immediately. No `ConnectFuture` registers a connect waiter on this path.

Their docs say "The `on_connect` callback fires when the TCP handshake completes (or fails)". `AsyncEventHandler` has no `on_connect`, so a caller cannot learn when the connect completes either.

Options:
1. Give `DriverCtx` connects a completion path (e.g. an `on_connect` handler callback, or spawn a task with the `ConnCtx`) and mark these connections as owned so the orphan guard skips them.
2. Document that outbound connections are made with `ringline::connect(...)` from a task, and deprecate or remove the `DriverCtx` connect methods (breaking; batch into the next coordinated release).

Either way, the `on_connect` references in `handler.rs` are wrong today.

Partial fix for #638. Does not close it.

## Change

A connection's sends can take received buffers out of `recv_hold` or `pending_recv_bufs`:
- a direct-echo gather or single send;
- a `forward_held` send;
- a `forward_recv_buf` send of a lent receive buffer (`SendRecvBuf`).

A `forward_to` write also pins ring buffers. The receive throttle (`at_hold_cap`) counted none of these. So a direct-echo or `forward_held` connection whose peer stopped reading held its cap in `recv_hold`, plus up to 32 more buffers in its send. - `Driver::send_held_recv` counts, per connection, the received buffers its queued or in-flight sends hold.

agent_prs.body:
On io_uring, a park offer is now ignored while the connection holds request bytes the handler has not read, or when it is made from inside one of the connection's reader callbacks. Closes #669.

## The bug

`offer_for_park` set `park_offered` without looking at what the connection held. If the next request was already buffered, `park_blocker` refused the park while it was unread (`DataPending`), but the offer stayed set. Once the handler read the request, nothing refused the park. A handler that then awaited something other than the connection, for example a backend call, could be parked mid-request: its future was dropped and the request got no reply.

Found by reading the code; not observed. Park (#443) is not in a release.

## The change

- `Driver::holds_unread` is the `DataPending` check `park_blocker` already made (accumulator, a lent buffer in `pending_recv_bufs`, `segment_hold`, `recv_hold`, `segment_pinned`), moved into one function that `park_blocker` and the new `Driver::offer_park` share.
- `Driver::offer_park` declines an offer while `holds_unread` is true or the connection's reader callback is running. A decline also clears any earlier offer and its deposited `ParkState`, and counts `metrics::park_diag::OFFER_DECLINED`. `ConnCtx::offer_for_park` calls it after its generation check.
- The callback check is a thread-local set by a guard around each reader callback (`with_data`, `with_bytes`, `with_segments`, `try_with_data`), io_uring only. `with_bytes`, and a `forward_recv_buf` that sends the whole lent buffer or accumulator, take the bytes out of the driver before the callback can offer, so `holds_unread` alone would let such an offer stand. Only the innermost running callback is recorded. An offer for connection A from inside a nested callback on connection B is declined only while the runtime holds A's bytes; the docs say so.

The owner chose to decline and document in-callback offers, with the counter, rather than defer them until the read completes

On io_uring, a park offer stays set after the handler reads the next request, so a connection can be parked while its handler is in the middle of that request. Found by reading the code at 313a5e7; not reproduced.

## Sequence

1. While the handler is still working on request 1, request 2 arrives. `handle_recv_multi` calls `withdraw_park_offer`, which clears any offer, and buffers or lends the bytes.
2. The handler sends response 1 and calls `offer_for_park`. This sets `park_offered`. `park_blocker` returns `DataPending` while request 2 is unread, so nothing parks yet.
3. The handler reads request 2 with `with_data` or `with_bytes`. The connection now holds no unread bytes, and `park_offered` is still `true`.
4. The handler awaits something other than the connection, for example a backend call, before it replies to request 2.
5. `maybe_park_one` runs. `park_blocker` finds an open connection, no unread bytes, an offer, and no queued sends, and returns `None`, so the park proceeds. The handler's future is dropped on this worker, and request 2 gets no reply.

`park_offered` is cleared in only four places:
- `withdraw_park_offer` when bytes arrive (`backend/uring/event_loop.rs`);
- `close_connection` (`backend/uring/driver.rs`);
- the two slot resets at install and adoption.

Reading data does not clear it. The `offer_for_park` docs say "a handler offers once per idle point and never has to revoke". That holds only when no request bytes are buffered at the moment of the offer.

Fixes #642.

## Problem

On io_uring, a zero-copy send (`SendMsgZc`, the `.guard()` path of `send_parts`) from unregistered memory is charged to `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` while in flight (from Linux 6.15), and from 6.14 the rings are charged to the same limit. When the pages do not fit, the operation returns `-ENOMEM` and sends nothing. `handle_send_msg_zc` treated that as a send error. The send and every send queued behind it were dropped after `send_parts` had returned `Ok`, and the connection stayed open, so later bytes arrived with a gap.

## Change

- `-ENOMEM` on a CQE tagged `SendMsgZc` (not its drain), with no Close submitted, goes through the existing `-EAGAIN` drain (#603): a plain `send` of the entry's first non-empty unsent iovec, which pins nothing.

- `-ENOMEM` from the drain itself is a send error, as before.
- New `ringline/pool` counter `send_zc_enomem`, also listed in `ringline-bench`'s summary.
- Not covered: inside a `send_chain`, `-ENOMEM` still fails the chain, as any error does there.

On io_uring, consecutive queued copy sends on one connection, plaintext or TLS ciphertext, now go out as one `SendMsgCoalesced` even when they come from different `send` calls. Before, a coalescing run stopped at the first end-of-send slot, so N pipelined responses cost N send operations.

## Changes

- **Coalescing.** `submit_next_queued_inner` gathers every consecutive pool-backed send at the queue head, up to `MAX_IOVECS` (32).
- **Per-send settling.** The slab entry carries each awaited send in the run with its success length and where its bytes end (`SendRun`). On completion:
  - a partial write settles the sends it covers at once (`take_sent_sends`);
  - a full write settles each send with its own length;

- **TLS.** Queue order is wire order, so TLS records stay in sequence. Only a slot that carries an id settles anything, so each logical send still wakes once. ## Summary

On io_uring, two user sends on one connection never share an SQE. With one send in flight per connection, N small pipelined responses on a connection cost N `Send` SQEs and N completion round trips. The mio backend's `flush_sends` writes a connection's whole queue with one `writev`. Under the ring emulator (#621), which executes the driver's SQEs one at a time, the same N responses would cost N `write` calls where mio pays one.

## Where

`Driver::submit_next_queued_inner` (`ringline/src/backend/uring/driver.rs`) coalesces a run of copy sends from the head of a connection's queue into one `SendMsgCoalesced`, up to `MAX_IOVECS` (32). The run stops after the first slot marked end-of-send:

> Coalesce at most one logical send's tail per op: stop the run after the first chunk marked end-of-send. Otherwise a single coalesced completion could span two independent pipelined sends, while the slab entry carries only one send's id.

Every user send marks its last slot end-of-send (`handler.rs` `send_inner` and `send_bounded`), and a single-slot send is always end-of-send (`send_copy.rs`). So a run carries the chunks of one send larger than a slot, never two sends, and queued sends go out one SQE per completion (`submit_next_queued`, called from each send-family completion handler).

## Summary

`ConfigBuilder::sqpoll(true)` cannot start on the io_uring backend. Every worker fails at launch with `Error::RingSetup("io_uring_setup(2): Invalid argument (os error 22) (EINVAL) ...")`.

## Cause

`UringEngine::setup` (`ringline/src/backend/uring/engine/uring.rs`, before #625 `Ring::setup`) always sets `IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN`, and adds `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` when `sqpoll` is on. The kernel's `io_uring_create` refuses `COOP_TASKRUN`, `TASKRUN_FLAG` and `DEFER_TASKRUN` together with `SQPOLL` with `EINVAL`, since the SQ thread, not the submitter, runs task_work there. The code already leaves out `DEFER_TASKRUN` under SQPOLL, with a comment saying so, but not `COOP_TASKRUN`. The line has been there since the initial commit, and no test sets `sqpoll(true)`.

## Evidence

Found by #622's step 0 conformance tests: an offset-order test under SQPOLL failed at engine setup with the error above on Linux 6.12. Setting `COOP_TASKRUN` only without SQPOLL makes setup succeed; the same test then passes, and an echo round trip under `sqpoll(true)` (22 B, 8 KiB, 256 KiB) passes.

## Fix

Set `COOP_TASKRUN` only when SQPOLL is off, alongside `DEFER_TASKRUN`, and add an echo test under `sqpoll(true)`.

- A `send().await` queued behind something nothing awaits resolved with *that* send's byte count. The unawaited send could be a `send_nowait`, a `send_chain_nowait`, a direct echo, a `forward_recv_buf` or a `send_backpressured`.

- Two awaited sends in flight at once on one connection could hang.

mio passed the single-send case (`notify_len` marked the awaited entry), but it had the same single-waiter limit.

## The change

Every awaited send owns an entry in the per-worker completion table from #618: `send`, `submit_batch_await`, `send_chain` and `forward_held`, on both backends. The entry's `SendId` is stored on the resource whose completion ends the send:

| Send | Where the id is stored |
|---|---|
| Copy send | End-of-send pool slot, moved to the coalesced slab entry if the run is coalesced |
| TLS send | Final ciphertext chunk |
| Zero-copy batch | Slab entry |
| `forward_held` | Recv-forward entry |
| Chain | `ChainState` |
| mio | The queued `PendingSend` |

That completion settles exactly that id. Sends nothing awaits carry no id and settle nothing.

Failures:

- An error settles the in-flight send's id with its errno.
- A queue drain fails every id it drops with `ConnectionAborted`. Queued slab entries are now included.
- A forced close fails a chain's id.
- Retry give-ups fail the id of the send they give up on.

Removed:

- `Executor::send_waiters`, `IoResult::Send` and `wake_send`
- `ConnSendState::acked_bytes`, the chain's `total_bytes` and the slab's unread `end_of_send`
- mio's `notify_len`, its per-connection `send_completions` queue with its dirty list, and `mark_last_send_awaited`

On io_uring, a `SendRecvBuf` is a zero-copy send straight from a held receive buffer. `handle_send_recv_buf` tracks a partial send of one in two per-connection fields, `send_recv_buf_original_lens` and `send_recv_buf_remaining`. Two places set them when they built the send:

- `flush_direct_echo`, which builds only when nothing is in flight.

So the in-flight send's completion read the queued send's counts. In the new test:
1. A 100-byte send is in flight, with a 4096-byte send queued behind it.
2. The 100-byte send completes in full.

Fixes #613.

## Problem

On io_uring, `handle_send_recv_buf` resubmits the rest of a partially sent receive buffer. This is the `SendRecvBuf` used by `forward_recv_buf`, and by `run_direct_echo` when one buffer is held. If the resubmit could not be pushed because the submission queue was still full after a submit, the handler:
- returned the buffer to the ring with the remainder unsent;
- submitted the connection's next queued send.

So the stream carried on with that remainder missing. That breaks Domain Invariant 7: a send whose SQE cannot be pushed is parked and retried, never dropped.

## Change

The remainder is parked at the head of the connection's send queue. A new helper, `Driver::park_at_queue_head`, does this. The queue keeps `in_flight` and the buffer stays held, so nothing queued behind the remainder can go first. `drain_send_retries` then pushes the remainder, as it does for any parked send.

- `drain_conn_send_queue` releases the queue, which returns a `SendRecvBuf` entry's buffer;

The first submit of a `SendRecvBuf` already parked this way through `submit_or_queue_send`. Only the partial-send resubmit did not.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #604.

## Problem

On io_uring, `ConnCtx::run_direct_echo` drops the bytes it received just before the peer's FIN.

A direct-echo connection does not echo each receive as it arrives. It holds the received provided buffers (`recv_hold`), and the flush pass at the end of each completion batch gathers them into one send. When the peer's FIN arrived in the same batch as the last data, two things went wrong:
- The receive handler called `close_connection`, which drains the hold and returns those buffers to the ring unsent.
- `DirectEchoFuture` resolved as soon as the read side finished. Its task then ended, which also requests a close.

A client that sent 8 MiB, half-closed, and then read got its echo about 12 KB short, every time.

## Change

- **On FIN, if bytes are still held:** the receive handler records the EOF and leaves the connection open. If nothing is held, the handler closes the connection as before.
- **When the hold drains:** if the flush pass drains the hold of a connection whose read side has finished, it wakes the direct-echo future and requests the close. The close waits for the in-flight send before it finalizes (`try_finalize_close`). A connection with bytes held at the FIN therefore closes in the same way as one with an empty hold, whatever the handler does after `run_direct_echo().await`.
- **`DirectEchoFuture`:** it resolves only once the read side has finished and the hold is empty, so a wake that arrives while bytes are still held cannot end the task early.

A peer that half-closes and never reads now keeps the connection open indefinitely: the held bytes are never sent, and no deadline applies to plaintext connections. This is the same as a queued send to such a peer. Worker shutdown still cancels it, as `shutdown_does_not_wait_out_a_direct_echo_to_a_half_closed_peer` checks. A receive error still closes the connection at once.

`run_direct_echo`'s docs now say when the future resolves. They also say that the method exists only on io_uring

issues.body:
On io_uring, `ConnCtx::run_direct_echo` closes the connection when the peer's FIN arrives without echoing the bytes received just before it.

## Seen

A client sends 8 MiB to a `run_direct_echo` server, then calls `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`, then reads. It gets EOF about 12 KB short. This was found while writing a test for #603; it happens with and without that fix (`main` at 8c9394b, Linux 6.12 arm64).

A CQE trace of the server shows how it ends:

```
... RecvMulti res=4096   (×32), SendRecvBufsCoalesced res=131072, repeated
RecvMulti res=4096
RecvMulti res=4096
RecvMulti res=3766
RecvMulti res=0          (peer FIN)
<close lead>
Close res=0
```

Every echo send completed in full. The last three receives, 11,958 bytes, were held for the next gather. The FIN then closed the connection, and those bytes were never sent.

## Likely cause (from the trace, not the code)

Direct echo flushes held buffers in `flush_direct_echoes`, at the end of a CQE drain. The FIN's `res=0` in the same drain appears to request the close before that flush runs. With nothing in flight, the close then finalizes, and the held bids are replenished instead of echoed.

## Expected

A peer's half-close should not drop data the server has already received. Every received byte should be echoed before the close finalizes, as a plain `send` queued before a FIN is.

`run_direct_echo` is used by `ringline-bench`'s echo servers.

Fixes #394.

## Problem

`udp_send_to_unreachable_peer_does_not_kill_worker` failed occasionally on mio under load with this message:

```
follow-up send to live peer must succeed after spamming a dead peer
```

The handler sends "alive" to the client and then increments `follow_up_ok`. The test asserted `follow_up_ok == 1` as soon as its `recv_from` returned "alive". On mio, `send_to` has already sent the datagram by the time it returns. If the worker is preempted between the send and the increment, the client reads the counter while it is still 0. On io_uring, `send_to` only queues the send. The ring submits it after the handler's poll returns, so the increment always comes first (SQPOLL is off in this test).

## Reproduction

A blocking 50 ms `std::thread::sleep`, inserted temporarily between the send and the increment, widens that window. With it, `main`'s test failed 5/5 on mio with the message from #394, and passed 5/5 on io_uring.

## Change

The test reads the counter after shutting down and joining the workers. The handler does not await between `send_to` and the increment, so the increment runs in the same poll as the send, before the worker can exit. The comments at the send and at the read now state this, because an `.await` there would let shutdown drop the parked task first. The check that the client receives "alive" stays where it was.

A real failed follow-up send is caught by the client's `recv_from` timing out. The counter check still fails if `send_to` reports an error for a datagram that was sent.

The handler's comments no longer say the sends can fail through ICMP. Linux drops ICMP errors for an unconnected UDP socket without `IP_RECVERR`, and ringline does not set it.

| Check | io_uring | mio |
|---|---|---|
| With the temporary blocking 50 ms sleep | 20/20 passed | 20/20 passed |
| Whole `udp` binary, 16 CPU busy loops on 8 CPUs | not run | 100/100 passed |

issues.body:
Observed on the `Test (mio)` CI job for #392, whose diff contains **zero** changes under `ringline/` (it touches `ringline-bench/` and `ringline-quic/tests/peer.rs` only).

```
test udp_send_to_unreachable_peer_does_not_kill_worker ... FAILED
ringline/tests/udp.rs:1779: assertion `left == right` failed:
  follow-up send to live peer must succeed after spamming a dead peer
```

Re-running the same job on identical code went green, and the test passes 8/8 in isolation locally.

## Why this is filed rather than waved away

This is the **fourth** distinct mio-suite flake seen in one working session, all with the same signature: pass in isolation, fail only under full parallel suite load.

- `async_join3_mixed` — fixed, measured (#389); root cause was a racy assumption in the test, not a runtime bug.
- `signal_wait_on_signal_shutdown` — fixed by isolating it into its own test binary (#389); its SIGTERM is process-wide and was killing sibling tests' servers.
- `large_payload_round_trip_via_endpoint_api` — #393; two reasoned fixes have missed.
- this one.

The cost is not the individual re-runs. It is that `Test (mio)` currently cannot distinguish a real regression from noise without a human deciding, per failure, whether the diff could plausibly have caused it — which is the judgement CI exists to remove.

## Suggested approach, learned from the two that were fixed

Do **not** characterise it by running the test alone: isolation is the condition under which it cannot fail. Use the full binary under parallel load with >=100 runs per arm. An n=30 comparison on `async_join3_mixed` produced a convincing result that reversed at n=120.

For that one the mechanism was a racy assumption *in the test*. Worth checking first here too — the assertion is that a follow-up send to a live peer succeeds after spamming an unreachable one, which plausibly depends on how promptly the worker drains ICMP-driven errors, i.e. on timing the test does not control.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #597.

## Problem

`udp_port_zero_resolves_once_for_every_worker` failed once in CI. It found 2 of the 3 worker sockets on the reported port. The job was Test (tls-unbuffered), `cargo nextest run --profile ci`, at 3de9c89 on 2026-10-02 (job 110726996332).

The test counted the lines in one read of `/proc/net/udp` that matched the port. The kernel produces that file in chunks and resumes each chunk by position. If sockets open or close in the same network namespace during a read, the read can skip an entry or list it twice:
- **Under nextest**, every test is its own process. `UDP_SLOT_LOCK` is a mutex inside one process, so it does not serialize the `udp.rs` tests, and other tests' sockets change while this one reads.
- **Under `cargo test`**, the lock does serialize them. `run_udp_client`'s echo server is still a source: its socket closes up to 5 s after its test returns.

It is not a startup race. Each worker binds its UDP sockets in `AsyncEventLoop::new`, before it reports startup, and `launch()` waits for every worker's report.

## Change

The test reads the table ten times. From every line whose local address equals the bound address exactly (IP and port), it collects the socket's inode, then counts the distinct inodes. A duplicate line is the same socket, so it counts once. A socket is missed only if all ten reads skip it.

## Verification

"Churn" below means a second process that holds about 2000 UDP sockets on `127.0.0.1` and keeps replacing them. All runs used Linux 6.12, arm64.

**Author's runs:**

| Commit | io_uring | mio |
|---|---|---|
| `main`'s test | 16/200 failed (counts 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) | not run |
| cb4ac0a (first commit) | 300/300 passed | 300/300 passed |
| c8c61b1 (final) | 200/200 passed | 200/200 passed |

**Runs by two review agents**, using the same churn and a heavier one (about 18,000 table lines):

| Test | io_uring | mio |
|---|---|---|
| `main`, same churn | 22/200 and 26/200 failed | 19/200 and 17/200 failed |
| `main`, heavie

Several tests in `ringline/tests/` hold a thread with a fixed sleep and assume it is still running when the test checks. This is the pattern behind #595, #555 and #596. None of these has been seen failing; they were found by reading the code during the review of the fix for those three.

| `accept_queue_shutdown.rs:99`, `:188`, `:271` | worker sleeps 300/400/300 ms; a 50 ms sleep at `:156` | Normal priority, but no guard that the worker was still blocked at shutdown. |
| `blocking.rs:256` | `SCHED_IDLE` closure sleeps 200 ms; 10 s wait at `:285` | Can starve under load. |
| `teardown_drops.rs:287` | `SCHED_IDLE` closure sleeps 200 ms; 10 s wait at `:323` | Can starve under load. |

## Suggested fix

Fixes #603. Fixes #553.

## Problem

On io_uring, a send that fills the socket of a peer that has half-closed and is not reading spun the worker's event loop at about 26,000 iterations a second (Linux 6.12 arm64). Every connection on that worker shared the core. #553's test bound (50× idle) was being tripped by this spin (34×), not by a slow host.

A standalone io_uring probe showed why. Once the peer has sent its FIN, with the send buffer full (Linux 6.12 arm64/x86_64, 7.1 x86_64):

| op | no FIN | after FIN |
|---|---|---|
| `Send` + `MSG_WAITALL` | waits | waits |
| `SendMsg` + `MSG_WAITALL` | waits | `-EAGAIN` |
| `SendMsgZc` | waits | `-EAGAIN` |
| `Writev` | waits | `-EAGAIN` |
| `PollAdd(POLLOUT)` | waits | completes with `POLLRDHUP` |

io_uring reports `POLLRDHUP` on every poll, so the `sendmsg`, `POLLOUT`, `sendmsg` retry loop never waited. That affected:
- coalesced copy sends;
- `run_direct_echo`;
- `forward_to` / `forward_to_conn` socket and connection sinks.

A guard send (`SendMsgZc`) treated the EAGAIN as an error: it failed with `WouldBlock` and drained the connection's queue.

## Change

- **The drain send.** On EAGAIN, each of those paths submits a plain `send` of the entry's first non-empty unsent iovec, under a `*Drain` tag (`SendMsgCoalescedDrain`, `SendRecvBufsCoalescedDrain`, `ForwardWriteDrain`, and the new `SendMsgZcDrain`).
- **Its completion** is a partial write of the same entry. It goes through the entry's own handler, which advances the iovecs and resubmits the rest. The entry stays the connection's one in-flight operation, so byte order holds.
- **Zero-copy:** the drain is a copying `send`, and the entry still waits for every notification owed by the earlier ops.
- **Removed:** the `*PollOut` tags, handlers and submitters. The metric `op` labels change (CHANGELOG, Changed).
- **Unchanged:** plain `Send` paths keep `SendPollOut`. A `send` with `MSG_WAITALL` does not return EAGAIN in this state.
- **Docs:** `docs/send-completion-design.m

`deferred_close_does_not_spin_on_half_closed_peer` (`ringline/tests/echo.rs`) fails every run on one Linux host. The test passes in GitHub CI, but its bound has little margin.

## Measured

Docker on Apple silicon (aarch64, kernel 6.12.72-linuxkit), io_uring backend, at `main` (efa9608) and on #548. Every run failed, in debug and release, alone and in the full binary:

```
event loop spun while a close was deferred: 13277 ticks in 500 ms (idle baseline 251, bound 12550)
```

| | ticks / 500 ms |
|---|---|
| idle baseline on this host | 243–255 |
| with the deferred close (healthy loop) | 12,800–13,300 (about 52× idle) |
| bound (`baseline.max(200) * 50`) | 12,150–12,750 |
| the original spin bug (from the test's comment) | ~270,000 |

The bound is relative to idle cadence. The healthy retained/idle ratio depends on the host: the test's comment gives about 11× on the validation host, and this host measures about 52×. So the 50× bound sits just below this host's healthy rate.

The test's comments also disagree with each other about the validation host's idle rate. The baseline comment says io_uring idle "ran ~5,300 ticks per 500 ms". The bound comment says "473 idle vs 5,317 retained".

## Options

- Add an absolute floor below the spin rate, e.g. `bound = (baseline.max(200) * 50).max(50_000)`. That keeps about 5× margin under the 270k spin and about 4× over this host's healthy rate.
- Measure the healthy cadence with sends outstanding but no deferred close, and compare against that instead of against idle.

Either way, the bug's signature (~270k) stays an order of magnitude above every healthy rate measured so far.

Fixes #594.

## Problem

`udp_repeated_launch_does_not_leak_fds` counted fds 50 ms after a warm-up and again after 6 launches, then asserted the count grew by less than 6. Every pool thread holds each worker's wake fd until the thread exits. Blocking-pool threads run at `SCHED_IDLE`, so on a busy host they exit seconds after the workers join. A count taken before they exit includes their fds, and the test failed under load.

## Change

- The test moves out of `udp.rs` into its own binary, `ringline/tests/udp_launch_fds.rs`, as the repo's other fd-counting tests are. It runs alone in its process, so no other test's runtime can add fds or threads.
- It records the process's thread ids before the first launch. Before both counts, it waits up to 30 s until only those threads remain.
- It then requires the two counts to be equal.
- On failure it lists the fds open at the baseline and after the launches.

An earlier version on this branch waited for the fd count to stop changing. Review showed that under load that baseline still held the warm-up's wake fds, and their release cancelled out an injected leak: it passed 10/10. Waiting for the threads to exit closes that hole. Waiting by thread id, not by a `ringline-*` name, covers pool threads that have not run yet: the resolver, spawner and blocking pools are started on the thread that calls `launch()`, and a new thread carries its creator's name until it first runs.

`wake_fd_lifetime` and `late_result_fds` each set up a thread that must still be running, or still inside open(2), when the `Runtime` drops. They did it with fixed sleeps:

#588 removed the problem on Linux 6.13+. Before 6.13, a connection close still runs `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` on the worker's bounded io-wq pool. That pool also runs file and path operations the kernel cannot finish inline, so a worker whose file I/O fills the pool closes its connections late. The other remedy #586 listed, a FIN without io-wq on old kernels, would need a raw fd per connection, which undoes the fixed-file design.

## `fs` module docs: "Blocking file I/O and connection closes (io_uring)"

- **What io-wq and its bounded pool are.** The pool belongs to the worker thread, or to the SQPOLL thread when `sqpoll` is set.

That fixed #581: before Linux 6.13, a socket removed from the fixed-file table is not released while earlier requests are in flight. The kernel always runs `shutdown` on io-wq (`REQ_F_FORCE_ASYNC`), and it uses the **bounded** pool (6.12 `opdef.c`: no `unbound_nonreg_file`). That pool also takes regular-file I/O that would block, such as `fs::fsync`.

So a close's FIN can wait behind file I/O on the same worker.

## Measured

SystemsLab experiment `01a102f5-2690-7100-04c1-5b82c440f2b2`, run on delta in a 16-vCPU VM with Linux 6.12. Kernel bounded limit 64.
- Workload: `ringline-bench`'s `close-latency` (#584's PR). The server answers one request per connection and closes it; the client times its wait for EOF.
- One server worker on CPUs 0–3; 32 `write_from` + `fsync` loops on the VM disk.
- Mean of 5 reps:

| arm | conns/sec | EOF wait p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| no fsync load | 35,590 | 0.20 ms | 0.44 ms |
| fsync, kernel limit (64) | 13,074 | 0.21 ms | 11.8 ms |
| fsync, `iowq_max_workers(16)` | 1,149 | 11.6 ms | 37.6 ms |
| fsync, `iowq_max_workers(4)` | 537 | 28.2 ms | 82.3 ms |

- Once a worker's blocking file operations fill its bounded pool, every close waits for an fsync.
- At the kernel limit, the p99 still rises 27×. CPU contention on the server's 4 CPUs is probably part of that, but was not separated out.

issues.body:
On Linux 6.14+, every io_uring ring and provided buffer ring is charged to `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` (see `ringline/src/memlock.rs`). The `ringline` lib test binary sets up many test event loops in one process. Under the common 8 MiB soft limit it now runs out partway through: `make_test_loop` gets `ENOMEM` from `io_uring_setup` and aborts the binary on purpose ("cannot create the test event loop on this host, aborting the test binary so this is reported once").

## Observed

Debian backports image, kernel `7.1.13+deb13-amd64`, memlock soft limit 8192 KiB, `cargo test -p ringline --lib`:

- **Main + #588's first commit (4870f6e):** the full suite passed, 1331 tests.
- **#588 at 21e4005,** which adds about 8 tests that set up rings: the lib binary aborted at `proptest_cqe::zc_sequence_no_slab_leak` with `io_uring_setup(2): Cannot allocate memory`. The abort happens in a test that predates #588.
- **Same commit with `prlimit --memlock=unlimited`:** passed, 1336 tests.

So the binary was already close to the limit. The kernel releases a closed ring's charge asynchronously (`io_ring_exit_work`), so rings from finished tests may still count when later ones start; I haven't confirmed that.

## Why it matters

- Any 6.14+ CI runner or developer machine with the default limit fails the lib tests, and the failure looks unrelated to the change being tested.
- Under nextest (one process per test) this does not happen. Under `cargo test`, which CI also runs (`cargo test --doc`) and the local gate list uses, it does.

## Options

1. Have the test harness raise its own soft memlock limit to the hard limit at startup, as `Runtime` launch already does for `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, and say so when the hard limit is too low.
2. Share one ring across the unit tests that only need a ring, not a full loop.
3. Document `ulimit -l` next to the `RLIMIT_NOFILE` note in CLAUDE.md.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #584.

Adds `ConfigBuilder::iowq_max_workers(n)`, which caps the threads in each worker's bounded io-wq pool. **The default is 0, the kernel's limit, so nothing changes unless it is set.** #584 proposed defaulting to 64; the measurement below is why it doesn't.

## Implementation

- `Ring::setup` registers the cap with `IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS`. That call applies to the calling thread's io-wq, and the ring is set up on its worker's own thread.
- The cap is an **upper bound only**. Setup first reads the current limit (a zero slot reads without changing it) and registers the cap only if it is lower. The kernel's limit is `min(sq_entries, 4 × online CPUs)`, so on an 8-CPU host it is 32, and registering 64 would have doubled it.
- Validation rejects values above `i32::MAX`, which the kernel would refuse.
- New bench tools:
  - `bench-server --iowq-max-workers`;
  - a new bin, `close-latency`: a server that answers once and closes, optionally with `fsync` loops per worker, and a client that times its wait for EOF.

## Tests

Unit tests in `backend/uring/ring.rs` read the limit back from the kernel, for the default, a configured cap, a cap above the kernel limit, and 0. Removing the upper-bound check fails two of them; removing the registration fails the configured-cap test.

## Measurement

SystemsLab `01a102f5-2690-7100-04c1-5b82c440f2b2`: delta, 16-vCPU VM, Linux 6.12, so the kernel limit is 64. One server worker on CPUs 0–3.

**Churn, no file I/O** (`connect-bench`, 16 threads). Each rep's first run was slow (about 30k/s) whatever the cap; those runs are excluded consistently.

| cap | conns/sec | CPU per conn | peak io-wq threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 47,539 | ~60 µs | 64–65 |
| 64 | 47,219 | ~60 µs | 64–66 |
| 16 | 47,633 | ~60 µs | 16–17 |
| 4 | 47,285 | ~60 µs | 4 |

**Server-initiated close under 32 `fsync` loops on the VM disk** (`close-latency`):

| arm | conns/sec | EOF wait p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| no load, cap 0 | 35,590 | 0.20 ms

issues.body:
Since #583, every io_uring connection close pushes a `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` linked ahead of its `Close`. The kernel always runs `shutdown` on an io-wq worker thread (`REQ_F_FORCE_ASYNC` in `io_shutdown_prep`), so io-wq threads now appear under connection churn.

## Observed

The #583 A/B ran a churn workload on a 16-vCPU VM (Linux 6.12) with one server worker. It peaked at 64–65 io-wq threads in the server process; `main` had none. Throughput and CPU per connection improved (see the comment on #583), so the threads cost nothing measurable there.

## Why cap it

Each ringline worker thread has its own io-wq. The kernel limits the bounded pool to the smaller of the SQ size and 4 × online CPUs; on the 16-vCPU VM that was 64. On larger hosts the default grows with the core count, for example 384 per worker at 96 cores. Shutdown work is short, so that many threads per worker is unlikely to help.

## Proposal

- Register `IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS` on each worker's ring at setup. This needs Linux 5.15, below the crate's 6.1 floor.
- Default bounded cap: 64. Leave the unbounded pool alone unless something uses it.
- Make it a `ConfigBuilder` knob, e.g. `iowq_max_workers(bounded)`, so a deployment can change it. `Config` stays opaque.
- Measure before settling on the default: the #583 churn A/B with caps of 4, 16 and 64 on a host with more cores than 16. A small cap may cost nothing, since shutdowns are quick.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #582.

`BlockingJoinHandle` (from `spawn_blocking`) and `ResolveFuture` (from `resolve`) had no `Drop`. When a handle was dropped before its result arrived, its `pending_blocking` / `pending_resolves` entry stayed with the worker for the worker's lifetime. That happened both to a `select!`/`timeout` loser and to a future owned by a connection's task at teardown. A closure's result delivered into the leaked entry was never dropped, so a returned file, buffer or guard stayed alive until the worker exited.

## Fix

Same pattern as #578:
- Each future records its owning worker (`waker::current_worker()`) and does nothing when dropped on another thread. Both futures are `Send`.
- Inside a task poll, `Drop` removes the entry. Outside one, it queues `Orphan::Blocking` or `Orphan::Resolve` for `runtime::release_orphans`.
- A result that arrives after its entry is gone is dropped in `deliver_blocking` / `deliver_resolve`, which already ignored unknown ids.
- `spawn_blocking` and `resolve` inserted the entry before sending the request. On a failed send they now remove the entry before returning the error.
- `BlockingJoinHandle`'s docs say that dropping the handle does not stop the closure, and that the result is dropped when it arrives.

## Tests

| Test | On `main` |
|---|---|
| `blocking.rs` `a_result_whose_handle_was_dropped_is_dropped_on_arrival` (handle dropped by a `timeout`, inside a poll) | fails: result never dropped |
| `teardown_drops.rs` `a_blocking_handle_dropped_with_its_connection_drops_the_result` (teardown, outside a poll) | fails: result never dropped |
| unit `a_dropped_resolve_future_leaves_no_entry` (mio harness: failed send, in-poll drop, deferred drop) | — (new) |
| unit `a_failed_blocking_request_leaves_no_entry` | — (new) |
| unit `a_handle_dropped_on_another_worker_releases_nothing` (request ids repeat across workers) | — (new) |

The integration tests run on both backends. Mutation checks:
- removing the in-poll release fails the timeout test

issues.body:
`ResolveFuture` (from `ringline::resolve`) and `BlockingJoinHandle` (from `ringline::spawn_blocking`) have no `Drop` impl. Each registers an entry when it is created:

- `resolve`: `executor.pending_resolves.insert(request_id, (task_id, None))` (`runtime/io.rs`).
- `spawn_blocking`: `executor.pending_blocking.insert(request_id, (task_id, None))`.

Only a `poll` that takes the result removes the entry. A future dropped first, whether a `select!`/`timeout` loser or owned by a connection's task dropped at teardown, leaves its entry for the worker's lifetime. The same leak #575 fixed for `spawn`, `Child::wait`, `sleep` and `connect`.

## Consequences

- The maps grow by one entry per abandoned request.
- `deliver_blocking` stores the closure's return value (`Box<dyn Any + Send>`) in the leaked entry. A closure that returns a file, a buffer or a guard keeps it alive until the worker exits.
- `deliver_resolve` / `deliver_blocking` call `wake_task(task_id)` for the dropped task. If the task slot has been reused, the new task gets a spurious wake. That is harmless but wasted.

## Fix shape

Same as #578:
- Give each future a `Drop` that removes its entry inside the executor and, outside it, queues an `Orphan` for `runtime::release_orphans`.
- Record the owning worker and skip the release on a foreign thread.
- Store a delivered result only while its entry exists. `deliver_*` already ignores unknown ids, so removing the entry is enough.

Tests: a `timeout` that drops each future before it completes (`spawn_blocking` of a sleeping closure, `resolve` of a slow name), plus the teardown case from `tests/teardown_drops.rs`. Assert the map is empty afterwards.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #581.

## Cause

On io_uring, the server processed the peer's FIN, and its `Close` SQE completed, but the client never saw EOF. Removing a socket from the fixed-file table does not release it while requests submitted before the removal are still in flight. Any connection's request counts, so another connection's multishot recv holds the closed socket open, and no FIN goes out, until that recv ends. In #581's repro that was when the other connection's 60 s sleep ended.

Kernel source (per review): before 6.13, io_uring frees removed fixed files in node order, so any earlier request on a registered file or buffer delays the release. 6.13 made the references per-file. Measured on 6.12 here and on a Pi VM (6.12.107 arm64); not run on 6.13+.

## Fix

- `Ring::submit_close` pushes `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` hard-linked ahead of the `Close`. A shutdown sends the FIN whatever holds the socket.
- The two SQEs go in as one `push_multiple`, so a submit cannot split them. A hard link (not `IO_LINK`) keeps the `Close` running when the shutdown fails, e.g. `ENOTCONN` on an outbound socket that never connected.
- The shutdown's completion has its own tag (`OpTag::CloseShutdown`) and is ignored. The `Close` CQE still drives teardown.
- **Exception:** a park handover (#443) installs a real fd for another worker and then closes its slot, relying on that close not sending a FIN. `handle_park_install` sets `ConnectionState::socket_handed_off`, and `Driver::close_shuts_down` skips the shutdown for it.
- `try_finalize_close` and the close retry go through `close_shuts_down`. Worker exit clears any pending close and pushes one plain `Close`, leaving the release to the ring's teardown.
- **Breaking:** config validation now requires `sq_entries >= 2`, since a close pushes the shutdown and `Close` as one pair.

mio is unaffected and unchanged.

`ringline/tests/peer_fin.rs`, both backends:

issues.body:
On io_uring, a peer FIN on a connection whose task is not reading is not acted on until the task ends, once more than one connection is open. On mio the server closes at once.

Measured on `main` at 54716d0 (Linux 6.12 arm64, one worker, default config).

## Repro

The handler's task only sleeps: `ringline::try_sleep(Duration::from_secs(60))`, then awaits it. The client:

1. Opens `n` connections and waits 50 ms.
2. Calls `shutdown(Write)` on the first connection.
3. Times a blocking `read` on it, with a 70 s timeout.

| backend | open connections | EOF after |
|---|---|---|
| io_uring | 1 | 69 µs |
| io_uring | 2 | **59.9 s** (when the 60 s sleep ends) |
| mio | 1, 4 | < 150 µs |

With 4 connections open and a 5 s read timeout, every one of 12 rounds timed out on io_uring. That happened with `timer_slots` of 4 or 1024, and with `tick_timeout_us` of 1000 or 0. mio returned EOF at once in every case.

## Expected

The connection state model (`docs/connection-state-model-design.md`) says a peer FIN sets `read` and then requests the close. So the connection should close, and its task be dropped, without waiting for the task to finish. mio does this.

## Notes

- First seen while writing `teardown_drops.rs` (#578). Clients that fully close (drop the `TcpStream`) were not checked separately. The churn test there waits on a task-drop counter rather than the client's EOF, so it does not depend on this.
- With one connection the FIN is handled at once, so the multishot recv seems to deliver the EOF. What differs with two connections is not yet known.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #575.

A connection's task is dropped by `remove_connection` outside any task poll, so `try_with_state` returns `None` and futures that released state in `Drop` skipped it. On `main`:

- a `sleep`/`timeout` held its timer slot (and on io_uring its armed timer) for the worker's life;
- a `spawn` future leaked the child's pidfd;
- a channel sender or receiver dropped with its task did not wake the other side;
- a `Child::wait` future left its waiter and result entries behind;
- an outbound `connect` future left its connection established with no task to use it.

## Fix

- `runtime::defer_release` queues an `Orphan` (timer slot, spawn, pidfd wait, connect) on a per-worker thread-local; `runtime::release_orphans` releases them. `fs::release_orphans` calls it first, so it runs before and after each task-poll pass on both backends.
- Each future records its owning worker and skips the release when dropped on another thread (they are `Send`).
- A channel wake outside a task poll goes on the worker's `READY_QUEUE`.
- `release_timer_slot` cancels an unfired io_uring timer before freeing the slot; a late CQE is rejected by generation.
- `release_connect` clears the connect waiter/result and closes the connection if it opened. On mio, a TCP or TLS connect that completes with no `ConnectFuture` waiting is closed, as on io_uring already. This includes connects started with `DriverCtx::connect`, which never register a waiter.
- Orphans are also released before each blocking wait, so an idle worker does not hold them.
- `wake_pidfd` stores a result only when a waiter was registered.

## Tests

`ringline/tests/teardown_drops.rs`, both backends (pidfd test Linux-only). Each fails on `main`:

| Test | On `main` |
|---|---|
| `a_sleep_dropped_with_its_connection_frees_its_timer_slot` | slots stay allocated/armed |
| `a_freed_timer_slot_is_available_to_the_next_connection` (4 slots, 30 rounds) | pool exhausted |
| `a_spawn_dropped_with_its_connection_closes_its_pidfd` | 10 pidfds

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #574.

On io_uring, dropping a `fs::read_into` or `fs::write_from` future could free its buffer while the kernel was still using it, and another disk-I/O future could resolve with the wrong result or never resolve. A completion is matched to its operation by a 32-bit key that repeats, and results were stored under it with nothing to say whose they were. A result nothing had taken was taken by a later operation with the same key, whether it was left by:
- a dropped `DiskIoFuture` / `StatFuture`;
- an NVMe or direct-I/O operation submitted through `DriverCtx`, which has no future;
- a future not yet polled (e.g. a prefetched `stat`).

The issue's reproduction:
1. Drop a `stat`.
2. Await enough operations for the key to come round.
3. Drop a pending FIFO `read_into`.

On `main` the read's buffer is freed at once.

## Design

**Held keys** (a per-worker thread-local, `runtime::disk_io_key_held`):
- A key is held from a future's creation (`Executor::wait_disk_io`) until it takes its result (`take_disk_io_result`) or is dropped (`abandon_disk_io`).
- `wake_disk_io` stores a result only for a held key. Graveyard buffers are freed first, as before. Any other result is discarded.
- A future dropped outside the executor (connection teardown) queues its key on `ORPHANED_KEYS`, and `release_orphans` releases it.

**Key allocation never hands out a key that may still be in use:**
- **io_uring:** keys are `subsystem(2) | sequence(14) | slab index(16)`, so fs, direct I/O and NVMe, whose slabs each number slots from 0, never collide. A busy slab slot keeps an in-flight key unique, and `disk_io_key` also skips held keys. If every key of a slot is held (16,384), allocation fails with an error and the caller releases its slot.
- **mio:** keys are a u32 sequence. `submit_disk_io` skips held keys and keys whose pool operation has not been drained yet (`Driver::disk_io_in_flight`). Without that second check, the key of a dropped future's still-running operation could be reissued af

issues.body:
## Summary

On io_uring, a `read_into` / `write_from` buffer can be freed while the kernel can still write into it. A stale entry in `Executor::disk_io_results`, left by a different disk-I/O future dropped earlier under the same key, is taken as proof that the read or write has completed.

Found by the adversarial review of the #568 fix and reproduced. The bug predates that fix, which only makes the same code reachable from the connection-teardown path.

## How

- `fs::park_buffer` (inline, and through `release_orphans`) and `ReadFuture::poll` / `WriteFuture::poll` treat `disk_io_results.remove(&seq).is_some()` as "this operation completed".
- `DiskIoFuture::drop` (`ringline/src/runtime/io.rs`) and `StatFuture::drop` (`ringline/src/fs.rs`) remove their waiter but never remove a result. So a disk-I/O future dropped before it resolves leaves its result in `disk_io_results` for good. That covers fsync, rename, remove, mkdir, stat, NVMe and direct I/O.
- The io_uring key is `u16 seq << 16 | slab_idx` (`ringline/src/handler.rs`), so it repeats after 65,536 operations. With one operation in flight, the free list (last in, first out) hands out the same slab slot each time, so the repeat is exact.

## Reproduction

A temporary test by the reviewer, io_uring, release build:
1. Open a regular file, and a FIFO with `READ_WRITE` so a read on it blocks in the kernel.
2. `drop(fs::fsync(data))` before it resolves. Its result stays in `disk_io_results`.
3. Await 65,535 more `fsync` calls, so the key comes round again.
4. `read_into(fifo, 0, BytesMut::with_capacity(..))` and drop it.

Results:
- **Bug:** the buffer is freed at once (`frees right after dropping the pending fifo read: 1`), with nothing ever written to the FIFO.
- **Control:** with the first fsync awaited instead of dropped, the buffer is not freed (`0`).

`ReadFuture::poll` trusts the same stale entry, so it would hand the buffer back early too.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #568.

`park_or_drop` (`ringline/src/fs.rs`), called from `ReadFuture::drop` / `WriteFuture::drop`, ran `mem::forget` on the buffer whenever `CURRENT_DRIVER` was unset, on the premise that this "shouldn't happen". It does whenever a connection closes while its task awaits `read_into` or `write_from`: `executor.remove_connection` drops the task outside any task poll (mio `drain_pending_closes`, io_uring `handle_close`). Fixes #559: a runtime `Waker` woken from another thread now schedules its task on the worker that owns it.

**Before.** A waker's data was the bare task id, and `wake` pushed it onto the *calling* thread's thread-local `READY_QUEUE`. ## Summary

`Waker`s handed to futures by the runtime can only be woken from the worker
thread that polled them. Waking from any other thread silently misroutes: the
parked task is never scheduled, and the waking thread schedules an unrelated
task instead. `std::task::Waker` is `Send + Sync` and its contract allows
`wake()` from any thread, so this breaks any future that stores its waker —
including futures from outside this crate.

## Where it comes from

`runtime/waker.rs` keeps the ready queue in a `thread_local!`:

```rust
thread_local! {
    pub(crate) static READY_QUEUE: RefCell<VecDeque<u32>> = ...;
}
```

and `wake_by_ref_fn` pushes onto whichever thread calls it:

```rust
unsafe fn wake_by_ref_fn(data: *const ()) {
    let conn_index = data as usize as u32;
    READY_QUEUE.with(|q| q.borrow_mut().push_back(conn_index));
}
```

The waker's data is a bare index — `conn_waker(conn_index)` /
`standalone_waker(task_idx)` — with no thread identity in it, so
`wake_by_ref` has no way to reach the owning worker. The restriction is
already documented on `conn_waker` ("Must only be used on the same thread
where the executor runs"), but it is not expressible in the type system and
not what a `Future` author will assume, because storing the waker from
`Context` and waking it later is the normal way to write one.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than documenting

Two failures happen at once, and both are silent:

1. The parked task is never scheduled. If it is awaited without a timeout,

2. The waking thread pushes the index onto its own ready queue, so it polls
   whichever of *its* tasks holds that index — an unrelated task, with no
   error anywhere.

Any synchronisation primitive built on wakers has this shape: an async mutex,
a channel, a semaphore, a `Notify`, a barrier. The waiter parks on one worker
and is released by whichever worker frees the resource, which is usually a

Closes #561 (with #562): listener sockets get one owner.

Each listener's sockets are now a `ListenerSockets` (`Vec<OwnedFd>`), shared by `Arc`:

- `RuntimeShutdown` and the listen gates hold it until shutdown.

Fixes #547. Task panics are caught and returned to the caller as errors by
default, and `TaskPanicPolicy::Shutdown` lets a caller choose to shut the
whole runtime down on a task panic instead.

## Breaking changes (0.7.0)

- `JoinHandle` (from `spawn_with_handle`) and `BlockingJoinHandle` (from
  `spawn_blocking`) resolve to `Result<T, JoinError>` instead of `T`.
  `JoinError` converts into `io::Error`, so `?` works in `io::Result`
  functions.
- `signal::Signal` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and gains `Signal::TaskPanic`.

## What was wrong

| where a panic happens | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `spawn_blocking` closure | pool thread died; handle pending forever | caught; handle `Err(JoinError)`; thread survives |
| `spawn_with_handle` task | handle pending forever | handle `Err(JoinError)` |
| `JoinHandle::abort` / `id().cancel()` | handle pending forever | handle `Err(cancelled)`; awaiting task woken |
| `abort` after the task finished | cancelled whatever task reused the slot | does nothing |

  drained return `Ok(())`.

issues.body:
A `spawn_blocking` closure that panics kills its pool thread, and the task awaiting it never resolves.

## What happens

`blocking_thread` (`ringline/src/blocking.rs`) runs `(req.work)()` with no `catch_unwind`. A panic unwinds the pool thread, so:

- no `BlockingResponse` is sent, and the awaiting `BlockingJoinHandle` stays pending for the rest of the task's life;
- the pool loses a thread; with the default 4 threads, a few panics leave the pool unable to run anything, and every later `spawn_blocking` hangs.

Shutdown still completes and nothing leaks; it is the caller's task and the pool's capacity that are lost.

Found by the third adversarial review of #541 and reproduced there on both backends. Present on `main`.

## Intended behaviour (owner decision)

By default, a panic in a task is caught and returned to the caller as an error. It does not kill the pool thread, the worker or the process. The caller can opt in to having a task panic take down the whole runtime.

## Proposed fix

- The pool thread wraps `(req.work)()` in `catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(..))` and sends the outcome as the response, so the thread survives and the awaiting task resolves.
- `BlockingJoinHandle` resolves to an error carrying the panic (e.g. an `io::Error` or a dedicated error type that holds the payload, so a caller can `resume_unwind` it if they want the panic). This is a public contract change for `spawn_blocking`'s return type and belongs in a coordinated release.
- A `ConfigBuilder` knob (name to be decided) makes a task panic abort the runtime instead: the caught panic triggers shutdown, or is re-raised on the worker, for callers who prefer fail-fast.
- Worth checking the same policy against the other task boundaries (`on_accept`/`on_start` futures, standalone `spawn`ed tasks) so "task panics are errors by default" holds runtime-wide, not only for the blocking pool.

issues.body:
A disk-I/O `open` or a `spawn` that completes after its worker has exited leaks the resulting fd.

## What happens

Pool threads send results back to the requesting worker over a per-worker crossbeam channel. If the worker has exited, `send` fails (or the result sits in a channel that is then dropped), and the response is dropped. Two responses carry an fd as a raw integer, so dropping them leaks it:

- **Disk I/O (mio).** `DiskIoResponse { result: i32, .. }` mirrors an io_uring CQE: for `fs::open` the `result` is the new fd, for every other operation it is a byte count or `-errno`.
- **Spawn.** `SpawnResult { pidfd: RawFd, .. }`.

## Reproduction

Found while adding a test for #541. On mio, `fs::open` a FIFO with no writer from `on_start`, drop the `Runtime` and join the workers, then open the writer. The disk-I/O thread's `open` completes, its response reaches no worker, and the FIFO fd stays open indefinitely (`/proc/self/fd/N -> .../fifo (deleted)`). The spawn case was found by review and not reproduced. Present on `main`, not introduced by #541; #541's test excludes this fd from its leak check and points here.

## Proposed fix

Make the responses own their fds:

- `SpawnResult::pidfd` becomes `OwnedFd`, a straight type change.
- `DiskIoResponse` gains `fd: Option<OwnedFd>`, set only for an `open`. `result: i32` stays the CQE-shaped status, so the change is not a pure wrapper swap.

A dropped response then closes its fd.

**Not solved by this:** a spawned child whose result reaches no worker is never `wait`ed, so it stays a zombie until the ringline process exits. Closing the pidfd does not reap it. That needs a reaper or a kill-on-drop policy, which is a separate decision.

issues.body:
Accepted connections still queued in a worker's accept channel when the runtime shuts down are never closed.

## What happens

`AcceptedConn` (`ringline/src/acceptor.rs`) carries the socket as a `RawFd`:

```rust
pub struct AcceptedConn {
    pub fd: RawFd,
    pub listener: crate::ListenerId,
    pub peer: crate::connection::PeerAddr,
}
```

The acceptor thread `accept4`s a connection and sends an `AcceptedConn` to a worker's bounded crossbeam channel. If the worker exits before draining the channel, which is what happens at shutdown with connections in flight, the channel drops with `AcceptedConn`s still in it. Nothing closes their fds.

## Reproduction

Found by the third adversarial review of #541. 20 launch/drop cycles, each connecting 8 clients and dropping them at once: 2–8 socket fds were still open 5 s after shutdown, on both io_uring and mio. Present on `main` (051a375), not introduced by #541.

## Proposed fix

Carry the fd as `OwnedFd`. A queued connection then closes when the channel drops. The worker calls `into_raw_fd()` where it registers the connection, the point where it actually takes ownership. The acceptor's "every worker is full" path, which closes the fd by hand today, gets the `AcceptedConn` back from `try_send` and drops it. Merged mode's `peer_accept` handoff uses the same struct and is covered by the same change.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #535.

## Problem

`ConnCtx::close` passed the slot index to `close_connection` without comparing `self.generation`. A `ConnCtx` held past its connection's close and the slot's reuse closed whichever connection held the slot now. The `close` methods on the owned handle types delegate to `ConnCtx::close`, so they had the same bug.

## Audit

I checked every `ConnCtx` method that touches connection state by index. #535 calls `close` "the exception"; it isn't the only one.

| method | stale-handle effect before |
|---|---|
| `close` | closed the slot's new occupant |
| `set_recv_sink` | installed the sink on the new occupant, so **its received bytes would be written into the stale caller's buffer** |
| `take_recv_sink` | removed the new occupant's sink |
| `recv_timestamp` | returned the new occupant's timestamp |

The other 45 `pub` methods either compare the generation or go through a `ConnToken` that carries it.

## Fix

All four return early (or 0) on a stale handle, as `is_alive`, `enable_recv_forward` and #437's entry points already do. `close` keeps its null-safe `CURRENT_DRIVER` lookup, since it runs from `Drop` outside a task poll. The check is in shared runtime code, so both backends get it.

The `is_alive()` guards in the `ringline-redis` / `-memcache` / `-ping` pools (the #533 workaround) are now redundant but harmless; left as is.

## Tests

These are io_uring unit tests, following #437's stale-handle pattern:
- `close_ignores_a_stale_handle`, which also checks, as a control, that the current handle still closes;
- `set_recv_sink_ignores_a_stale_handle`;
- `take_recv_sink_ignores_a_stale_handle`;
- under `timestamps`, `recv_timestamp_ignores_a_stale_handle`.

Each failed before the fix. Removing each check turns exactly its own test red.

- clippy is clean with default, `force-mio`, `timestamps` and `tls-unbuffered`, and on macOS.
- The workspace suite passes in debug and release on io_uring, except

`ConnCtx::close` checks that a driver is installed, then calls
`driver.close_connection(self.conn_index)` with the index alone. Neither side
compares `self.generation` against the slot's current generation:

- `ringline/src/runtime/io.rs` — `ConnCtx::close`
- `ringline/src/backend/uring/driver.rs:1778` — `close_connection(&mut self, conn_index: u32)`
- `ringline/src/backend/mio/driver.rs:509` — same signature

Every other accessor on `ConnCtx` that reads connection state compares the
generation first (`is_alive`, `listener`, and the completion handlers, per
domain invariant 3 in `CLAUDE.md`: "Stale CQEs are normal. Slots recycle;
every completion must be validated against the connection generation").
`close` is the exception, and it is the one that mutates.

The consequence: a `ConnCtx` held across the point where its connection is
closed and its slot reused will, on `close()`, close whichever connection now
occupies that slot. `close_connection` returns early on `close_requested()`,
so this is only reachable once the slot has been recycled into a new
`Lifecycle::Open` connection — but that is exactly the case a generation
check exists to catch.

Found while reviewing #533. The connection pools in `ringline-redis`,
`ringline-memcache` and `ringline-ping` hold a client across arbitrary user
code and can be dropped after the runtime has closed the connection
underneath them. They now gate every `close()` on `is_alive()`, which does
compare the generation, as a local workaround:

- `PooledClient::drop` (both close paths)
- `Pool::close_all`

`Pool::mark_disconnected` was already safe because it matches on
`ConnToken`, which carries the generation.

The fix belongs in the runtime rather than in each caller: either compare the
generation in `ConnCtx::close` before calling through, or give
`close_connection` a token-taking form. Doing it in `ConnCtx::close` keeps
the internal callers that legitimately close by index unchanged.

issues.body:
An accepted connection arrives as an owned `Connection`. An outbound connection from `connect()` arrives as a `ConnCtx`. The caller, or a client crate, then has to claim the halves with a fallible `split()`. This proposes making `connect()` resolve to a `Connection` too, before 0.7.0 ships.

## Current state (main, `df93bff`)

- `on_accept(&self, conn: Connection)`. The event loop builds the `Connection` with `Connection::for_accept` and sets the read claim itself, because `spawn_accept_task` runs outside a task poll where `split()` could reach the driver.
- `ConnectFuture::Output = io::Result<ConnCtx>`, for `connect`, `connect_with_timeout`, `connect_unix`, `connect_tls` and `connect_tls_with_timeout`, both the free functions and the `ConnCtx` methods.
- The client crates take the token and claim inside construction, so construction is fallible:
  - `ringline_redis::Client::{new, builder(..).build()}`
  - `ringline_memcache::Client::{new, builder(..).build(), builder(..).build_binary()}`
  - `ringline_ping::Client::{new, builder(..).build()}`
  - `ringline_http::H2Conn::from_conn` (and the private `H1Conn::new`)

  All of these call `conn.split()?` and return `Result`, with `EBUSY` if a half is already out or `EPIPE` if the handle is stale.

`docs/connection-handle-ownership-design.md` describes `ConnCtx` as a copyable name (identity, lifecycle, and minting the halves) and `Connection` as the claimed halves. Its original sketch for step 4 had outbound connections take their read half with `take_recv()` as a separate change. Nothing in the doc argues that connect should keep returning the name.

## Why change it

- **The claim can fail at construction time for reasons the caller did not cause.** A downstream load generator had to add a setup-failure path to each of its five connection tasks: close the connection, undo the connection-count metrics, count a failed connect, sleep and reconnect. That path exists only because `build()` can fail after a connect succeeded.

## The bug

`Ring::submit_shutdown` builds `Shutdown::new(Fixed(conn_index), SHUT_WR)` — the socket
is named as the **registered-file slot**, not as an fd. Nothing pinned that slot for the
operation's lifetime:

- a `Shutdown` is not a queued send, so `try_finalize_close`'s drained check

- its completion was discarded outright — `OpTag::Shutdown => {}`;

could be submitted and complete first, the next accept could register the slot, and the
kernel could then execute the FIN **against that new connection** — a live peer, cleanly
half-closed, whose next send fails `EPIPE`.

## Summary
- `drive_park_drains` runs once per event-loop iteration. Its early return tested `park_drain.is_empty()`, but `park_drain` is `vec![None; max_connections]`, so every tick scanned all slots. At the default 16,000 that was 37% of a client worker's cycles at 64 connections / 100K req/s (measurements in #514).
- The drive now visits `park_drain_pending`, a list of the connection indices with a drain outstanding, instead of scanning `park_drain`. Every write to `park_drain` goes through `Driver::set_park_drain`, which pushes the index on a `None → Some` transition and never adds a duplicate. Clears leave the index for the next drive to drop. The per-connection handling in the loop body is unchanged.
- This is the same shape as `pending_send_retries` and the other retry lists: per-slot state for lookup by index, plus a list of the slots with work. `park_carry` and `adopt_pending` stay HashMaps because they are only looked up by key and never visited per tick.
- The first commit used a count of live drains. That made the idle case free but still scanned up to the last live slot while any park was draining; the second commit replaces it with the list.
- Not in a release: introduced in #483, and `release/0.6.x` has no `drive_park_drains`.

`maybe_park_one` has the same kind of guard (`park_offered.is_empty()` on a dense `Vec<bool>`). It is left alone here: in pool mode it returns on `worker_loads` before any scan, so clients do not pay for it. In merged-accept mode it scans `park_offered` only when `choose_park_target` finds an imbalance.

issues.body:
Observed on `Test (mio, release)` for #499, whose diff touches only io_uring-gated code (`#[cfg(has_io_uring)] forward_held`, `backend/uring`). Rerunning the job on the same head went green.

```
test udp_gso_invalid_segment_size_returns_error ... FAILED
ringline/tests/udp.rs:2087: assertion `left == right` failed:
  follow-up send_to_gso must succeed after the invalid-arg errors
  left: 0
 right: 1
```

## Mechanism (from reading the code, not reproduced)

The race is in the test, not the runtime. The handler does:

```rust
if udp.send_to_gso(peer, &[0u8; 600], 200).is_ok() {
    ok_count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
}
```

The client thread receives the three 200-byte datagrams, then asserts `SANE_OK == 1`.

On mio, `send_to_gso` is three inline `send_to` calls, each a blocking `sendto` syscall (`runtime/io.rs`, the `#[cfg(not(has_io_uring))]` variants). All three datagrams are on loopback **before `send_to_gso` returns**, so before the `fetch_add`. The client can wake, drain them and read the counter in that window, and it sees 0.

io_uring doesn't hit this. The send is only pushed to the ring at the end of the loop iteration, after the handler has incremented.

## Suggested fix

Make the assertion wait for the increment rather than racing it: poll `SANE_OK` until it reaches 1, with a deadline (e.g. 2 s), before asserting. Alternatively, record success before the datagrams can be observed, though the counter's purpose is to confirm the send's return value, so polling is the more faithful fix.

Verify by mutation: sleep ~50 ms between `send_to_gso` and `fetch_add`. The current test should then fail reliably on mio, and the fixed one should pass.

Fixes #487.

## Root cause

ringline predicted whether a `SendMsgZc` notification will follow from `result > 0`, and released the send-slab entry at once on an error or zero result. The kernel's signal is `IORING_CQE_F_MORE` on the main CQE, and it sets that flag on those results too (`io_uring/net.c`):

- `io_sendmsg_zc` / `io_send_zc` end with `io_req_set_res(req, ret, IORING_CQE_F_MORE)` whatever `ret` is.
- `io_sendrecv_fail` sets `IORING_CQE_F_MORE` on a failed ZC request that allocated its notification (`REQ_F_NEED_CLEANUP`).

So a ZC send that completed with, say, `-ECONNRESET` still got a notification, after its entry had been released. If the next send reused the entry first, the late notification passed the `in_use` check and decremented the **new** send's count. In debug that's the `notification underflow` panic in #487. In release it's a wrapped count, or the new send's entry released while the kernel may still hold its pages.

## Fix

Count a pending notification **exactly when the main CQE carries `IORING_CQE_F_MORE`**, at all four sites:

- the main path;
- the stale-identity path;
- the chain path, whose `-ECANCELED` and error arms released the entry unconditionally;
- the shutdown drain in `driver.rs`.

The partial-send resubmission still keys on `result > 0`, since only bytes actually sent advance the iovecs.

   - `a_late_notification_never_reaches_a_reused_entry` panicked with **`notification underflow for slab entry 0`**, the #487 panic;

2. **`fix(uring)` commit:**
   - `stale_zc_cqe_for_reused_index_resource_only` and `zc_sequence_no_slab_leak` injected a successful main CQE without `F_MORE`, which no kernel produces, and now set it;
   - the ZC property test gains an `ErrorThenNotif`

Fixes #460.

## The bug

`tcp_nodelay(true)` was applied inside the acceptor thread's accept loop. `AcceptMode::Merged` has no acceptor thread — each worker arms its own multishot accept on an `SO_REUSEPORT` socket — so the option was silently dropped for every merged-mode connection.

Plaintext echo barely notices. TLS does: a handshake is several short round trips, so Nagle holds each small record waiting for an ACK that the peer's 40 ms delayed-ACK timer is holding back. Merged mode measured **29x slower than the pool with its workers idle**.

## The fix

One `apply_accepted_sockopts(fd, nodelay, timestamps)` in `acceptor.rs`, called from both accept paths, so the two cannot drift apart again. The acceptor keeps its `AF_UNIX` guard by passing `tcp_nodelay && !is_unix`; a merged listener is never a Unix socket, because `SO_REUSEPORT` does not apply to one.

The second commit closes the other gap the same audit found: `AcceptMulti` passed no `accept_flags`, where the pool path uses `accept4(SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC)`. See that commit message for why the CLOEXEC window is real but narrow, and why `SOCK_NONBLOCK` is parity rather than a known bug.
